docs.title: CVE-2026-110264 — GitLab: Unauthenticated RCE via Integer Overflow in Regex Compilation
docs.text: Field Value Severity Critical — CVSS 10.0 (v3.1) Product GitLab CE/EE — the DevOps platform (self-managed instances) Type Integer overflow (CWE-190) in regular-expression compilation leading to remote code execution Vector Unauthenticated remote attacker submits a specially crafted regular expression → integer overflow while GitLab compiles it → memory corruption → arbitrary code execution on the GitLab server

docs.title: Root cause
docs.text:
GitLab compiles user-influenced regular expressions server-side (search, filtering, integrations). The compiler computed a buffer size from attacker-controlled repeat counts using fixed-width integer arithmetic. A crafted pattern made that multiplication wrap around to a tiny value, so the allocator handed back a buffer far smaller than the compiled output — and the compiler then wrote past the end of it:

# Simplified vulnerable pattern
def compile_pattern(repeat_count, unit_size):
    buf_len = (repeat_count * unit_size) % 2**32  # BUG: wraps on overflow
    buf = allocate(buf_len)                        # far too small
    write_compiled_bytecode(buf, repeat_count * unit_size)  # heap overflow

# Simplified fixed pattern
def compile_pattern_fixed(repeat_count, unit_size):
    buf_len = checked_multiply(repeat_count, unit_size)  # errors on overflow
    buf = allocate(buf_len)
    write_compiled_bytecode(buf, buf_len)

No login, no interaction, network-reachable: the classic recipe for a 10.0.

docs.title: Proof of concept (conceptual)
docs.text:
1. Attacker crafts a regular expression whose repetition counts overflow a 32-bit size calculation.
  2. The pattern reaches GitLab's server-side regex compiler (e.g. via search/filter input).
  3. The overflowed length allocates an undersized heap buffer.
  4. Compiled bytecode is written past the buffer — corrupting heap metadata.
  5. Carefully shaped overflow turns the corruption into arbitrary code execution as the GitLab user.

The accompanying poc.py demonstrates the pattern safely: wrapping vs. checked integer arithmetic for a buffer-size computation. Offline, no server, no exploit.

docs.title: Mitigation
docs.text:
• Upgrade immediately: 18.11.13 / 19.0.10 / 19.1.9 / 19.2.9 / 19.3.6 / 19.4.3 / 19.5.1. There is no workaround — patching is the fix.
  • Assume exposure: any internet-facing instance was remotely exploitable without credentials; hunt for unexpected processes, new SSH keys, and runner registrations.
  • Rotate secrets stored in or reachable from the GitLab server (tokens, CI variables, deploy keys).
  • Restrict network access to the instance until patched (VPN / allow-list).

docs.title: CVE-2026-110353 — HAProxy: CPU Exhaustion via Truncated HTTP/2 PING Frame
docs.text: Field Value Severity High — CVSS 7.5 (v3.1) Product HAProxy 3.2 before 3.4.6 — the high-performance load balancer Type Unchecked return value (CWE-252) — truncated HTTP/2 PING frame never consumed, tasklet spins forever Vector Unauthenticated remote attacker sends a truncated HTTP/2 PING frame → h2c_handle_ping skips the short-read check → frame can never be processed nor consumed → H2 multiplexer tasklet re-woken endlessly → worker thread pinned at 100% CPU until http-request timeout; many connections sustain the exhaustion

docs.title: Affected versions
docs.text: HAProxy 3.2 before 3.4.6. Fixed in 3.4.6.

docs.title: Root cause
docs.text:
h2c_handle_ping in src/mux_h2.c never checked for a short read — unlike every other H2 frame handler. A truncated PING frame can therefore neither be processed nor consumed: its data stays pending, and the H2 multiplexer tasklet is woken again and again by that same pending data, making no progress:

# Simplified vulnerable pattern
def handle_ping(frame):
    process(frame)          # BUG: no length check; stub never consumed
    # tasklet re-woken by pending bytes -> infinite retry at 100% CPU

# Simplified fixed pattern
def handle_ping_fixed(frame):
    if len(frame) < PING_LEN:
        drop_connection()   # no progress possible -> bail out
        return
    process(frame)
Any retry loop over untrusted input needs a progress guarantee.

docs.title: Proof of concept (conceptual)
docs.text:
1. Attacker opens a connection to HAProxy and sends a truncated HTTP/2 PING frame.
  2. The handler cannot parse the stub and never consumes its bytes.
  3. The multiplexer tasklet is re-woken by the pending data in an endless loop.
  4. The worker thread spins at 100% CPU until the http-request timeout; opening many such connections sustains high CPU across workers.

The accompanying poc.py demonstrates the pattern safely: parsers must bail out when no progress is possible: the demo contrasts the spinning handler with one that validates length and drops the connection. Offline, no server, no exploit.

docs.title: Mitigation
docs.text:
• Upgrade now: HAProxy 3.4.6.
  • Enforce connection and rate limits at the edge.
  • Alert on sustained worker-thread CPU — it is the signature of this class.

docs.title: CVE-2026-110354 — HAProxy: Persistent CPU Exhaustion via HTTP/1.1 Chunked Parsing
docs.text: Field Value Severity High — CVSS 7.5 (v3.1) Product HAProxy 3 before 3.4.6 Type Loop with unreachable exit condition (CWE-835) — HTTP/1.1 chunked parser re-processes the same bytes without progress Vector Unauthenticated remote attacker sends a crafted HTTP/1.1 chunked request → H1 multiplexer drains the request but the parser re-processes the same bytes endlessly → worker thread stuck at 100% CPU even after timeouts expire and the client disconnects → repeated requests consume all workers until restart

docs.title: Affected versions
docs.text: HAProxy 3 before 3.4.6. Fixed in 3.4.6.

docs.title: Root cause
docs.text:
The HTTP/1.1 multiplexer drained the request before closing the stream, but the chunked-transfer parser repeatedly re-processed the same bytes without making progress — a loop whose exit condition could never be reached. The thread stayed at 100% CPU after timeouts expired and even after the client disconnected:

# Simplified vulnerable pattern
def parse_chunked(buf):
    while not done(buf):
        parse(buf)          # BUG: same bytes, no progress, no exit

# Simplified fixed pattern
def parse_chunked_fixed(buf):
    while not done(buf):
        consumed = parse(buf)
        if consumed == 0:
            abort_stream()  # no progress -> stop, don't spin
            return
Only a process restart recovered the workers.

docs.title: Proof of concept (conceptual)
docs.text:
1. Attacker sends a crafted HTTP/1.1 chunked request.
  2. The parser re-processes the same bytes without advancing.
  3. The worker thread pins at 100% CPU — surviving timeouts and client disconnect.
  4. Repeated requests consume every worker; the process must be restarted.

The accompanying poc.py demonstrates the pattern safely: every parse loop needs a progress check: the demo contrasts the stuck parser with one that aborts on zero progress. Offline, no server, no exploit.

docs.title: Mitigation
docs.text:
• Upgrade now: HAProxy 3.4.6.
  • Cap request sizes and timeouts aggressively at the edge.
  • Keep a tested restart playbook — this bug class needs one.

docs.title: CVE-2026-110372 — OttoKit: Forged Header Bypasses Connection Authentication
docs.text: Field Value Severity Critical — CVSS 9.8 Product OttoKit (formerly SureTriggers) WordPress automation plugin, 100k+ sites Type Missing Authorization (CWE-862) Vector Unauthenticated, network → administrator account creation

docs.title: Affected versions
docs.text: OttoKit through 1.1.40. Fixed in versions past 1.1.40.

docs.title: Root cause
docs.text:
The create_wp_connection endpoint identifies its caller by the request's User-Agent header — a value anyone can forge — and then skips the capability check that should gate privileged actions. The application-password verification misfires on top, so empty or invalid credentials still open the door. Identity by claim, not proof.

// Simplified vulnerable pattern
if ($_SERVER['HTTP_USER_AGENT'] === 'OttoKit') {
    create_wp_connection($details);  // trusted by header alone
}
// fixed: verify a signed credential AND current_user_can('manage_options')

docs.title: Proof of concept (conceptual)
docs.text:
The attack chain is:

  1. The attacker sends a crafted REST request to the plugin's connection endpoint — no login, no password — with the User-Agent set to OttoKit and forged connection details.
  2. The plugin accepts the header as identity and mishandles the application-password verification.
  3. The attacker receives an authenticated session and creates a new administrator account (or takes over an existing one).

The accompanying poc.py demonstrates the pattern safely: a mock connection endpoint whose vulnerable variant trusts the header, versus the fixed variant that requires a signed token plus a capability check. Fully offline, synthetic data — no exploit, no network calls.

From there it is the standard playbook: backdoored plugins, stolen customer data, defaced pages, ransomware-style lockouts.

docs.title: Mitigation
docs.text:
• Update OttoKit past 1.1.40 immediately.
  • Audit your users for accounts you did not create — especially new administrators.
  • Check for recently installed or modified plugins; scan for backdoors.
  • Force password resets and rotate API keys.

docs.title: CVE-2026-110373 — Login with Phone Number: Privilege Escalation After Verification
docs.text: Field Value Severity High — CVSS 8.1 Product Login with Phone Number WordPress auth plugin Type Incorrect Privilege Assignment (CWE-266) Vector Unauthenticated (self-registration), network → administrator

docs.title: Affected versions
docs.text: Login with Phone Number through 1.8.77. Fixed in versions past 1.8.77.

docs.title: Root cause
docs.text:
During the phone-number login flow the plugin assigns capabilities or roles without properly checking what the account should hold. Verifying a phone number proves who owns the number — it says nothing about what the account may do. The plugin conflated the two: successful verification flowed straight into privileged assignment with no allow-list and no capability check.

// Simplified vulnerable pattern
if (verify_phone($number)) {            // proves number ownership only
    $account->set_role('administrator'); // ...yet grants privileges anyway
}
// fixed: assign the role from an allow-list, defaulting to the
// account's existing role — never from the login flow itself

docs.title: Proof of concept (conceptual)
docs.text:
The attack chain is:

  1. The attacker registers with any phone number they control — a prepaid SIM is enough.
  2. They complete the legitimate verification step; the code arrives, the check passes.
  3. The flawed assignment logic promotes the session beyond what it should hold — up to administrator.

The accompanying poc.py demonstrates the pattern safely: a mock phone login whose vulnerable variant takes the role from the flow, versus the fixed variant that keeps the account's pre-existing role. Fully offline, synthetic data — no exploit, no network calls.

An attacker with nothing but a prepaid number walks into wp-admin — and from there it is new admin users, malicious plugins, and stolen data, all through the front door built for convenience.

docs.title: Mitigation
docs.text:
• Update Login with Phone Number past 1.8.77 immediately.
  • Audit recent registrations for accounts with unexpected roles; demote or remove them.
  • Force password resets for affected accounts.
  • Keep authentication (who are you) and authorization (what may you do) as separate, explicit steps.

docs.title: CVE-2026-110382 — Simply Schedule Appointments: Stored XSS in Booking Notes
docs.text: Field Value Severity High — CVSS 7.1 Product Simply Schedule Appointments WordPress booking plugin Type Improper Neutralization of Input During Web Page Generation ('Cross-site Scripting') (CWE-79), stored variant Vector Unauthenticated booking → script executes in the admin's browser

docs.title: Affected versions
docs.text: Simply Schedule Appointments through 1.6.12.35. Fixed in versions past 1.6.12.35.

docs.title: Root cause
docs.text:
Appointment input is saved without proper sanitization and rendered without escaping in the admin area. Unlike reflected XSS, this one waits: the payload is stored cleanly, then executed later in the most privileged context on the site — the wp-admin dashboard.

// Simplified vulnerable pattern
save_booking(['notes' => $_POST['notes']]);  // stored raw
echo $booking['notes'];                      // rendered raw in wp-admin
// fixed: sanitize on save, escape with esc_html() on output

docs.title: Proof of concept (conceptual)
docs.text:
The attack chain is:

  1. The attacker books a normal-looking appointment with a script hidden in the notes field. Nothing looks wrong at booking time.
  2. Days later, the site owner opens the bookings list in wp-admin.
  3. The script runs in the owner's browser, with the owner's admin session — and creates a new administrator account for the attacker.

The accompanying poc.py demonstrates the pattern safely: a mock booking store plus admin renderer, vulnerable (raw save, raw render) versus fixed (sanitized save, escaped render). Fully offline, synthetic data — no exploit, no network calls.

The attacker's script executes with full administrator privileges: new accounts, backdoor plugins, data exfiltration — all while the owner thinks they are just checking tomorrow's schedule.

docs.title: Mitigation
docs.text:
• Update Simply Schedule Appointments past 1.6.12.35 immediately.
  • Purge suspicious bookings — especially ones with markup in notes.
  • Check for unknown administrator accounts and remove them.
  • Treat every input field as hostile: sanitize on input, escape on output, always.

docs.title: CVE-2026-110383 — E-Signature for Fluent Forms: IDOR Exposes Signed Documents
docs.text: Field Value Severity High — CVSS 7.5 Product Electronic Signature add-on for Fluent Forms (WordPress) Type Authorization Bypass Through User-Controlled Key (CWE-639) Vector Unauthenticated/low-privilege, network → read any signed document

docs.title: Affected versions
docs.text: Electronic Signature add-on for Fluent Forms through 2.0.5. Fixed in versions past 2.0.5.

docs.title: Root cause
docs.text:
The plugin fetches a signed document using an ID taken straight from the request, without checking that the requester owns it or may see it. Knowing a document's ID is treated as permission to read it — and sequential, predictable IDs make enumeration trivial.

// Simplified vulnerable pattern
$doc = get_document($_GET['doc_id']);  // no ownership check
serve($doc);
// fixed:
if ($doc->owner_id !== current_user_id()) { deny(); }

docs.title: Proof of concept (conceptual)
docs.text:
The attack chain is:

  1. The attacker signs one document legitimately and notes its ID.
  2. They simply increment the number — doc 1024, 1025, 1026 — requesting each in turn. No hacking tools, just a browser and patience.
  3. The plugin serves every document back: contracts, personal data, handwritten signatures.

The accompanying poc.py demonstrates the pattern safely: a mock document store whose vulnerable serve function honors any ID, versus the fixed one that enforces ownership. Fully offline, synthetic data — no exploit, no network calls.

Every signed document on the site becomes readable and downloadable by anyone who can count — a privacy breach and, depending on the data, a regulatory incident.

docs.title: Mitigation
docs.text:
• Update the Electronic Signature add-on past 2.0.5 immediately.
  • Check access logs for sequential doc_id enumeration patterns.
  • Notify affected clients if documents were exposed.
  • Enforce ownership checks on every object fetched by a request-supplied ID; prefer unguessable identifiers.

docs.title: CVE-2026-110653 — LatePoint OTP Race Condition → Authentication Bypass
docs.text: Field Detail Severity Critical 9.1 (CVSS 3.1) Product LatePoint (WordPress appointment booking plugin), ≤ 5.7.4 Type Authentication bypass via race condition / TOCTOU (CWE-287) Attack vector Network · unauthenticated request_otp / verifyOTP endpoints

docs.title: Affected versions
docs.text: All versions up to and including 5.7.4.

docs.title: Root cause
docs.text: verifyOTP increments the OTP attempt counter with a non-atomic read-modify-write: the counter is read into memory, incremented there, and written back with no SELECT ... FOR UPDATE row lock and no conditional UPDATE ... WHERE attempts < 10 guard. Concurrent requests therefore all read the same stale value, so the 10-attempt lockout never engages (time-of-check to time-of-use). The anti-CSRF nonce does not mitigate this because the unauthenticated request_otp endpoints issue nonces freely.

docs.title: Proof of concept
docs.text:
Conceptual attack chain (educational only): 1. The attacker knows the victim's email or phone number (often public for businesses that take bookings). 2. The attacker calls request_otp for the victim's account. 3. The attacker fires dozens of OTP guesses at verifyOTP concurrently. 4. Every concurrent request reads the same stale attempt count, so the lockout never trips. 5. One guess lands → authenticated session as the victim → victim's bookings readable.

The bundled poc.py simulates the vulnerable counter versus an atomic counter under concurrent threads. It touches no real system — pure local simulation.

docs.title: Mitigation
docs.text:
• Update LatePoint past 5.7.4 immediately.
  • Audit recent logins and sessions for unknown devices.
  • Enforce rate limits atomically: conditional updates (UPDATE ... WHERE attempts < N), row-level locks, and limits checked in the database rather than in application memory.

docs.title: CVE-2026-110720 — Consul-k8s: Cross-Namespace Authorization Bypass
docs.text: Field Value Severity Critical — CVSS 9.9 (v3.1) Product HashiCorp Consul-k8s — Kubernetes integration for Consul service mesh Type Incorrect authorization (CWE-863) — component ACL binding rules Vector An attacker with Kubernetes permissions in another namespace creates a ServiceAccount, takes its token, and authenticates as a Consul component. The binding rules do not consistently restrict authentication to ServiceAccounts in the namespace hosting the Consul deployment, so the foreign identity receives the component's elevated Consul privileges.

docs.title: Affected versions
docs.text: Consul-k8s 0.42.0 through 2.0.4 with automated system ACL management enabled. Fixed in 2.1.0 and 1.8.18.

docs.title: Root cause
docs.text: When system ACL management is enabled, consul-k8s sets up Kubernetes authentication and binding rules so its components can obtain Consul tokens. Those rules are supposed to link each component's Kubernetes ServiceAccount to its corresponding Consul role, confined to the namespace where Consul runs. The affected rules did not consistently enforce that namespace restriction, so an identity from another namespace could authenticate as a component and inherit its privileges. Authorization that checks identity but not origin is only half a check.

docs.title: Proof of concept (conceptual)
docs.text:
1. Attacker has permission to create a ServiceAccount and obtain its token in some other namespace.
  2. Attacker presents that token to the Consul API.
  3. The binding rule matches the identity to a Consul component role without checking the namespace.
  4. The attacker receives the component's elevated privileges.

The accompanying poc.py demonstrates the pattern safely: a binding matcher that ignores namespace (vulnerable) versus one that requires the ServiceAccount to live in the Consul namespace (fixed). Offline, no cluster, no exploit.

docs.title: Mitigation
docs.text:
• Upgrade now: consul-k8s 2.1.0 or 1.8.18.
  • Audit ACL binding rules for cross-namespace grants you did not approve.
  • Restrict network access to the Consul API to trusted workloads only.
  • Rotate tokens that may have been issued through a foreign namespace.

docs.title: Jackson Protobuf Map Keys: An 8-Byte Message Crashes the JVM (DoS)
docs.text:
Educational material only. Do not use against systems you do not own or have explicit permission to test.

Field Value CVE CVE-2026-110747 Severity High — CVSS 7.5 Product com.fasterxml.jackson.dataformat:jackson-dataformat-protobuf (2.x) and tools.jackson.dataformat:jackson-dataformat-protobuf (3.x) Type Integer Overflow to Uncontrolled Resource Allocation (CWE-190, CWE-770, CWE-789) Vector An unauthenticated attacker who can submit protobuf data for parsing sends an 8-byte message containing a map entry whose string-key length is declared as Integer.MAX_VALUE. The map-key reader adds position plus length in 32-bit signed arithmetic, the sum overflows negative, the check passes with no key data present, and the text buffer expands toward the declared length, throwing OutOfMemoryError.

docs.title: Affected versions
docs.text: 2.x releases 2.21.6–2.21.7 and 2.22.0–2.22.3 (2.18–2.20 lines do not contain the map-key path) and 3.x releases with map support including 3.2.0–3.2.3. The 3.x branches fixed the map-key site in branch HEAD; the corresponding 2.x branches were still unguarded as of 2026-10-06, including branches targeting 2.21.8 and 2.22.4 — verify your build carries the guard.

docs.title: Root cause
docs.text:
This is the same integer-overflow pattern as CVE-2026-104016, missed at one call site: the map string-key reader. The remediation for CVE-2026-104016/104017 corrected this site on the 3.x branches only, leaving the 2.x branches exposed. As with the string-field path, StreamReadConstraints do not prevent the failure, and with exit-on-out-of-memory configured the JVM terminates.

# Simplified vulnerable pattern (map-key reader)
def read_string_key(ptr, length, end):
    if int32(ptr + length) <= end:  # BUG: wraps negative near MAX_INT
        return finish_text(length)  # huge allocation, no key data present

# Simplified fixed pattern
def read_string_key_fixed(ptr, length, end):
    if length < 0 or length > (end - ptr):
        raise ValueError("key length overflows input")
    return finish_text(length)

docs.title: Proof of concept
docs.text:
Educational, conceptual demo only — it models the vulnerable pattern with synthetic, offline objects. It is not a working exploit and cannot be aimed at real systems.

  1. Attacker sends 8 bytes: a map entry whose key length is declared 0x7FFFFFFF, with no key data at all.
  2. The map-key reader adds position plus length, the sum overflows negative, and the check passes.
  3. The parser expands its text buffer toward the declared length.
  4. The JVM throws OutOfMemoryError; with exit-on-error configured the process terminates.

The demo in poc.py contrasts the vulnerable pattern against the fixed pattern, using only synthetic values and no network access.

docs.title: Mitigation
docs.text:
• Update now: jackson-dataformat-protobuf to a release where the map-key guard is present (verify on 2.x builds).
  • Guard every length path, including map keys — not just string fields.
  • Reject oversized declared lengths before any buffer expansion.
  • Do not rely on StreamReadConstraints or heap size alone on this path.

docs.title: Jackson-databind: A Hidden Class Inside a Type Name Runs Any Gadget (RCE)
docs.text:
Educational material only. Do not use against systems you do not own or have explicit permission to test.

Field Value CVE CVE-2026-110879 Severity Critical — CVSS 9.8 Product com.fasterxml.jackson.core:jackson-databind (2.x) and tools.jackson.core:jackson-databind (3.x) Type Improper Control of Generation of Code / Deserialization of Untrusted Data (CWE-502, CWE-470) Vector An unauthenticated attacker who controls polymorphic JSON in a network-facing deployment names a generic wrapper around a gadget class. Jackson validates the outer class but not the classes inside its generic arguments, so the gadget is instantiated even though the same class would be rejected as a direct type ID. With Spring on the classpath, map-key discovery passes attacker-controlled JSON to a one-string constructor that loads attacker XML and starts a process.

docs.title: Affected versions
docs.text: jackson-databind from 2.10.0 (2.x) and from 3.0.0 (3.x). Fixed in 2.18.12, 2.21.8, 2.22.4, 3.1.8 and 3.2.4. Note: the earlier fix releases for CVE-2026-54512 (2.18.8, 2.21.4, 3.1.4) do NOT fix this bypass.

docs.title: Root cause
docs.text:
Polymorphic type validation is supposed to judge every class named in a type ID. The generic-argument path only judged the outer class: arguments were validated against the outer base type instead of their declared generic binding, and array element types were skipped once the base type was approved. Approving an outer type could also swap in a permissive validator, removing the restriction on embedded arguments entirely.

# Simplified vulnerable pattern
def resolve_type_id(type_id, base):
    if validator.allows(type_id.outer, base):  # only the wrapper is checked
        return build(type_id)                 # hidden arguments never judged

# Simplified fixed pattern
def resolve_type_id_fixed(type_id, base):
    for cls in type_id.all_classes():          # outer, arguments, array elements
        if not validator.allows(cls, base):
            raise ValueError("type not allowed")
    return build(type_id)
The fix validates every class named in a type ID with the configured validator, as if it were a direct type ID.

docs.title: Proof of concept
docs.text:
Educational, conceptual demo only — it models the vulnerable pattern with synthetic, offline objects. It is not a working exploit and cannot be aimed at real systems.

  1. Attacker sends JSON with a type ID naming a generic wrapper around a gadget class, where a plain map was declared.
  2. Jackson approves the harmless-looking outer type and builds the wrapper.
  3. Map-key discovery passes the attacker-controlled JSON property name to the gadget class one-string constructor.
  4. With Spring present and attacker-controlled XML loadable, the constructor loads the XML and starts a process under the application account.

The demo in poc.py contrasts the vulnerable pattern against the fixed pattern, using only synthetic values and no network access.

docs.title: Mitigation
docs.text:
• Update now: jackson-databind to 2.18.12, 2.21.8, 2.22.4, 3.1.8 or 3.2.4.
  • Disable class-name polymorphism for untrusted data if you cannot update yet.
  • Use narrow subtype rules instead of broad allowlists.
  • Remove gadget-bearing dependencies you do not need from the classpath.
  • Never let attackers write serialized cache or session values your app later deserializes.

docs.title: CVE-2026-110886 — Conversational Forms for ChatBot: PHP Object Injection
docs.text: Field Value Severity Critical — CVSS 9.8 Product Conversational Forms for ChatBot WordPress plugin Type Deserialization of Untrusted Data (CWE-502) Vector Unauthenticated, network → remote code execution via gadget chain

docs.title: Affected versions
docs.text: Conversational Forms for ChatBot through 1.5.1. Fixed in versions past 1.5.1.

docs.title: Root cause
docs.text:
The plugin takes attacker-controlled input and passes it straight to PHP's unserialize(), which rebuilds live objects — and runs their magic methods — from raw bytes off the network. unserialize() does not just parse data: it instantiates classes and runs their constructors, destructors, and __wakeup hooks. Without a signature or integrity check on the input, the attacker chooses which objects come alive.

// Simplified vulnerable pattern
$data = unserialize($_POST['chat_state']);  // attacker-controlled bytes
// fixed: $data = json_decode($_POST['chat_state'], true);
//        plus HMAC verification of the payload

docs.title: Proof of concept (conceptual)
docs.text:
The attack chain is:

  1. The attacker crafts a serialized payload chaining gadget classes already present in WordPress — a POP chain — and submits it as chat state.
  2. The plugin unserializes it; the chain fires: file writes, database writes.
  3. With the right gadgets, the chain reaches arbitrary PHP execution on the server.

The accompanying poc.py demonstrates the pattern safely: a mock chat state handler whose vulnerable variant instantiates attacker-named classes, versus the fixed variant that only accepts JSON-decoded plain data with a verified signature. Fully offline, synthetic data — no exploit, no network calls.

Object injection on a server that unserializes blind is as bad as remote code execution.

docs.title: Mitigation
docs.text:
• Update Conversational Forms past 1.5.1 immediately.
  • Scan uploads and plugin folders for unexpected files.
  • Review recent admin activity for actions you did not take.
  • Never unserialize data you did not sign yourself — use JSON plus an HMAC for round-tripped state.

docs.title: CVE-2026-110887 — HivePress: Unauthenticated Remote Code Inclusion
docs.text: Field Value Severity Critical — CVSS 9.9 Product hivepress WordPress plugin (directory / listings) Type Code Injection / Remote Code Inclusion (CWE-94) Vector Unauthenticated remote attacker makes the plugin include and execute arbitrary PHP

docs.title: Affected versions
docs.text: HivePress through 1.7.32. Fixed in past 1.7.32.

docs.title: Root cause
docs.text: A file/template name taken from the incoming request is passed to PHP's include without any validation. In PHP, including a file is executing it — so a request-controlled path becomes remote code execution. Reported by Patchstack; unauthenticated, network-reachable, low complexity — hence the 9.9 score.

docs.title: Proof of concept (conceptual)
docs.text:
The attack chain is:

  1. Attacker sends one crafted request carrying a file/template parameter.
  2. The plugin feeds that value straight into include.
  3. PHP loads and executes the attacker's payload with web-server privileges.
  4. Attacker drops a web shell, steals wp-config.php credentials, pivots.

The accompanying poc.py demonstrates the pattern safely: a vulnerable mock versus the fixed pattern. Fully offline, synthetic data — no exploit, no network calls.

docs.title: Mitigation
docs.text: Update HivePress past 1.7.32 immediately. Scan wp-content/uploads and plugin dirs for PHP files you did not put there. Assume breach: review access logs and admin users for the exposure window. Put a WAF rule in front of the template/file parameters as a stopgap.

docs.title: CVE-2026-110895 — Support Genix: SQL Injection in Ticket Filters
docs.text: Field Value Severity High — CVSS 8.5 Product Support Genix WordPress support ticket plugin Type Improper Neutralization of Special Elements used in an SQL Command (CWE-89) Vector Unauthenticated, network → full users table dump

docs.title: Affected versions
docs.text: Support Genix through 1.4.54. Fixed in versions past 1.4.54.

docs.title: Root cause
docs.text:
A ticket filter parameter flows into a database query without escaping or prepared statements. The query is built by concatenating user input into SQL text, so the database treats attacker input as instructions. Prepared statements with bound parameters keep data as data — the one fix that kills the entire class.

# Simplified vulnerable pattern
query = "SELECT * FROM tickets WHERE status = '" + ticket_filter + "'"
db.execute(query)
# fixed: db.execute("SELECT * FROM tickets WHERE status = %s",
#                   (ticket_filter,))

docs.title: Proof of concept (conceptual)
docs.text:
The attack chain is:

  1. The attacker submits a filter like ' UNION SELECT user_login, user_pass FROM wp_users -- through the ticket form. No support contract needed — just the ability to ask the plugin a question.
  2. The database obeys, and the plugin returns the rows as if they were tickets: logins, emails, password hashes, all of it.
  3. Cracked offline, those hashes become working logins, and working logins become admin sessions.

The accompanying poc.py demonstrates the pattern safely: a mock ticket database whose vulnerable filter concatenates input (a UNION probe leaks the fake users table), versus the fixed filter that binds parameters. Fully offline, synthetic data — no exploit, no network calls.

docs.title: Mitigation
docs.text:
• Update Support Genix past 1.4.54 immediately.
  • Grep slow-query and access logs for UNION and quote probes.
  • Force password resets for every user and rotate secrets.
  • Audit any data the plugin exposes through filterable listings.

docs.title: CVE-2026-110897 — PowerPack Lite for Beaver Builder: Stored XSS in Widget Settings
docs.text: Field Value Severity High — CVSS 7.1 Product PowerPack Lite add-on for Beaver Builder (WordPress) Type Improper Neutralization of Input During Web Page Generation ('Cross-site Scripting') (CWE-79), stored variant Vector Low-privilege (contributor), network → script served to every visitor

docs.title: Affected versions
docs.text: PowerPack Lite for Beaver Builder through 1.3.1. Fixed in versions past 1.3.1.

docs.title: Root cause
docs.text:
A widget field — editable by a low-privilege contributor — is saved without sanitization and printed into the page without escaping. The widget trusts content from a low-privilege role and amplifies it to the entire audience with no output encoding.

// Simplified vulnerable pattern
update_widget(['heading' => $_POST['heading']]);  // saved raw
echo $widget['heading'];                          // printed raw to visitors
// fixed: sanitize on save, escape with esc_html() on output

docs.title: Proof of concept (conceptual)
docs.text:
The attack chain is:

  1. An attacker with a mere contributor account edits a PowerPack widget and hides a script in a text field.
  2. The page is published. Now every visitor runs the attacker's JavaScript — including admins previewing the page.
  3. Session cookies are harvested; an admin preview hands over the keys to the kingdom.

The accompanying poc.py demonstrates the pattern safely: a mock widget store whose vulnerable renderer prints settings raw, versus the fixed renderer that escapes them. Fully offline, synthetic data — no exploit, no network calls.

One unescaped field turns a contributor account into a broadcast attack: session hijacking at scale, defacement, skimmers, and redirects riding along on the site's most trusted pages.

docs.title: Mitigation
docs.text:
• Update PowerPack Lite past 1.3.1 immediately.
  • Review pages edited by low-privilege users and strip suspicious scripts from widget settings.
  • Limit who can publish — contributor content should be reviewed.
  • Escape all widget output, regardless of the role that entered it.

docs.text:
Educational only. This writeup explains the vulnerability pattern for defensive learning. Test only in controlled environments you own.

Field Value Severity CRITICAL 9.8 (CVSS 3.1) Product asVereinbase WordPress plugin Type Improper authentication (CWE-287) Vector Network: unauthenticated attacker Fixed in 1.1.8

docs.title: Affected versions
docs.text: asVereinbase before 1.1.8.

docs.title: Root cause
docs.text: The plugin does not require a valid password or a genuine second factor before authenticating a user: it treats an empty stored credential value as a match. An unauthenticated attacker can therefore log in as any user, including an administrator, simply by submitting a login with empty credentials.

docs.title: Proof of concept
docs.text: Conceptual illustration: poc.py models a login check that accepts an empty stored value as a match (vulnerable) versus one that rejects empty credentials and verifies both password and second factor (fixed). No real credentials or live site are involved.

docs.title: Mitigation
docs.text:
• Update asVereinbase to 1.1.8 or later.
  • Force a password reset for every account and review the administrator list for accounts you do not recognize.
  • Enable real two-factor checks and monitor login logs for anomalous admin sessions.

docs.title: CVE-2026-110975 — Kruize Autotune: Unauthenticated REST API Leaks Datasource Secrets in Cleartext
docs.text: Field Value Severity High — CVSS 7.4 (v3.1) Product Kruize Autotune (Kubernetes resource autotuning) — before the auth/serialization fix Type Plaintext storage / transmission of credentials (CWE-256); missing authentication (CWE-306) Vector Network-adjacent attacker calls GET /datasources or the datasource-metadata endpoint — no authentication required — and the service serializes datasource objects with a default Gson configuration (no field-exclusion strategy) → basic-auth passwords, bearer tokens, API keys and OAuth2 client secrets are returned in cleartext → harvested credentials reused against the backing monitoring stack

docs.title: Affected versions
docs.text: Kruize Autotune before the fix in pull request 2038 (adds an authentication layer to the REST API and a field-exclusion strategy so secret fields are never serialized). Upgrade to a release containing that fix.

docs.title: Root cause
docs.text: Two failures compounded. First, the REST API shipped with no authentication layer at all — anyone who could reach the service could call every endpoint. Second, the endpoints that describe configured datasources serialized the full datasource objects, including their credential fields, with a default serializer that excludes nothing. An API that answers unauthenticated requests must never carry secrets in its responses; the serializer should have treated secret fields as non-serializable by default.

docs.title: Proof of concept
docs.text:
The vulnerable pattern, simplified (Python modeling of the serializer behavior):

# VULNERABLE - default serialization includes secret fields
def serialize_datasource(ds):
    return json.dumps(ds)  # ds contains password, token, api_key...

# FIXED - exclude secret fields by default
SECRET_FIELDS = {"password", "token", "api_key", "client_secret"}

def serialize_datasource(ds):
    return json.dumps({k: v for k, v in ds.items()
                       if k not in SECRET_FIELDS})

The demo poc.py models both behaviors with synthetic datasource objects — no network calls, no real credentials.

Educational material only. Do not use against systems you do not own or have explicit permission to test.

docs.title: Mitigation
docs.text: Upgrade to the Autotune release containing PR 2038. Additionally: rotate every credential stored in Autotune datasource configs (basic-auth passwords, bearer tokens, API keys, OAuth2 client secrets), restrict network access to the Autotune service to trusted administrators only, and audit monitoring-stack access logs for logins that used the exposed credentials.

docs.title: CVE-2026-111057 - Mercury: The Missing Comma That Broke the Blocklist
docs.text: Field Value Severity Critical - CVSS 10.0 Product Mercury 3.0.0-3.2.3 (Jupyter notebooks as web apps) Type Incorrect Regular Expression / Improper Access Control (CWE-185, CWE-284) Vector Remote attacker reaches blocked Jupyter endpoints because the path blocklist silently fused two rules into one

docs.title: Affected versions
docs.text: Mercury 3.0.0 through 3.2.3.

docs.title: Root cause
docs.text: The BLOCKED_PATTERNS list was missing a single comma between the /lab and /api/terminals entries. In Python, two adjacent string literals in a list concatenate - so instead of two regexes, Mercury compiled one fused pattern that matched neither real path. The blocklist that was supposed to keep strangers out of Jupyter's lab interface and terminal API quietly stopped blocking anything.

docs.title: Proof of concept (conceptual)
docs.text:
The attack chain is:

  1. Mercury deploys notebooks as public web apps with a path blocklist.
  2. A missing comma fuses two regex entries into one dead pattern.
  3. Attacker requests /lab or /api/terminals - nothing blocks them.
  4. Terminals and kernels become reachable: command execution follows.

The accompanying poc.py demonstrates the pattern safely: a vulnerable mock versus the fixed pattern. Fully offline, synthetic data - no exploit, no network calls.

docs.title: Mitigation
docs.text: Upgrade Mercury to 3.2.4 or later. Audit access logs for hits on /lab and /api/terminals from untrusted IPs. Enable linting that flags implicit string concatenation in security lists. Treat blocklist tests as security tests: assert each pattern matches its path.

docs.title: CVE-2026-111058 - Mercury: Tokenless Deployments Hand Out Anonymous Code Execution
docs.text: Field Value Severity Critical - CVSS 9.8 Product Mercury before 3.2.6 (Jupyter notebooks as web apps) Type Missing Authorization (CWE-862) Vector Unauthenticated remote attacker creates Jupyter kernels and sends execute requests

docs.title: Affected versions

docs.title: Root cause
docs.text: Mercury's default deployment ran without an auth token, and in that mode anonymous clients could hit the kernel API directly: create a Jupyter kernel, then send execute_request messages to it.   2. Anonymous attacker calls the kernel creation endpoint.
  3. Attacker sends an execute request carrying OS commands.

docs.title: CVE-2026-111066 - aiohttp: Unbounded File Descriptors Turn One Request Into a DoS
docs.text: Field Value Severity High - CVSS 8.2 Product aiohttp 2.0.0-3.14.4 (async Python web framework) Type Uncontrolled Resource Consumption (CWE-400, CWE-770) Vector Unauthenticated remote attacker sends multipart requests that pile up open file descriptors

docs.title: Affected versions
docs.text: aiohttp 2.0.0 through 3.14.4.

docs.title: Root cause
docs.text: Multipart request processing could retain an unbounded number of open file descriptors while parsing. A single unauthenticated client streaming a crafted multipart body made the server hold descriptor after descriptor until the process hit its limit - then it could not serve anyone. Cheap for the attacker, total outage for the service.

docs.title: Proof of concept (conceptual)
docs.text:
The attack chain is:

  1. Attacker opens a connection to an aiohttp server and streams multipart data.
  2. The parser retains file descriptors with no cap.
  3. The process exhausts its descriptor limit.
  4. Legitimate requests fail: full denial of service from one client.

The accompanying poc.py demonstrates the pattern safely: a vulnerable mock versus the fixed pattern. Fully offline, synthetic data - no exploit, no network calls.

docs.title: Mitigation
docs.text: Upgrade aiohttp past 3.14.4. Set conservative file-descriptor and connection limits on app servers. Rate-limit multipart endpoints and bound request body sizes. Monitor descriptor usage; alert on abnormal growth per connection.

docs.title: CVE-2026-111079 — Goose terminal history leaked to LLM providers
docs.text: Severity Product Type Vector HIGH 7.4 Goose (Block open-source AI agent) Sensitive information disclosure (CWE-497) Network

docs.title: Affected versions
docs.text: Goose with the terminal integration feature enabled. Any build shipping that integration is in scope.

docs.title: Root cause
docs.text: When terminal integration is on, Goose captures the user's shell command history and forwards it verbatim to the configured language-model provider endpoints during queries. There is no sanitization or redaction step: typed secrets (API tokens, passwords, environment variables) are treated as ordinary context and cross the trust boundary into external provider endpoints and request logs.

docs.title: Proof of concept (conceptual, educational only)
docs.text:
Educational purposes only. This demonstrates the idea of the leak — no real secrets, no real provider calls.

# redaction_demo.py — shows what Goose SHOULD do before sending context
import re

SECRET_HINTS = re.compile(
    r"(api[_-]?key|token|password|passwd|secret|aws_secret)", re.IGNORECASE
)

def redact(commands: list[str]) -> list[str]:
    """Replace likely-secret tokens before context leaves the machine."""
    safe = []
    for cmd in commands:
        if SECRET_HINTS.search(cmd):
            safe.append("[REDACTED — possible secret in shell history]")
        else:
            safe.append(cmd)
    return safe

history = [
    "git status",
    "export STRIPE_API_KEY=sk_live_xxx",  # placeholder, not a real key
    "ls -la",
]
print("Sent to provider:", redact(history))

docs.title: Mitigation
docs.text:
• Disable Goose's terminal integration unless you explicitly need it.
  • Rotate every credential that ever crossed a terminal Goose could observe (API keys, passwords, tokens, cloud keys).
  • Review your LLM provider's request logs for stored history payloads.
  • Keep secrets out of shells the agent can watch; prefer environment files outside the visible history.
  • Update Goose once the sanitization fix is released.

docs.title: CVE-2026-111090 — Stormshield Network Security: Logic Error Accepts Unsigned Update and License Files
docs.text: Field Value Severity High — CVSS 7.8 (AV:L/AC:L/PR:N/UI:R/S:U/C:H/I:H/A:H) Product Stormshield Network Security (SNS) firewalls — the appliance that filters all of your network traffic Type Improper Verification of Cryptographic Signature (CWE-347) Vector Local — a logic error in the signature verification routine accepts unauthenticated update and license files, which are then installed as if genuine; proof-of-concept code exists

docs.title: Affected versions
docs.text:
• SNS 5.1.0 to 5.1.3
  • SNS 5.0.0 to 5.0.9
  • SNS 4.8.0 to 4.8.19
  • SNS 4.3.0 to 4.3.44

Fixed in SNS 5.1.4 EA, SNS 5.0.10, and SNS 4.8.20 LTSB (Stormshield advisory STORM-2026-031, 2026-10-16).

docs.title: Root cause
docs.text:
Before installing a firmware update or license file, the appliance is supposed to verify the vendor's signature. A logic error in that verification routine means files that were never authenticated are accepted. The gate checks that a file exists and is shaped like an update, but the cryptographic proof-of-origin check does not actually reject forgeries — so trust is granted on presence alone.

# Simplified vulnerable pattern
def verify_vulnerable(file):
    if looks_like_update(file):   # logic error: never actually rejects
        return True               # unsigned file treated as authentic

# Simplified fixed pattern
def verify_fixed(file, vendor_key):
    if not signature_valid(file, vendor_key):
        return False              # origin must be proven, not assumed
    return True

docs.title: Proof of concept (conceptual)
docs.text:
1. The attacker builds a forged update or license file and gets it onto the appliance's update path.
  2. The appliance's signature routine accepts the unauthenticated file as genuine.
  3. An administrator (or automated process) applies the update normally.
  4. The forged file runs with full appliance privileges — confidentiality, integrity, and availability of the firewall are all impacted.

The accompanying poc.py demonstrates the pattern safely: a verification model that accepts files on presence alone versus one that rejects anything not signed by the vendor key. Purely synthetic, offline, no firmware, no exploit.

docs.title: Mitigation
docs.text:
• Upgrade now: SNS 5.1.4 EA, SNS 5.0.10, or SNS 4.8.20 LTSB, depending on your branch.
  • Verify hashes: check the SHA-256 hash of every update file against the reference hashes in the MyStormshield portal before installing.
  • Source discipline: retrieve updates only from MyStormshield servers, or use automatic verification via SNS.

docs.title: CVE-2026-111183 — GStreamer: Malformed Audio Packet Becomes Remote Code Execution
docs.text: Field Value Severity Critical — CVSS 9.8 (v3.0) Product GStreamer — the multimedia framework behind Linux desktops, browsers and video apps Type Heap-based buffer overflow (CWE-122) — the rtpL16depay element copies RTP payload data without validating the declared length (ZDI-26-775) Vector Remote attacker sends a crafted RTP audio packet with an oversized length field → the handler copies past the heap buffer → memory corruption → arbitrary code execution in the decoding process

docs.title: Affected versions
docs.text: GStreamer versions containing the vulnerable rtpL16depay element. Fixed upstream via commit 80c184b4c5ee8ba28b2540ba58f40b8d44b61622 — update through your distribution's security release.

docs.title: Root cause
docs.text: The depayloader trusted the length field carried inside the network packet and passed it straight to the memory copy as the number of bytes to copy. Because the declared length could exceed the destination heap buffer, a remote peer could write past the buffer and corrupt the heap — the classic precondition for code execution.

docs.title: Proof of concept
docs.text:
The demo contrasts copy_vulnerable() (declared length trusted) with copy_fixed() (length clamped to the real buffer size before copying).

The poc.py file next to this writeup demonstrates the vulnerable pattern versus the fixed pattern as a safe, offline logic demo — no network, no shell, no exploit.

docs.title: Mitigation
docs.text:
• Upgrade now: apply your distribution's GStreamer security update.
  • Rebuild or update every application bundling its own GStreamer copy.
  • Treat RTP/media streams from untrusted peers as hostile input.
  • Fuzz media parsers: they remain the highest-value attack surface in multimedia stacks.

docs.title: CVE-2026-111322 — Archon Unauthenticated Control API
docs.text: Field Detail Severity Critical 9.8 (CVSS 3.1) Product Archon agent harness, 0.2.13 – 0.11.1 Type Missing authentication (CWE-306) → unauthenticated remote control of the AI coding agent Attack vector Network · /api/* binds to 0.0.0.0:3090 with no login

docs.title: Affected versions
docs.text: Archon 0.2.13 through 0.11.1. No patch available as of 2026-10-17.

docs.title: Root cause
docs.text:
The agent control API (/api/*) requires no authentication — no token, no password — and the server binds to 0.0.0.0:3090 by default, i.e. every network interface. Anyone with network reach can send messages to the AI coding agent, which runs with bypassed permissions, and even "approve" actions the agent paused to ask the real user about. The agent cannot tell the attacker's approval from yours.

// simplified: the vulnerable defaults
app.listen(3090, '0.0.0.0');   // reachable from the whole network
POST /api/messages -> agent    // no auth check anywhere

docs.title: Proof of concept
docs.text:
poc.py is an educational illustration of the vulnerable defaults vs. the mitigated configuration. It audits the server settings locally — no network calls, no exploit code. For learning purposes only.

python3 poc.py

Conceptual attack chain:

  1. Attacker discovers the Archon API on the LAN (port 3090, no login).
  2. Attacker sends a message to the agent through /api/messages.
  3. The agent, running with bypassPermissions, treats it as a legit instruction — including approving steps it had paused for the real user.
  4. Commands execute on the host as the Archon user: files, code, shells.

docs.title: Mitigation
docs.text:
There is no patch yet. Mitigate now:

  • Set HOST=127.0.0.1 so the API binds to localhost only.
  • Or place an authenticated reverse proxy in front of the API.
  • Firewall port 3090 from the LAN; never expose it to the internet.

docs.title: CVE-2026-111382 — FreeRDP Client Heap Out-of-Bounds Write
docs.text: Field Detail Severity High 8.8 (CVSS 3.1) Product FreeRDP client, before 3.32.0 Type Heap out-of-bounds write (CWE-787) → memory corruption, possible RCE Attack vector Network · the server attacks the connecting client

docs.title: Affected versions
docs.text: FreeRDP before 3.32.0 (client side). Fixed in 3.32.0.

docs.title: Root cause
docs.text:
When decoding RDPGFX AVC444 / AVC444v2 video frames, general_LumaToYUV444 and general_ChromaV2ToYUV444 write past the U/V planes when a region rect has an odd height ending exactly at the surface height. The plane offset math is never bounds-checked:

// simplified: offset math without validation
write_plane(U, V, height);   // odd height -> writes past the plane end

A malicious (or man-in-the-middled) RDP server sends the crafted frame; the victim's client corrupts its own heap.

docs.title: Proof of concept
docs.text:
poc.py is an educational illustration of the unchecked offset math vs the fix. Pure arithmetic on a simulated buffer — no memory unsafety, no network. For learning purposes only.

python3 poc.py

Conceptual attack chain:

  1. Victim connects to a malicious RDP server (or session is intercepted).
  2. Server sends a crafted AVC444 frame: odd-height region at surface edge.
  3. Client writes past the U/V planes → heap corruption → potential code execution on the victim's machine, inside their network.

docs.title: Mitigation
docs.text:
• Update FreeRDP to 3.32.0+.
  • Only connect to fully trusted RDP servers; prefer VPN/gateway paths.
  • Treat unexplained RDP client crashes as potentially hostile.

docs.text: Field Value Severity High — CVSS 7.7 Product mapsvg-lite-interactive-vector-maps WordPress plugin (MapSVG) Type Path Traversal (CWE-22) Vector Remote attacker escapes the intended directory to read or delete server files

docs.title: CVE-2026-111406 — MapSVG: Unrestricted File Upload Plants Web Shells
docs.text: Field Value Severity Critical — CVSS 9.9 Product mapsvg-lite-interactive-vector-maps WordPress plugin (MapSVG) Type Unrestricted Upload of File with Dangerous Type (CWE-434) Vector Remote attacker uploads a PHP web shell through the plugin's upload handler

docs.title: CVE-2026-111408 — Quiz And Survey Master: Deserialization → PHP Object Injection
docs.text: Field Value Severity High — CVSS 8.8 Product quiz-master-next WordPress plugin (Quiz And Survey Master) Type Deserialization of Untrusted Data (CWE-502) Vector Remote attacker submits crafted serialized data that becomes live PHP objects

docs.title: Affected versions
docs.text: Quiz And Survey Master through 11.2.7. Fixed in past 11.2.7.

docs.title: Root cause
docs.text: Quiz/survey input from the request is passed to PHP's unserialize(). That function rebuilds full objects — including their magic methods (__destruct, __wakeup) — from attacker-controlled text. Chained with gadget classes present in WordPress, this yields file deletion, option changes, and potentially RCE. Reported by Patchstack.

docs.title: Proof of concept (conceptual)
docs.text:
The attack chain is:

  1. Attacker crafts a serialized payload naming gadget classes.
  2. Submits it as ordinary quiz answer data.
  3. unserialize() builds the chosen objects; magic methods fire.
  4. File deletion, stolen data, rogue admins — RCE in the worst chains.

The accompanying poc.py demonstrates the pattern safely: a vulnerable mock versus the fixed pattern. Fully offline, synthetic data — no exploit, no network calls.

docs.title: Mitigation
docs.text: Update Quiz And Survey Master past 11.2.7 immediately. If installed but unused, delete it — dormant plugins are forgotten doors. Audit admin accounts and recent file changes. Never unserialize() request data; use JSON into plain arrays.

docs.title: CVE-2026-111440 — openGauss JDBC: Unsafe Reflection Turns a Logger Setting into Arbitrary Class Loading
docs.text: Field Value Severity High — CVSS 7.0 Product openGauss-connector-jdbc — the official openGauss JDBC driver, versions 1.1.0 through 6.x / 7.0.0-RC3 Type Unsafe reflection (CWE-470): LogFactory builds a logger class straight from the JDBC URL with no type check before instantiation Vector Network-adjacent, low complexity, no privileges → whoever controls the logger connection parameter triggers arbitrary class instantiation on the client

docs.title: Affected versions
docs.text: • openGauss-connector-jdbc 1.1.0 through 6.x and 7.0.0-RC3. Fixed in 7.0.0-LTS.

docs.title: Root cause
docs.text:
LogFactory reads the logger class name directly from the JDBC URL's logger parameter, calls Class.forName on that attacker-controlled string, then reflects a String constructor and instantiates it — before ever checking that the class actually implements the Log interface. The cast to Log comes after construction, so any class on the client's classpath with a String constructor gets built, and its constructor side effects (file writes, network calls, deserialization chains) fire inside your application. The check comes after the damage.

// Simplified vulnerable pattern
Class<?> c = Class.forName(loggerName);          // attacker-controlled string
Constructor<?> k = c.getConstructor(String.class);
Log log = (Log) k.newInstance(arg);              // side effects already fired

// Simplified fixed pattern: validate BEFORE constructing
Class<? extends Log> c = Class.forName(name).asSubclass(Log.class);
Log log = c.getConstructor(String.class).newInstance(arg);

docs.title: Proof of concept (conceptual)
docs.text:
1. The target app connects to openGauss with a JDBC URL whose logger parameter the attacker influences (config injection, untrusted connection string).
  2. The attacker names a gadget class already present in the client's classpath.
  3. LogFactory loads it via Class.forName and invokes its String constructor — the gadget's side effects execute.
  4. Only then does the cast to Log fail — too late.

The accompanying poc.py demonstrates the pattern safely: a factory that builds a class before validating it versus one that validates with an interface check first. Fully offline, synthetic data — no exploit, no network calls.

docs.title: Video walkthrough
docs.text: Watch the explainer Short

docs.title: Mitigation
docs.text:
• Upgrade openGauss-connector-jdbc to 7.0.0-LTS, which validates with asSubclass before constructing.
  • Never let untrusted input reach JDBC URLs — treat connection strings as security-sensitive configuration.
  • Audit your classpath for gadget classes reachable from connection-parameter-driven reflection.

docs.title: CVE-2026-111759 — markdown-it: Quadratic Blowup in the Smartquotes Rule
docs.text: Field Value Severity High — CVSS 7.5 (CVSS 3.1) Product markdown-it (JS Markdown parser) Type Uncontrolled Resource Consumption (CWE-400 / CWE-407) Vector Before 14.3.2 and 15.0.2, with typographer: true, crafted Markdown (many opening double quotes followed by unmatched closing single quotes) makes the smartquotes rule repeatedly scan the opener stack — quadratic processing time that hangs servers rendering untrusted Markdown; default config (typographer: false) is not affected

docs.title: Affected versions
docs.text: markdown-it before 14.3.2 and before 15.0.2. Fixed in 14.3.2 and 15.0.2.

docs.title: Root cause
docs.text: When typographer is enabled, the smartquotes rule pairs opening and closing quotes by scanning a stack of openers. A document with many opening double quotes followed by unmatched closing single quotes forces the rule to rescan the opener stack for every quote — O(n²) processing. A tiny crafted document keeps a CPU core busy long enough to hang a rendering worker, and the default config (typographer: false) never runs this rule, which is why only typography-enabled setups are exposed.

docs.title: Proof of concept (conceptual)
docs.text:
The attack chain is:

  1. Attacker submits Markdown: a run of opening " quotes, then unmatched closing ' quotes.
  2. The app renders it with typographer: true.
  3. The smartquotes rule rescans the opener stack on every quote — quadratic time.
  4. The rendering worker hangs; the server stops responding.

The accompanying poc.py demonstrates the pattern safely: a vulnerable mock versus the fixed pattern. Fully offline, synthetic data — no exploit, no network calls.

docs.title: Mitigation
docs.text: Upgrade to markdown-it 14.3.2 or 15.0.2 — both lines are fixed. Disable typographer if you do not need smart quotes (default is off). Bound the size of untrusted Markdown you render in request handlers.

docs.title: CVE-2026-111812 — Apache Traffic Server: origin_server_auth Signs Attacker-Chosen AWS Headers
docs.text: Educational content only. This writeup explains the vulnerability conceptually. Nothing here is a working exploit. Do not test against systems you do not own.

docs.title: Summary
docs.text:
Field Value Severity CRITICAL — CVSS 3.1 10.0 (AV:N/AC:L/PR:N/UI:N/S:C/C:H/I:H/A:N) Product Apache Traffic Server Type Incorrect Authorization (CWE-863) Attack vector Network — unauthenticated

This CVE is one of three CVSS 10.0 flaws disclosed together in Apache Traffic Server's October 2026 security bulletin, alongside six sibling issues (CVE-2026-111814, CVE-2026-111815, CVE-2026-111811, CVE-2026-111809, CVE-2026-111805, CVE-2026-111808, CVE-2026-111810, CVE-2026-112381).

docs.title: Root cause
docs.text:
The origin_server_auth plugin signs requests forwarded to AWS backends using the proxy's own IAM credentials (AWS SigV4). It builds the signed payload from the request headers as received from the client, without distinguishing headers the proxy generated itself from headers supplied by the remote client. Any client can therefore submit attacker-chosen headers and have them stamped with the proxy's real cloud identity.

In short: a signature proves the request passed through the proxy, but the proxy never verified who wrote the headers. Signing is not the same as trusting the sender.

docs.title: Proof of concept
docs.text:
Conceptual only — educational. The attack chain works like this:

  1. The attacker sends an HTTP request to the proxy carrying custom headers that mimic AWS-signed API request fields.
  2. The plugin treats the client-supplied headers as legitimate signing input and signs the whole set with the proxy's IAM credentials.
  3. The signed request is forwarded to the AWS backend, which validates the signature against the proxy's identity.
  4. The backend cannot distinguish the attacker's request from genuine proxy traffic, so the attacker operates with the proxy's cloud privileges.

No secret keys are stolen — the proxy is tricked into lending its identity.

docs.title: Mitigation
docs.text:
• Update immediately to Apache Traffic Server 9.2.16, 10.1.5, or 10.2.1.
  • Until patched, disable the origin_server_auth plugin (and the experimental tsmemcache plugin, affected by CVE-2026-111811).
  • Audit cloud access logs for API calls signed by the proxy that the proxy never legitimately issued; rotate IAM credentials if forgery is suspected.

docs.title: CVE-2026-111813 — Apache Traffic Server: Unsigned ImageMagick Arguments Become Remote Shell
docs.text: Field Value Severity Critical — CVSS 10.0 (v3.1) Product Apache Traffic Server — the high-performance caching reverse proxy Type Argument injection (CWE-88) — unauthenticated client controls ImageMagick convert arguments in the experimental magick plugin's default (unsigned) configuration Vector Unauthenticated remote attacker sends a crafted image URL → the magick plugin passes the query string into ImageMagick convert as command-line arguments → arbitrary OS command execution on the proxy

docs.title: Root cause
docs.text: The experimental magick plugin built a shell command by concatenating the request's query string into ImageMagick convert arguments. In the default configuration there was no signature or allowlist on those arguments, so attacker-controlled text reached a command line verbatim — a textbook argument-injection path to remote code execution.

docs.title: Proof of concept
docs.text:
The demo contrasts handle_vulnerable() (query string spliced straight into a command) with handle_fixed() (arguments must carry a valid HMAC signature before anything is executed).

The poc.py file next to this writeup demonstrates the vulnerable pattern versus the fixed pattern as a safe, offline logic demo — no network, no shell, no exploit.

docs.title: Mitigation
docs.text:
• Upgrade now: Traffic Server 9.2.16, 10.1.5 or 10.2.1.
  • Workaround: disable the experimental magick plugin (and audit every other experimental plugin before enabling it).
  • Search access logs for unusual image URLs carrying extra convert arguments.
  • Never pass unsigned, client-controlled strings into shell commands.

docs.title: CVE-2026-111823 — Mage AI: OAuth Error Path Creates an Authenticated Session
docs.text: Field Value Severity Critical — CVSS 9.8 Product mage-ai data pipeline orchestration Type Detection of Error Condition Without Action (CWE-390) Vector Unauthenticated, network → full authenticated session

docs.title: Affected versions
docs.text: Mage OSS versions through 0.9.80. Fixed in the commit after 0.9.80 (upstream PR mage-ai/mage-ai#6204, change 76c4f46).

docs.title: Root cause
docs.text:
In the OAuth callback handler, when the login flow encounters an unknown OAuth provider, the code detects the error condition — and then keeps going. Session creation is not aborted, so an unauthenticated request that merely triggers the error path ends up with a valid, authenticated session.

# Simplified vulnerable pattern
if provider not in KNOWN_PROVIDERS:
    log("unknown oauth provider")   # error detected...
create_session(user)                 # ...but the flow continues anyway

docs.title: Proof of concept (conceptual)
docs.text:
The attack chain is:

  1. The attacker starts the Mage OAuth login flow and steers the callback into the "unknown provider" error path.
  2. The error is logged, but the handler proceeds to session creation.
  3. The attacker holds a valid authenticated session — no credentials, no real identity provider involved.

The accompanying poc.py demonstrates the pattern safely: a mock OAuth callback that detects an unknown provider and (in the vulnerable variant) still mints a session, versus the fixed variant that aborts. Fully offline, synthetic data — no exploit, no network calls.

A public proof of concept for the real vulnerability has been observed in the wild; treat any internet-facing Mage instance as potentially probed.

docs.title: Mitigation
docs.text:
• Update Mage AI past 0.9.80 to the fixed commit immediately.
  • Rotate every credential stored in Mage (S3 keys, Snowflake, Salesforce tokens, etc.) — assume they were readable.
  • Audit active sessions for logins that bypassed OAuth providers.
  • Restrict Mage's network exposure; it should not be reachable from the open internet without additional access controls.

docs.title: CVE-2026-111830 — WP Mailster: One Fake Signup Hides a Live Script in Your Dashboard
docs.text: Field Value Severity High — CVSS 7.1 (v3.1) Product WP Mailster — the WordPress newsletter / mailing-list plugin Type Stored cross-site scripting (CWE-79) — unsanitized signup data rendered in the admin panel Vector Attacker submits a newsletter signup carrying script markup → the value is stored raw in the subscriber list → when the site owner opens the admin panel the script executes in their session → session hijack, admin takeover

docs.title: Affected versions
docs.text: WP Mailster from n/a through 1.9.1.0. Fixed in 1.9.2.0.

docs.title: Root cause
docs.text:
A newsletter signup was stored without sanitization and later rendered as HTML inside the admin panel. Stored cross-site scripting turns a database field into a payload that fires in a privileged browser:

# Simplified vulnerable pattern
def add_subscriber(email):
    db.save(email)                     # BUG: stored raw
def admin_list():
    return "<li>%s</li>" % db.get()    # BUG: rendered as HTML

# Simplified fixed pattern
def add_subscriber_fixed(email):
    db.save(sanitize(email))           # neutralize on the way in
def admin_list_fixed():
    return "<li>%s</li>" % escape(db.get())  # encode on the way out
Treat every stored value as hostile text until it is encoded for its output context.

docs.title: Proof of concept (conceptual)
docs.text:
1. Attacker submits a newsletter signup containing script markup.
  2. WP Mailster stores the value raw in the subscriber list.
  3. The site owner opens the subscriber list in the admin panel.
  4. The stored markup executes as live script in the admin's session — hijacking it, and with it the site.

The accompanying poc.py demonstrates the pattern safely: stored input is not safe input: the demo contrasts raw storage and rendering with sanitization plus output encoding. Offline, no server, no exploit.

docs.title: Mitigation
docs.text:
• Upgrade now: WP Mailster 1.9.2.0.
  • Hunt the subscriber list for suspicious entries and remove them.
  • Rotate admin credentials and revoke sessions — assume the admin browser was exposed.
  • Encode on output as a standing rule: sanitizing on input alone is not enough.

docs.title: CVE-2026-111832 & CVE-2026-111834 — Unrestricted File Upload → Web Shell → Server Takeover
docs.text: Field CVE-2026-111832 CVE-2026-111834 Severity Critical 10.0 (CVSS v3.1) Critical 9.9 (CVSS v3.1) Product WP Mailster (WordPress plugin) Mang Board WP (WordPress plugin) Type Unrestricted Upload of File with Dangerous Type Unrestricted Upload of File with Dangerous Type Vector Network, low complexity, no privileges, no user interaction (S:C) Network, low complexity, low privileges, no user interaction (S:C) Weakness CWE-434 CWE-434

docs.title: Affected versions
docs.text:
• WP Mailster: from n/a through 1.9.1.0 (update past 1.9.1.0)
  • Mang Board WP: from n/a through 2.4.4 (update past 2.4.4)

docs.title: Root cause
docs.text: Both plugins expose public-facing upload features — subscriber attachments in the Mailster newsletter plugin and guest post image uploads in the Mang Board plugin — without properly validating the type or content of the uploaded file. The check (if any) inspects only the attacker-controlled file name/extension, so a web shell renamed to look harmless is stored in a web-accessible uploads directory. Mang Board's boards allow guest posts by default, so exploitation can be unauthenticated. This is the classic CWE-434 unrestricted-upload pattern: the application trusts metadata the attacker controls instead of verifying the file's real content.

docs.title: Proof of concept
docs.text:
Conceptual attack flow (educational illustration only — no working payload):

  1. Attacker submits an upload form with a file carrying a dangerous extension disguised as an image (e.g. shell.php.jpg semantics where only the name is checked).
  2. The plugin stores the file inside the site's uploads folder, reachable via URL.
  3. Attacker requests the uploaded file's URL; the server executes it.
  4. The web shell now runs commands with the web server's privileges (www-data): reading wp-config.php, database credentials, dropping further malware.

See poc.py for a safe, offline demonstration of the validation logic difference between an unsafe name-based check and a safe allow-list + content validation.

docs.title: Mitigation
docs.text:
1. Update WP Mailster past 1.9.1.0 and Mang Board WP past 2.4.4 immediately.
  2. Allow-list safe file extensions server-side; reject everything else by default.
  3. Validate file content (magic bytes / mime sniffing), never trust the file name alone.
  4. Store uploaded files outside the web root or with randomized names and no extension.
  5. Disable script execution in upload directories (php_flag engine off / server config).
  6. Use a WAF/virtual patch as a stopgap while you roll out the update.

docs.title: CVE-2026-111841 — FunnelKit Automations for WordPress: Cross-Site Request Forgery (CSRF)
docs.text: Field Value Severity High — CVSS 8.8 (CVSS:3.1/AV:N/AC:L/PR:N/UI:R/S:U/C:H/I:H/A:H) Product FunnelKit Automations for WordPress (wp-marketing-automations), through 3.8.5.2 Type Cross-Site Request Forgery (CWE-352) Vector Network, low complexity, no privileges required, user interaction required, scope unchanged

docs.title: Affected versions
docs.text:
• FunnelKit Automations for WordPress from n/a through 3.8.5.2.
  • Some plugin actions do not verify that a request genuinely originated from the site's own dashboard, so a request triggered from another site is executed with the victim administrator's session.

docs.title: Root cause
docs.text:
The plugin performs state-changing actions without a per-action security token (nonce) check. Browsers attach the victim's session cookies to every request, even one triggered by a page on a different site. Without a token proving the request came from the site's own dashboard, the plugin cannot distinguish a legitimate administrator click from a forged request (CWE-352: cross-site request forgery).

// Simplified vulnerable pattern (conceptual)
// action handler without a nonce check
function handle_automation_action() {
    // no check that this request came from our own dashboard
    update_automation_rules($_REQUEST);
}

docs.title: Proof of concept (conceptual)
docs.text:
The attack chain:

  1. The attacker builds a malicious page that silently fires requests against the victim site's automation endpoints.
  2. They lure a logged-in WordPress administrator to open the page, for example through a phishing email.
  3. The administrator's browser sends the requests with full admin cookies.
  4. The plugin executes the forged requests: automation rules are rewritten, customer emails redirected, and order data exposed.

The accompanying poc.py demonstrates the pattern safely and offline: a request handler that executes any request (vulnerable) versus one that requires a valid per-session token (fixed). No site, no network, no exploit.

docs.title: Mitigation
docs.text:
• Update FunnelKit Automations past version 3.8.5.2 immediately.
  • Audit automation rules for changes you did not make, including redirected emails and altered workflows.
  • Log out of WordPress when you are done, and avoid clicking links in unexpected emails while logged in as an administrator.
  • Plugin authors should verify a nonce on every state-changing action.

docs.title: CVE-2026-111851 — Royal Elementor Addons: This Widget Runs Attacker Code
docs.text: Field Value Severity High — CVSS 7.6 (v3.1) Product Royal Elementor Addons (by WProyal) — widgets and extensions for the Elementor page builder Type Code injection via unsafe reflection (CWE-470) — class name taken from the request and instantiated Vector Authenticated remote attacker sends a request naming an arbitrary class → the widget handler loads that class through reflection with no allowlist → attacker code executes on the server: backdoors, defacement, data theft

docs.title: Affected versions
docs.text: Royal Elementor Addons from n/a through 1.7.1068. Fixed in 1.7.1069.

docs.title: Root cause
docs.text:
A widget handler took a class name straight from the request and loaded it via reflection — with no allowlist. Reflection turns a string into behavior; when the string is attacker-controlled, so is the behavior:

# Simplified vulnerable pattern
def render_widget(request):
    cls = load_class(request["widget"])   # BUG: any class, attacker's pick
    return cls().render()

# Simplified fixed pattern
ALLOWED = {"Heading", "Button", "Gallery"}
def render_widget_fixed(request):
    name = request["widget"]
    if name not in ALLOWED:               # fixed menu only
        raise ValueError("unknown widget")
    return load_class(name)().render()
Never build a class name from request data — map input to a fixed allowlist and reject everything else.

docs.title: Proof of concept (conceptual)
docs.text:
1. Attacker, logged in with any account, names an arbitrary class in a widget request.
  2. The handler loads that class through reflection — no allowlist, no check.
  3. The attacker's chosen code runs on the server with the site's privileges.
  4. Backdoors, defaced pages, stolen data: the server obeys the attacker's class.

The accompanying poc.py demonstrates the pattern safely: reflection must only reach a fixed allowlist: the demo contrasts loading any named class with a strict menu of known-safe widgets. Offline, no server, no exploit.

docs.title: Mitigation
docs.text:
• Upgrade now: Royal Elementor Addons 1.7.1069.
  • Scan for unknown admin accounts and strange files — assume the worst on exposed sites.
  • Review recently modified content for injected scripts or iframes.
  • Rotate credentials and secrets reachable from the site.

docs.title: CVE-2026-111852 — Blind SQL Injection in WPdreams Ajax Search Lite
docs.text: Field Value Severity CRITICAL 9.3 (CVSS 3.1 / AV:N/AC:L/PR:N/UI:N/S:C/C:H/I:N/A:L) Product WPdreams Ajax Search Lite (WordPress plugin, ajax-search-lite) Type Improper Neutralization of Special Elements used in an SQL Command — SQL Injection (CWE-89), blind variant Vector Network, no privileges required, no user interaction

docs.title: Affected versions
docs.text: Ajax Search Lite from n/a through 4.14.6. Fixed in 4.14.7 and later.

docs.title: Root cause
docs.text:
The plugin's search handler builds its database query by concatenating the visitor's search keyword directly into a raw SQL string instead of using a prepared statement. A quote character in the keyword breaks out of the intended string literal, and the remainder of the input is interpreted as SQL. Because this is the blind variant, the attacker gets no query output back — only a yes/no signal per request — but by asking thousands of boolean questions through the public search box they can exfiltrate the entire database bit by bit (usernames, password hashes, post content, etc.).

// conceptual illustration of the vulnerable pattern (simplified)
$sql = "SELECT * FROM posts WHERE title LIKE '%" . $search_keyword . "%'";
//     ^ attacker-controlled quote in $search_keyword breaks out of the string literal

docs.title: Proof of concept
docs.text:
Educational, conceptual demo only — no working exploit. poc.py uses a local SQLite toy database to show the difference between the vulnerable pattern (string concatenation, where an injected quote alters the query logic) and the safe pattern (parameterized queries, where the input stays plain data).

Run it with: python3 poc.py

docs.title: Mitigation
docs.text:
1. Update Ajax Search Lite to 4.14.7 or later immediately (mass exploitation campaigns are expected for this class of bug).
  2. Enable WordPress plugin auto-updates so the window of exposure stays small.
  3. If you develop plugins: never interpolate user input into SQL — always use $wpdb->prepare() / parameterized queries so the query shape is locked.
  4. Until patched, a web application firewall rule blocking suspicious quotes in search parameters reduces exposure (defense in depth only — update is the fix).
