docs.title: Authlib: Two Key-Handling Bugs Let Attackers Forge Login Tokens
docs.text: Educational material only. Do not use against systems you do not own or have explicit permission to test. | | | |---|---| | CVE | CVE-2026-114615 | | Severity | High — CVSS 7.4 (v3.1) — covers CVE-2026-114615 + CVE-2026-114616 | | Product | Authlib (Python OAuth / OpenID Connect library) 1.3.1 – 1.9.0 | | Type | Key confusion in OctKey.import_key() (CWE-184) + empty HMAC secrets accepted (CWE-287) | | Attack vector | Remote attacker forges login tokens: a public key with a leading space is accepted as an HMAC secret, or an empty secret signs arbitrary claims |

docs.title: Affected versions
docs.text: Authlib 1.3.1 through 1.9.0. Fixed in 1.9.1 — upgrade.

docs.title: Root cause
docs.text:
Two flaws in how Authlib imported HMAC keys, both leading to forged tokens:

Bug 1 (CVE-2026-114615) — OctKey.import_key() checked asymmetric-key markers only at byte zero, while the PEM loaders accepted leading whitespace, comments, or a byte-order mark. A public key prefixed with a space slipped past the "is this asymmetric?" test and was treated as an HMAC secret — so an attacker who knew the public key bytes could sign tokens with them.

Bug 2 (CVE-2026-114616) — import_key() and the HMAC sign/verify path accepted zero-length key material. If an application's secret lookup returned an empty string, an attacker could compute the deterministic HS256/HS384/HS512 signature for arbitrary claims and be treated as authentic.

# Simplified fixed pattern
def import_key_fixed(raw):
    key = raw.strip()                 # normalize first
    if not key:
        raise ValueError("empty key rejected")
    if looks_asymmetric(key):
        raise ValueError("public key is not an HMAC secret")
    return OctKey(key)
Key material must be normalized, non-empty, and type-checked before use.

docs.title: Proof of concept
docs.text:
1. Attacker learns the application's public-key bytes (often public by design).
  2. (Bug 1) Attacker prefixes the public key with a space and presents it as the HMAC secret — Authlib accepts it.
  3. (Bug 2) Alternatively, attacker triggers an empty secret lookup and signs claims with the empty key.
  4. Attacker mints a token with arbitrary claims (e.g. admin) and a valid HMAC signature.
  5. Authlib verifies the signature against the confused/empty key — the forged token is accepted as authentic.

See poc.py — a safe, fully synthetic demo of the vulnerable vs. fixed pattern. key material must be normalized, non-empty, and type-checked: the demo contrasts accepting a spaced public key / empty secret with rejecting both.

docs.title: Mitigation
docs.text:
• Upgrade to Authlib 1.9.1 now — both bugs are fixed there.
  • Audit token issuance logs for tokens signed with unexpected keys.
  • Never let secret lookups return empty — fail closed on missing secrets.
  • Pin and separate HMAC secrets from asymmetric keys in configuration.

docs.title: CVE-2026-114625 — Arista VeloCloud Orchestrator: Authenticated SQL Injection to Superuser
docs.text: Field Value Severity Critical — CVSS 9.9 (v3.1, AV:N/AC:L/PR:L/UI:N/S:C) Product Arista VeloCloud Orchestrator (VCO) — on-prem SD-WAN management plane Type SQL injection in the web interface → privilege escalation to superuser operator Vector Any authenticated user (even a read-only tenant/customer account) submits crafted input through the VCO web UI → injected SQL runs against the orchestrator database → the session escalates to operator, then masquerades as a local "superuser operator" → internal-only functionality exposed, VCO host impacted

docs.title: Affected versions
docs.text: VCO 5.2 train before 5.2.3.18, 6.1 train before 6.1.3.10, 6.4 train before 6.4.2.12. Fixed in 5.2.3.18, 6.1.3.10, 6.4.2.12. On-prem deployments only.

docs.title: Root cause
docs.text:
The VCO web interface passes user-controlled input into database queries without proper sanitization or parameterization. Because the database session and the authorization model are coupled, an injected query does more than read rows — the resulting database session inherits escalated privileges. A read-only tenant becomes an operator, then impersonates the built-in superuser operator. Injection plus a privilege model that trusts the database session is the whole vulnerability.

# Simplified vulnerable pattern
def get_tenant(username):
    query = "SELECT * FROM tenants WHERE name = '" + username + "'"
    return db.execute(query)          # attacker input runs as SQL

# Simplified fixed pattern
def get_tenant_fixed(username):
    query = "SELECT * FROM tenants WHERE name = ?"
    return db.execute(query, (username,))   # input stays data, never code

docs.title: Proof of concept (conceptual)
docs.text:
1. Attacker logs in with a low-privilege tenant account (even read-only).
  2. A web form field is filled with input containing SQL metacharacters.
  3. The unsanitized input breaks out of the intended query; injected SQL executes.
  4. The database session's privilege context escalates to operator.
  5. The attacker masquerades as a local "superuser operator", reaching internal-only functions and the VCO host.

The accompanying poc.py demonstrates the pattern safely: string-interpolated vs. parameterized query construction, offline, against a local throwaway SQLite database with synthetic data. No network, no exploit.

docs.title: Mitigation
docs.text:
• Upgrade immediately: 5.2.3.18 / 6.1.3.10 / 6.4.2.12. Arista confirms active exploitation — treat this as an incident, not a routine patch.
  • Restrict VCO web access to trusted admin networks until patched.
  • Hunt: known attacker IPs 74.82.197.86 and 38.54.50.151; unusual URL-like paths or encoded characters in web logs; unexpected admin/operator activity.
  • Review recent operator and superuser actions for anything unrecognized.

docs.title: CVE-2026-114635 — Traefik: SNI Check Bypass via HTTP/2 Scheme on Nil TLS State
docs.text: Field Value Severity High — CVSS 8.7 (v3.1) Product Traefik before 2.11.58 and before 3.7.14 — the cloud-native edge router / reverse proxy Type Authentication bypass using an alternate path (CWE-288) — SNI check skipped when request TLS state is nil Vector Unauthenticated remote attacker sends an HTTP/2 request with the :scheme pseudo-header set to http over a TLS connection (Go 1.27 builds) → Traefik sees an empty TLS state and skips the SNI check → request lands on routers requiring client certificates without presenting one

docs.title: Affected versions
docs.text: Traefik before 2.11.58 and before 3.7.14. Fixed in 2.11.58 and 3.7.14.

docs.title: Root cause
docs.text:
Traefik's SNI check guards routers that require client certificates: it inspects the request's TLS state to decide which certificate checks apply. On affected builds, when an HTTP/2 request arrives over TLS carrying the :scheme pseudo-header set to http, the request's TLS state reads as empty — and the SNI check is skipped entirely instead of failing closed:

# Simplified vulnerable pattern
def route_request(req):
    if req.tls_state is None:
        return skip_sni_check(req)      # BUG: empty state => no check
    return enforce_client_certs(req)

# Simplified fixed pattern
def route_request_fixed(req):
    if req.tls_state is None:
        return deny(req)                # fail closed: no state => no entry
    return enforce_client_certs(req)
An empty security context must deny, never wave through.

docs.title: Proof of concept (conceptual)
docs.text:
1. Attacker opens a TLS connection to Traefik (no client certificate).
  2. Attacker sends an HTTP/2 request with :scheme: http over that TLS socket.
  3. Traefik observes an empty TLS state and skips the SNI verification.
  4. The request is routed to a backend whose router demanded mutual TLS — with no certificate ever presented.
  5. Unauthenticated traffic now flows inside the mTLS-protected zone.

The accompanying poc.py demonstrates the pattern safely: a missing security context must fail closed: the demo contrasts skipping the check on empty state versus denying. Offline, no server, no exploit.

docs.title: Mitigation
docs.text:
• Upgrade now: Traefik 2.11.58 / 3.7.14 close this and seven sibling bypasses.
  • Audit routers that relied on client-certificate enforcement — assume unauthenticated traffic may have reached them.
  • Rotate backend credentials that sat behind the affected routers.
  • Hunt logs for unauthenticated hits on mTLS-protected routes.

docs.title: CVE-2026-114636 — Traefik: Ingress NGINX ssl-passthrough Ignores Access-Control Annotations
docs.text: Field Value Severity High — CVSS 8.7 (v3.1) Product Traefik 3.7.13 before 3.7.14 — Kubernetes Ingress NGINX provider Type Missing authentication for critical function (CWE-306) — access-control annotations never applied to ssl-passthrough HTTP router Vector Unauthenticated attacker reaches the HTTP entry point with the Ingress host → generated router never evaluates auth-type, auth-url, or whitelist-source-range annotations → protected backends served with nothing logged

docs.title: Affected versions
docs.text: Traefik 3.7.13 before 3.7.14. Fixed in 3.7.14.

docs.title: Root cause
docs.text:
For Kubernetes Ingresses using ssl-passthrough, Traefik generates an HTTP router on non-TLS entry points. That generated router was built without wiring in the Ingress's access-control annotations — auth-type, auth-url, and whitelist-source-range were silently dropped:

# Simplified vulnerable pattern
def build_http_router(ingress):
    router = Router(entrypoint="http", host=ingress.host)
    # annotations never copied -> no auth enforced
    return router

# Simplified fixed pattern
def build_http_router_fixed(ingress):
    router = Router(entrypoint="http", host=ingress.host)
    router.apply(ingress.annotations.auth_type,
                 ingress.annotations.auth_url,
                 ingress.annotations.whitelist)
    return router
Worse, the bypass left no trace in the logs.

docs.title: Proof of concept (conceptual)
docs.text:
1. Attacker identifies an ssl-passthrough Ingress with auth annotations.
  2. Attacker sends plain HTTP requests to the non-TLS entry point with the Ingress host.
  3. The generated HTTP router applies no access control at all.
  4. Backends meant to require auth-type / auth-url / IP whitelisting answer directly, silently.

The accompanying poc.py demonstrates the pattern safely: generated configuration must inherit every security annotation: the demo contrasts a router built with and without the annotations. Offline, no server, no exploit.

docs.title: Mitigation
docs.text:
• Upgrade now: Traefik 3.7.14.
  • Audit Ingress annotations on ssl-passthrough services — verify auth is actually enforced end to end.
  • Check access logs (and their absence) for unauthenticated access during the exposure window.

docs.title: CVE-2026-114637 — Traefik: FastProxy Pool Hands Victim NTLM Sessions to Strangers
docs.text: Field Value Severity High — CVSS 8.7 (v3.1) Product Traefik 3.2.0 before 3.7.14 — experimental FastProxy connection pool Type Exposure of data element to wrong session (CWE-488) — NTLM/Negotiate-authenticated backend connections not pinned to their frontend Vector Victim completes an NTLM/Negotiate handshake to a backend → connection returns to the shared pool → unauthenticated attacker is handed that pooled keep-alive → reads victim data and acts as the victim

docs.title: Affected versions
docs.text: Traefik 3.2.0 before 3.7.14. Fixed in 3.7.14.

docs.title: Root cause
docs.text:
The experimental FastProxy connection pool reuses backend keep-alive connections across frontend connections — but never pinned connections that carried an NTLM or Negotiate authentication handshake to the frontend that authenticated them:

# Simplified vulnerable pattern
pool = SharedPool()
def get_backend_conn(frontend):
    return pool.any_keepalive()   # BUG: may return victim's authed socket

# Simplified fixed pattern
def get_backend_conn_fixed(frontend):
    conn = pool.keepalive_for(frontend.session_id)  # pinned to owner
    if conn and conn.auth_owner != frontend.session_id:
        return new_connection()
    return conn
Connection pooling must never mix authenticated sessions across users.

docs.title: Proof of concept (conceptual)
docs.text:
1. Victim authenticates to a backend through Traefik with NTLM/Negotiate.
  2. The authenticated keep-alive connection returns to the shared pool.
  3. Attacker opens an unauthenticated frontend connection; the pool hands them the victim's socket.
  4. Attacker reads victim responses and issues requests as the victim.

The accompanying poc.py demonstrates the pattern safely: pooled resources must be pinned to their owner: the demo contrasts a shared pool with a session-pinned pool. Offline, no server, no exploit.

docs.title: Mitigation
docs.text:
• Upgrade now: Traefik 3.7.14; disable the experimental FastProxy pool if you cannot upgrade immediately.
  • Rotate credentials for backends reachable through the pool.
  • Review logs for sessions served on connections they did not open.

docs.title: CVE-2026-114638 — Traefik: Client CA Mix-Up via auth-tls-secret Name Collision
docs.text: Field Value Severity High — CVSS 8.7 (v3.1) Product Traefik 3.7.0 before 3.7.14 — Kubernetes Ingress NGINX provider (auth-tls) Type Improper authentication (CWE-287) — client CAs merged when auth-tls-secret names collide after dot-to-dash normalization Vector Attacker holds a certificate from another host's CA → secret-name collision merges the CAs → attacker's cert is accepted for a host requiring its own client CA, while legitimate clients are refused

docs.title: Affected versions
docs.text: Traefik 3.7.0 before 3.7.14. Fixed in 3.7.14.

docs.title: Root cause
docs.text:
When two auth-tls-secret names collide after dot-to-dash normalization, Traefik merged their client CA bundles instead of keeping them separate. A certificate issued by host A's CA was then accepted for host B — which required its own, different client CA — while host B's legitimate clients could be refused:

# Simplified vulnerable pattern
def load_ca(secret_name):
    key = secret_name.replace(".", "-")   # normalization collides
    ca_store[key].merge(load(secret_name))  # BUG: CAs mixed across hosts

# Simplified fixed pattern
def load_ca_fixed(secret_name):
    key = "ns/" + secret_name             # collision-free identity
    ca_store[key] = load(secret_name)     # never merged
Normalization must never erase security boundaries.

docs.title: Proof of concept (conceptual)
docs.text:
1. Attacker holds a client certificate from host A's CA.
  2. The auth-tls-secret names for host A and host B collide after normalization.
  3. Traefik merges the CA bundles; the attacker's cert validates for host B.
  4. Attacker accesses the mTLS-protected host B with the wrong CA's certificate.

The accompanying poc.py demonstrates the pattern safely: identifier normalization must preserve security boundaries: the demo contrasts merging versus isolated CA stores. Offline, no server, no exploit.

docs.title: Mitigation
docs.text:
• Upgrade now: Traefik 3.7.14.
  • Audit auth-tls-secret names for dot/dash collisions across hosts.
  • Re-issue client certificates if cross-host acceptance is suspected.

docs.title: CVE-2026-114639 — Traefik: Negotiate-Pooled Sockets Leak Authenticated Identity
docs.text: Field Value Severity High — CVSS 8.7 (v3.1) Product Traefik 2.11.0 before 2.11.58 and 3.0.0 before 3.7.14 — shared backend connection pool Type Improper authentication (CWE-287) — Negotiate-preauthenticated socket in the globally shared pool never isolated Vector Attacker's first request carries an Authorization: Negotiate token → socket enters the shared pool preauthenticated → unauthenticated attackers on separate frontends are assigned that NTLM/Kerberos-bound socket → reads/writes as the victim

docs.title: Affected versions
docs.text: Traefik 2.11.0 before 2.11.58 and 3.0.0 before 3.7.14. Fixed in 2.11.58 and 3.7.14.

docs.title: Root cause
docs.text:
A backend socket preauthenticated with an Authorization: Negotiate token was placed into the globally shared connection pool with no isolation. Any later frontend connection could be assigned that NTLM/Kerberos-bound socket and inherit the victim's identity:

# Simplified vulnerable pattern
def return_to_pool(sock):
    global_pool.append(sock)   # BUG: authed socket shared with everyone

# Simplified fixed pattern
def return_to_pool_fixed(sock, owner):
    if sock.is_negotiate_authenticated():
        owner_pools[owner].append(sock)  # pinned to its identity
    else:
        global_pool.append(sock)
Authenticated transport state must never be fungible.

docs.title: Proof of concept (conceptual)
docs.text:
1. Victim (or attacker) sends a request preauthenticated with a Negotiate token.
  2. The authenticated socket returns to the globally shared pool.
  3. An unauthenticated attacker on a separate frontend connection is assigned that socket.
  4. The attacker performs reads and writes with the victim's identity.

The accompanying poc.py demonstrates the pattern safely: authenticated transport state must not be shared: the demo contrasts a global pool with identity-pinned pooling. Offline, no server, no exploit.

docs.title: Mitigation
docs.text:
• Upgrade now: Traefik 2.11.58 / 3.7.14.
  • Rotate backend service credentials that traversed the shared pool.
  • Monitor for requests executed under unexpected identities.

docs.title: CVE-2026-114640 — Traefik: mTLS Identity Spoofing via Forwarded Ssl-Client Headers
docs.text: Field Value Severity High — CVSS 8.7 (v3.1) Product Traefik 3.7.0 before 3.7.14 — Kubernetes Ingress-NGINX provider Type Authentication bypass by spoofing (CWE-290) — client-supplied Ssl-Client-* headers forwarded on the plaintext HTTP router Vector Unauthenticated attacker sends Ssl-Client-Verify: SUCCESS plus a chosen certificate subject/issuer on the plaintext router (ssl-redirect disabled + auth-tls-pass-certificate-to-upstream) → upstream trusts the headers → attacker impersonates mTLS identities

docs.title: Affected versions
docs.text: Traefik 3.7.0 before 3.7.14. Fixed in 3.7.14.

docs.title: Root cause
docs.text:
With ssl-redirect disabled and auth-tls-pass-certificate-to-upstream enabled, the plaintext HTTP router forwarded client-supplied Ssl-Client-* headers straight to the upstream. Upstreams that trust those headers for identity saw Ssl-Client-Verify: SUCCESS — written by the attacker:

# Simplified vulnerable pattern
def proxy_to_upstream(req):
    headers = req.headers            # BUG: client-controlled Ssl-Client-*
    return upstream(headers)         # upstream trusts them as mTLS proof

# Simplified fixed pattern
def proxy_to_upstream_fixed(req):
    headers = strip_spoofable(req.headers, prefix="Ssl-Client-")
    headers["Ssl-Client-Verify"] = req.real_tls_verify_status()
    return upstream(headers)
Security headers must be set by the proxy, never accepted from the client.

docs.title: Proof of concept (conceptual)
docs.text:
1. Attacker targets an Ingress with ssl-redirect disabled and certificate pass-through on.
  2. Attacker sends plain HTTP with Ssl-Client-Verify: SUCCESS and a chosen subject/issuer.
  3. Traefik forwards the spoofed headers to the upstream untouched.
  4. The upstream accepts the attacker as the claimed mTLS identity.

The accompanying poc.py demonstrates the pattern safely: the proxy must author security headers itself: the demo contrasts forwarding client headers with overwriting them from verified TLS state. Offline, no server, no exploit.

docs.title: Mitigation
docs.text:
• Upgrade now: Traefik 3.7.14.
  • Enable ssl-redirect where possible so plaintext routers do not exist.
  • Make upstreams verify TLS themselves instead of trusting proxy headers.

docs.title: CVE-2026-114642 — Traefik: TLS Config Bypass via Shared NTLM Round-Tripper Slot
docs.text: Field Value Severity High — CVSS 8.7 (v3.1) Product Traefik 2.11.0 before 2.11.58 and 3.0.0 before 3.7.14 — backend round tripper Type Improper certificate validation (CWE-295) — NTLM/Kerberos round tripper stored in a slot not keyed by ServersTransport Vector Attacker arms the shared slot via a backend issuing an NTLM/Negotiate challenge → one service's TLS client configuration is reused for another service's backend → root CAs, server name, and certificate verification bypassed

docs.title: Affected versions
docs.text: Traefik 2.11.0 before 2.11.58 and 3.0.0 before 3.7.14. Fixed in 2.11.58 and 3.7.14.

docs.title: Root cause
docs.text:
The NTLM/Kerberos backend round tripper lived in a client-connection slot that was not keyed by ServersTransport — the per-service TLS configuration. One service's TLS client settings were therefore reused for another service's backend, bypassing its root CAs, expected server name, and certificate verification:

# Simplified vulnerable pattern
slot = {}                                   # one global slot
def get_roundtripper(service):
    return slot.setdefault("shared", make_rt(service.tls))  # BUG: first wins

# Simplified fixed pattern
def get_roundtripper_fixed(service):
    key = service.servers_transport_id     # keyed per TLS config
    return slot.setdefault(key, make_rt(service.tls))
TLS identity is per-service; caching must respect that boundary.

docs.title: Proof of concept (conceptual)
docs.text:
1. Attacker triggers a backend that issues an NTLM/Negotiate challenge, arming the shared slot.
  2. On the same keep-alive connection, the attacker reaches a different service.
  3. The first service's TLS configuration is reused for the second service's backend.
  4. Root CA pinning, server-name checks, and certificate verification are bypassed.

The accompanying poc.py demonstrates the pattern safely: security-relevant caches must be keyed by the full security context: the demo contrasts a global slot with a per-transport slot. Offline, no server, no exploit.

docs.title: Mitigation
docs.text:
• Upgrade now: Traefik 2.11.58 / 3.7.14.
  • Verify backend TLS settings per service after upgrading — especially pinned CAs.
  • Monitor for unexpected backend certificate acceptance.

docs.title: CVE-2026-114656 — Traefik: mTLS Bypass via Negated Host Matcher TLS Conflict
docs.text: Field Value Severity High — CVSS 7.5 (v3.1) Product Traefik before 2.11.58 and before 3.7.13 — TLS options / Host matchers Type Interpretation conflict (CWE-436) — negated Host matchers counted as served domains, TLS options conflict falls back to defaults Vector Attacker targets a router whose rule uses a negated Host() matcher → conflict resolves to default TLS options → RequireAndVerifyClientCert silently dropped → backends reachable without client certificates

docs.title: Affected versions
docs.text: Traefik before 2.11.58 and before 3.7.13. Fixed in 2.11.58 and 3.7.13.

docs.title: Root cause
docs.text:
Negated Host() matchers were counted as served domains when Traefik computed TLS options. The resulting options conflict fell back to the default TLS options — silently discarding RequireAndVerifyClientCert on routers that required it:

# Simplified vulnerable pattern
def tls_options(rule):
    if "!" in rule.host_matcher:
        served.add(negated_host)      # BUG: negated != served
    return resolve(served) or DEFAULT # conflict -> defaults, mTLS dropped

# Simplified fixed pattern
def tls_options_fixed(rule):
    served = {h for h in rule.hosts if not h.negated}
    return resolve_strict(served)     # conflict -> explicit, never silent
Fallbacks in security configuration must be explicit and loud.

docs.title: Proof of concept (conceptual)
docs.text:
1. Attacker finds a router whose rule contains a negated Host() matcher.
  2. The negated matcher is counted as a served domain, creating a TLS options conflict.
  3. Traefik falls back to default TLS options — client-cert verification dropped.
  4. Backends protected by RequireAndVerifyClientCert answer unauthenticated requests.

The accompanying poc.py demonstrates the pattern safely: security fallbacks must be explicit: the demo contrasts silent defaulting with strict resolution. Offline, no server, no exploit.

docs.title: Mitigation
docs.text:
• Upgrade now: Traefik 2.11.58 / 3.7.13.
  • Audit router rules using negated Host() matchers combined with mTLS.
  • Test mTLS enforcement end to end after upgrading.

docs.title: CVE-2026-114658 — Grav Login: Unauthenticated Invitation Grants Super-User
docs.text: Field Value Severity High — CVSS 8.8 (v3.1) Product Grav Login plugin 3.6.0 before 3.9.13 — user management for the Grav flat-file CMS Type Improper privilege management (CWE-269) — missing authorization in the login.invite task Vector Attacker defines an invitation form granting super access in page frontmatter → submits it unauthenticated → registers the invited address → super-user account created → full site control

docs.title: Affected versions
docs.text: Grav Login plugin 3.6.0 before 3.9.13. Fixed in 3.9.13.

docs.title: Root cause
docs.text:
The login.invite task performed no authorization check. Page authors could define an invitation form right in the page's frontmatter — including the privilege level granted — and the form could be submitted with no login at all. The plugin registered whatever the form specified:

# Simplified vulnerable pattern
def invite_task(form):
    create_user(form.email, groups=form.groups)  # BUG: no auth check

# Simplified fixed pattern
def invite_task_fixed(form, actor):
    require_role(actor, "admin")                  # only admins invite
    create_user(form.email, groups=form.groups)
Privilege must flow from a verified granter, never from the request itself.

docs.title: Proof of concept (conceptual)
docs.text:
1. Attacker crafts a page whose frontmatter defines an invite form with super-user privileges.
  2. Attacker submits the form unauthenticated.
  3. Attacker registers the invited address.
  4. The plugin creates a super-user account — full site administration.

The accompanying poc.py demonstrates the pattern safely: invitation flows must verify the inviter: the demo contrasts the unchecked task with one requiring the admin role. Offline, no server, no exploit.

docs.title: Mitigation
docs.text:
• Upgrade now: Login plugin 3.9.13.
  • Audit every user account for ones you did not create.
  • Review page frontmatter for rogue invitation forms; rotate admin credentials.

docs.title: CVE-2026-114661 — OpenRemote: Any Authenticated User Controls Gateway Tunnels
docs.text: Field Value Severity High — CVSS 8.5 (v3.1) Product OpenRemote 1.2.0 before 1.31.0 — open-source IoT device management platform Type Missing authorization (CWE-862) — GatewayServiceResource tunnel endpoints lack role checks Vector Any authenticated (non-admin) user sends POST/DELETE to the gateway tunnel endpoint → persistent bidirectional TCP circuits opened into edge gateway networks, or operator tunnels torn down

docs.title: Affected versions
docs.text: OpenRemote 1.2.0 before 1.31.0. Fixed in 1.31.0.

docs.title: Root cause
docs.text:
The gateway tunnel endpoints in GatewayServiceResource checked that the caller was authenticated but never checked that they were authorized — no admin role required. Starting, stopping, and querying tunnels was open to every logged-in user:

# Simplified vulnerable pattern
def tunnel_endpoint(user, action):
    require_login(user)          # BUG: authentication != authorization
    return apply(action)

# Simplified fixed pattern
def tunnel_endpoint_fixed(user, action):
    require_login(user)
    require_role(user, "admin")   # tunnels reshape the network
    return apply(action)
Being logged in proves who you are; it says nothing about what you may touch.

docs.title: Proof of concept (conceptual)
docs.text:
1. Attacker logs in with any ordinary, low-privilege account.
  2. Attacker POSTs to the gateway tunnel endpoint.
  3. The server opens a persistent bidirectional TCP circuit into the edge gateway's network.
  4. Attacker pivots to devices behind the gateway — or DELETEs operators' tunnels to blind them.

The accompanying poc.py demonstrates the pattern safely: privileged endpoints must check roles, not just login: the demo contrasts the login-only check with an admin-role check. Offline, no server, no exploit.

docs.title: Mitigation
docs.text:
• Upgrade now: OpenRemote 1.31.0.
  • Audit existing tunnels for ones you did not open.
  • Review low-privilege accounts and segment edge networks.

docs.title: CVE-2026-114662 — Obot: CLI Login Flow Leaks API Keys via Chosen Request IDs
docs.text: Field Value Severity High — CVSS 8.1 (v3.1) Product Obot before 0.26.0 — open-source AI agent platform Type Cross-site request forgery (CWE-352) — CLI login flow token request IDs are attacker-chosen Vector Attacker creates a token request with a chosen ID via POST /api/token-request → sends the login link to a signed-in victim → victim completes the login → attacker fetches the resulting non-expiring API key → account takeover

docs.title: Affected versions
docs.text: Obot before 0.26.0. Fixed in 0.26.0.

docs.title: Root cause
docs.text:
The CLI login flow issued token requests whose IDs the attacker chose. Nothing bound a request to the session that created it, so an attacker could pre-claim an ID, have the victim complete the login against it, and then collect the minted API key:

# Simplified vulnerable pattern
def create_token_request(chosen_id):
    store[chosen_id] = PENDING        # BUG: attacker picks the ID
def fetch_key(request_id):
    return store[request_id].api_key  # whoever knows the ID gets the key

# Simplified fixed pattern
def create_token_request_fixed(session):
    rid = secrets.token_urlsafe(32)   # random, unguessable
    store[rid] = PENDING(owner=session)
def fetch_key_fixed(request_id, session):
    req = store[request_id]
    assert req.owner == session       # bound to creator
    return req.api_key
Auth handshakes must use unguessable, single-use, session-bound identifiers.

docs.title: Proof of concept (conceptual)
docs.text:
1. Attacker POSTs /api/token-request with a chosen request ID.
  2. Attacker sends the resulting login link to a signed-in victim (disguised as routine).
  3. Victim completes the login legitimately; a non-expiring API key is minted.
  4. Attacker polls the known request ID and retrieves the key — full account takeover.

The accompanying poc.py demonstrates the pattern safely: handshake identifiers must be unguessable and session-bound: the demo contrasts chosen IDs with random, owner-bound ones. Offline, no server, no exploit.

docs.title: Mitigation
docs.text:
• Upgrade now: Obot 0.26.0.
  • Revoke all API keys and re-authenticate every CLI session — treat pre-fix keys as compromised.
  • Verify no rogue agents or sessions exist on the account.

docs.title: CVE-2026-114663 — Vyper: Name Shadowing Silently Replaces Imported Constants
docs.text: Field Value Severity High — CVSS 8.4 (v3.1) Product Vyper 0.4.0b1 through 0.5.0b1 — Python-like smart contract language for Ethereum Type Use of incorrectly-resolved name (CWE-706) — imported constants/default args resolved in the wrong scope Vector Contract imports a module constant but declares a same-named local fed by user input → compiler resolves the name in the function's scope → attacker-influenced value (even out-of-range for narrow types like uint8) replaces the constant → validation/accounting corrupted in deployed bytecode

docs.title: Affected versions
docs.text: Vyper 0.4.0b1 through 0.5.0b1. Fixed in later releases — recompile and redeploy.

docs.title: Root cause
docs.text:
The compiler miscompiled unfoldable constants and omitted default arguments from imported modules: parse_Name resolved their names in the using function's scope rather than at declaration. When a parameter, local, or loop variable shared such a name, it shadowed the constant — silently, with no warning:

# Simplified vulnerable pattern
def resolve_name_vuln(name, function_scope, module_scope):
    return function_scope.get(name) or module_scope.get(name)  # BUG: wrong order

# Simplified fixed pattern
def resolve_name_fixed(name, function_scope, module_scope):
    if name in module_scope.imported_constants:
        return module_scope.get(name)   # declaration site wins
    return function_scope.get(name)
A shadowed constant should be a loud compile error, never a quiet substitution.

docs.title: Proof of concept (conceptual)
docs.text:
1. Contract imports a module constant (e.g. a fee cap) and also declares a same-named local fed by user input.
  2. The compiler resolves the name in the function scope — the local wins.
  3. Validation and accounting logic now runs on attacker-influenced numbers, including out-of-range values.
  4. The miscompiled bytecode is deployed on-chain: immutable, guarding real funds.

The accompanying poc.py demonstrates the pattern safely: imported names must resolve at their declaration site: the demo contrasts wrong-scope resolution with declaration-site resolution. Offline, no server, no exploit.

docs.title: Mitigation
docs.text:
• Upgrade the compiler past the affected range immediately.
  • Recompile every contract built with 0.4.0b1–0.5.0b1 and redeploy affected bytecode.
  • Audit deployed contracts for shadowed names in validation/accounting logic.

docs.title: CVE-2026-114664 — Frappe: Blind SQL Injection in Event Listing
docs.text: Field Value Severity High — CVSS 7.1 (v3.1) Product Frappe Framework before 16.33.0 — the Python framework behind ERPNext Type SQL injection (CWE-89) — blind injection in the event get_events method Vector Authenticated attacker sends crafted input to the event listing → input built into SQL without neutralization → application behavior reveals true/false per condition → database contents reconstructed byte by byte

docs.title: Affected versions
docs.text: Frappe before 16.33.0. Fixed in 16.33.0.

docs.title: Root cause
docs.text:
The event listing method built user-supplied input straight into a SQL query without proper neutralization. Results were not returned directly — but the application's behavior differed for true versus false conditions, giving attackers a boolean oracle:

# Simplified vulnerable pattern
def get_events_vuln(filter_text):
    q = "SELECT * FROM events WHERE title LIKE '%%%s%%'" % filter_text
    return db.query(q)                       # BUG: input becomes SQL

# Simplified fixed pattern
def get_events_fixed(filter_text):
    q = "SELECT * FROM events WHERE title LIKE %s"
    return db.query(q, ("%" + filter_text + "%",))  # parameterized
Parameterized queries keep code and data strictly separate.

docs.title: Proof of concept (conceptual)
docs.text:
1. Attacker sends crafted conditions through the event filter (e.g. testing one character of a secret).
  2. The application behaves slightly differently for true versus false.
  3. Repeating the probe, the attacker reconstructs secrets byte by byte.
  4. Password hashes, tokens, and business data the DB user can read are exfiltrated.

The accompanying poc.py demonstrates the pattern safely: input must never become SQL: the demo contrasts string-built queries with parameterized ones. Offline, no server, no exploit.

docs.title: Mitigation
docs.text:
• Upgrade now: Frappe 16.33.0.
  • Hunt custom code for the same string-built-SQL pattern and parameterize it.
  • Rotate secrets the database user could read.

docs.title: CVE-2026-114716 — Roundcube: Mail Header Injection via Inline-Image Media Type
docs.text: Field Value Severity High — CVSS 8.5 (v3.1) Product Roundcube Webmail before 1.6.20 and 1.7.x before 1.7.5 — the open-source webmail client Type Mail header injection (CWE-99) — unvalidated media type from inline-image data URI Vector Authenticated remote attacker composes mail with an inline image whose data-URI media type hides CRLF sequences → extract_inline_images() pastes it into the outgoing MIME structure → arbitrary headers injected into mail sent from the victim's domain

docs.title: Affected versions
docs.text: Roundcube before 1.6.20 and 1.7.x before 1.7.5. Fixed in 1.6.20 and 1.7.5.

docs.title: Root cause
docs.text:
rcmail_sendmail::extract_inline_images() took the media type straight from an inline image's data URI and embedded it in the outgoing message — without validating it. Because a media type is attacker-controlled text, CRLF sequences inside it terminate the Content-Type line and begin brand-new MIME headers:

# Simplified vulnerable pattern
def build_part(data_uri):
    media_type = data_uri.split(";")[0]      # attacker-controlled
    return "Content-Type: %s\r\n" % media_type   # pasted raw!

# Simplified fixed pattern
def build_part_fixed(data_uri):
    media_type = data_uri.split(";")[0]
    if not is_mimetype_valid(media_type):     # strict allow-list
        raise ValueError("bad media type")
    return "Content-Type: %s\r\n" % media_type
Upstream fixed this by validating the media type with rcube_mime::is_mimetype_valid().

docs.title: Proof of concept (conceptual)
docs.text:
1. Attacker composes a message in Roundcube with an inline image.
  2. The image's data URI carries CRLF sequences inside its media type.
  3. Roundcube copies the media type verbatim into the outgoing MIME part.
  4. Each injected line break becomes an attacker-chosen header — spoofed attachments, hijacked Reply-To — in mail the victim's server sends.

The accompanying poc.py demonstrates the pattern safely: untrusted text must never be interpolated into structured output: the demo contrasts raw pasting with strict media-type validation. Offline, no server, no exploit.

docs.title: Mitigation
docs.text:
• Upgrade now: Roundcube 1.6.20 / 1.7.5.
  • Review recently sent mail for injected MIME headers and unexpected parts.
  • Treat unexpected MIME structure in outbound mail as hostile.

docs.title: CVE-2026-114720 — Roundcube: IMAP Command Injection via the Flag Parameter
docs.text: Field Value Severity High — CVSS 7.1 (v3.1) Product Roundcube Webmail before 1.6.20 and 1.7.x before 1.7.5 Type IMAP command injection (CWE-93) — CRLF in the _flag parameter of the mail/mark action Vector Authenticated remote attacker crafts the flag parameter with CRLF sequences → Roundcube forwards it to the IMAP server → injected commands execute inside the victim's IMAP session

docs.title: Affected versions
docs.text: Roundcube before 1.6.20 and 1.7.x before 1.7.5. Fixed in 1.6.20 and 1.7.5.

docs.title: Root cause
docs.text:
The mail/mark action forwarded its _flag parameter to the IMAP server without stripping control characters. IMAP is a line-based protocol, so CRLF sequences inside the flag terminate the intended command and begin another of the attacker's choosing — executed with the victim's mailbox privileges:

# Simplified vulnerable pattern
def mark_mail(flag):
    send_imap("STORE 1 +FLAGS (%s)" % flag)   # BUG: raw into protocol

# Simplified fixed pattern
def mark_mail_fixed(flag):
    if re.search(r"[\x00-\x20\x7f(){%*"\\\\]", flag):
        raise ValueError("bad flag")            # reject control/specials
    send_imap("STORE 1 +FLAGS (%s)" % flag)
Upstream now rejects flags containing control, whitespace, and IMAP-special characters.

docs.title: Proof of concept (conceptual)
docs.text:
1. Attacker crafts a flag value containing CRLF plus IMAP commands.
  2. Attacker triggers the mail/mark action with that flag.
  3. Roundcube forwards the tainted value down the victim's IMAP connection.
  4. The injected commands execute — reading folders, altering mailbox state — as the victim.

The accompanying poc.py demonstrates the pattern safely: values crossing into a line-based protocol must be sanitized: the demo contrasts raw forwarding with strict flag validation. Offline, no server, no exploit.

docs.title: Mitigation
docs.text:
• Upgrade now: Roundcube 1.6.20 / 1.7.5.
  • Apply least privilege to IMAP accounts used by webmail.
  • Review mail logs for unusual flag values.

docs.title: CVE-2026-114724 — Roundcube: Object Injection Primitive via Session Desync
docs.text: Field Value Severity High — CVSS 7.4 (v3.1) Product Roundcube Webmail before 1.6.20 and 1.7.x before 1.7.5 Type Deserialization of untrusted data (CWE-502) — object injection primitive in session unserialize via !-prefixed keys Vector Attacker influences stored session data with a key prefixed by ! → treated as valueless but still emitted → serialized stream desyncs → following bytes interpreted as a serialized PHP object

docs.title: Affected versions
docs.text: Roundcube before 1.6.20 and 1.7.x before 1.7.5. Fixed in 1.6.20 and 1.7.5.

docs.title: Root cause
docs.text:
rcube_session::unserialize() treated a session key prefixed with ! as having no value — but still emitted the key into the reconstructed serialized string. With a key but no corresponding value, the remainder of the input desynchronized: following session data was interpreted as a serialized value, yielding a PHP object injection primitive:

# Simplified vulnerable pattern
def unserialize_vuln(pairs):
    out = ""
    for k, v in pairs:
        if k.startswith("!"):
            out += serialize(k)          # BUG: key emitted, value dropped
        else:
            out += serialize(k) + serialize(v)
    return out                            # stream now misaligned

# Simplified fixed pattern
def unserialize_fixed(pairs):
    out = ""
    for k, v in pairs:
        if k.startswith("!"):
            continue                     # skip cleanly: no key, no shift
        out += serialize(k) + serialize(v)
    return out
One character of misalignment turns attacker bytes into live objects.

docs.title: Proof of concept (conceptual)
docs.text:
1. Attacker gets a !-prefixed key into stored session data.
  2. The session restore routine emits the key but drops its value.
  3. Every byte after that point shifts out of alignment.
  4. Trailing session bytes are reinterpreted as a serialized PHP object — an object injection primitive, one gadget chain away from code execution.

The accompanying poc.py demonstrates the pattern safely: deserializers must never trust the shape of their input: the demo contrasts the desyncing parser with one that skips cleanly. Offline, no server, no exploit.

docs.title: Mitigation
docs.text:
• Upgrade now: Roundcube 1.6.20 / 1.7.5.
  • Invalidate existing sessions after upgrading.
  • Audit everywhere session data can be influenced by users.

docs.title: CVE-2026-114727 — Roundcube: Unsafe ImageMagick Processing of Contact Photos
docs.text: Field Value Severity High — CVSS 8.3 (v3.1) Product Roundcube Webmail before 1.6.20 and 1.7.x before 1.7.5 Type Inclusion of functionality from untrusted control sphere (CWE-829) — SVG/EPS passed to ImageMagick on resize Vector Authenticated attacker uploads an SVG/EPS contact photo with external entities → Roundcube passes it to ImageMagick for resizing → delegates resolve external resources → server-side file reads / request forgery

docs.title: Affected versions
docs.text: Roundcube before 1.6.20 and 1.7.x before 1.7.5. Fixed in 1.6.20 and 1.7.5.

docs.title: Root cause
docs.text:
SVG and EPS were accepted as valid image types for contact photo upload and conversion. Both formats can reference external resources, and ImageMagick processes them through delegates — external helper programs. An uploaded "photo" therefore became a server-side fetch:

# Simplified vulnerable pattern
ALLOWED = {"png", "jpg", "gif", "svg", "eps"}   # BUG: svg/eps included
def resize_contact_photo(upload):
    assert upload.ext in ALLOWED
    return imagemagick_resize(upload)            # delegates + entities live

# Simplified fixed pattern
ALLOWED_FIXED = {"png", "jpg", "gif"}            # svg/eps removed
def resize_contact_photo_fixed(upload):
    assert upload.ext in ALLOWED_FIXED
    return sandboxed_resize(upload)
Upstream removed svg and eps from the accepted types.

docs.title: Proof of concept (conceptual)
docs.text:
1. Attacker uploads an SVG contact photo containing an external entity pointing at a sensitive file or internal URL.
  2. Roundcube accepts it and hands it to ImageMagick for resizing.
  3. ImageMagick resolves the entity — reading local files or reaching internal addresses from the server.
  4. Depending on installed delegates, this class of issue has historically escalated to remote code execution.

The accompanying poc.py demonstrates the pattern safely: powerful file processors must never see attacker formats unchecked: the demo contrasts the permissive allow-list with the hardened one. Offline, no server, no exploit.

docs.title: Mitigation
docs.text:
• Upgrade now: Roundcube 1.6.20 / 1.7.5.
  • Disable dangerous ImageMagick delegates server-wide (policy.xml).
  • Sandbox any image conversion that touches user uploads.

docs.title: CVE-2026-114730 — Roundcube: SSRF Filter Bypass via NAT64 Address Ranges
docs.text: Field Value Severity High — CVSS 7.2 (v3.1) Product Roundcube Webmail 1.6.14–1.6.19 and 1.7.0–1.7.4 Type Server-side request forgery (CWE-918) — SSRF filter bypass via NAT64 prefixes Vector Attacker supplies a URL with a NAT64-mapped address (e.g. http://[64:ff9b::7f00:1]/) → the is_local_url() blocklist omits 64:ff9b::/96, 64:ff9b:1::/48 and ::/128 → filter passes → server fetches loopback / link-local / cloud metadata

docs.title: Affected versions
docs.text: Roundcube 1.6.14 before 1.6.20 and 1.7.0 before 1.7.5. Fixed in 1.6.20 and 1.7.5.

docs.title: Root cause
docs.text:
The network blocklist used by the local-URL check omitted the RFC 6052 NAT64 prefix 64:ff9b::/96, the local-use NAT64 prefix 64:ff9b:1::/48, and the unspecified address ::/128. A URL encoding loopback inside one of those ranges passed the filter and reached loopback, link-local, and cloud metadata addresses:

# Simplified vulnerable pattern
BLOCKLIST = ["127.0.0.0/8", "::1/128", "169.254.0.0/16"]  # NAT64 missing!
def is_local_url_vuln(url):
    return any(ip_in(url.host, net) for net in BLOCKLIST)

# Simplified fixed pattern
BLOCKLIST_FIXED = BLOCKLIST + ["64:ff9b::/96", "64:ff9b:1::/48", "::/128"]
def is_local_url_fixed(url):
    return any(ip_in(url.host, net) for net in BLOCKLIST_FIXED)
A blocklist only protects what it enumerates.

docs.title: Proof of concept (conceptual)
docs.text:
1. Attacker crafts a URL with a NAT64-mapped loopback address.
  2. The incomplete blocklist finds no match and approves the URL.
  3. Roundcube's server fetches it — reaching its own loopback or link-local services.
  4. Cloud metadata endpoints answer, potentially leaking instance credentials.

The accompanying poc.py demonstrates the pattern safely: blocklists fail on the ranges they forget: the demo contrasts the gapped list with the completed one. Offline, no server, no exploit.

docs.title: Mitigation
docs.text:
• Upgrade now: Roundcube 1.6.20 / 1.7.5.
  • Add egress firewall rules so the webmail host cannot reach metadata or internal ranges at all.
  • Enable cloud metadata protection (IMDSv2 / disabled where unused).

docs.title: CVE-2026-114820 — Oracle Java SE / GraalVM JSSE Vulnerability
docs.text:
Educational only. This writeup explains the vulnerability pattern for defensive learning. Test only in controlled environments you own.

Field Value Severity CRITICAL 9.1 (CVSS 3.1) Product Oracle Java SE, Oracle GraalVM for JDK, Oracle GraalVM Enterprise Edition (JSSE component) Type Use of a broken or risky cryptographic algorithm (CWE-327) Vector Network: unauthenticated attacker via multiple protocols Fixed in October 2026 Critical Patch Update

docs.title: Root cause
docs.text: A weakness in JSSE, Java's secure socket extension, allows an unauthenticated attacker with network access to compromise the deployment through APIs in the component (for example via a web service that supplies data to those APIs). Successful attacks can create, delete or modify critical data and gain unauthorized access to all accessible data of the Java deployment.

docs.title: Proof of concept
docs.text: Conceptual illustration: poc.py models an application passing network-supplied data straight into a security-sensitive API (vulnerable) versus validating the data and running a patched runtime before trusting it (fixed). No real cryptographic code is involved.

docs.title: Mitigation
docs.text:
• Apply Oracle's October 2026 Critical Patch Update to every Java and GraalVM installation (runtimes 8, 11, 17, 21, 25, 27 and GraalVM editions).
  • Limit network exposure of Java services and audit services that feed external data into JSSE APIs.

docs.title: CVE-2026-115188 — Mautic 7: Unrestricted File Upload in Campaign Import
docs.text: Field Value Severity Critical — CVSS 9.9 (v3.1) Product Mautic 7 — open-source marketing automation, campaign import feature Type Code injection (CWE-94) / Unrestricted upload of dangerous file type (CWE-434) Vector An authenticated user with permission to create campaign imports uploads a campaign archive through the UI or the API (/api/campaigns/import). The application copies bundled asset files into a publicly accessible media directory without restricting file names or types. On web servers that honor per-directory configuration, such as the default Apache setup of the official Mautic Docker image, a planted server-side script executes with the privileges of the web server user. Administrator privileges are not required.

docs.title: Affected versions
docs.text: Mautic 7 releases prior to the security fix. Update to the latest patched Mautic 7 release.

docs.title: Root cause
docs.text: The campaign import handler treats an uploaded archive as trusted content: it extracts and copies the bundled files into the public media folder without validating file names or extensions, and without keeping executable content out of the web root. Two missing controls combine into remote code execution: no upload validation, and a destination directory the web server both serves and executes.

docs.title: Proof of concept (conceptual)
docs.text:
1. Attacker with campaign-import permission builds a campaign archive containing a server-side script file.
  2. Attacker imports it via the UI or /api/campaigns/import.
  3. Mautic copies the script into the public media directory, unchanged.
  4. Attacker visits the script's public URL; the web server executes it.

The accompanying poc.py demonstrates the pattern safely: an import handler that copies any file name (vulnerable) versus one that enforces an extension allowlist and stores uploads outside the web root (fixed). Offline, no server, no exploit.

docs.title: Mitigation
docs.text:
• Upgrade now: latest patched Mautic 7 release.
  • Limit campaign import permission to trusted staff only.
  • Block script execution in media directories at the web server level.
  • Audit uploaded media for unexpected files, especially scripts.

docs.title: CVE-2026-115214
docs.text: Field Detail Severity CRITICAL 9.8 Product Datawiza Proxy Auth Plugin (WordPress) Type Improper Privilege Management (CWE-269) Vector CVSS:3.1/AV:N/AC:L/PR:N/UI:N/S:U/C:H/I:H/A:H

docs.title: Affected versions
docs.text: Datawiza Proxy Auth Plugin before 1.1.1

docs.title: Root cause
docs.text: The plugin trusts user-identity and role information carried in HTTP request headers, without verifying that those headers were actually set by the trusted reverse proxy. Any client that can reach WordPress directly can present arbitrary headers.

docs.title: Proof of concept
docs.text:
Educational only. This section illustrates the vulnerable pattern versus the fixed pattern in simplified form, for learning and defense. It is not a working exploit, and it must only ever be tested in controlled environments you own.

The educational demo below shows the pattern only: a request handler that accepts identity headers at face value (vulnerable) versus one that accepts them solely from a configured trusted proxy address (fixed). No real credentials, tokens, or target hosts are used; everything runs against local dummy values.

See poc.py in this folder for the runnable illustration using dummy values only.

docs.title: Mitigation
docs.text: Update the plugin to 1.1.1 or later. Restrict network access so only the trusted reverse proxy can reach WordPress, have the proxy strip incoming identity headers from clients, and audit administrator accounts for unexpected entries.

docs.title: CVE-2026-115324 — mem0: Your Own Memories Became the SQL Injection
docs.text: Field Value Severity Critical — CVSS 9.2 (v3.1) Product mem0 — the open-source AI memory framework (memories, conversation context, agents) Type SQL injection (CWE-89) — stored memory text, metadata, and message names interpolated unescaped into insert() / update() queries in the Databricks vector store Vector An attacker influences text stored as a memory (crafted message, poisoned metadata) → mem0's Databricks vector store builds the SQL by string interpolation, escaping nothing → injected SQL executes on the configured Databricks SQL warehouse → attacker reads, alters, or deletes memories and warehouse data

docs.title: Affected versions
docs.text: mem0 0.1.117 up to (not including) 1.0.8. Fixed in 1.0.8 (commit a2ffca3, PR 4558).

docs.title: Root cause
docs.text:
In mem0/vector_stores/databricks.py, the insert() and update() operations assembled SQL by interpolating memory content directly into the query string. Memory text, metadata, and even message names — all attacker-influenceable — reached the database unescaped, so any quotes or keywords in a memory rewrote the command:

# Simplified vulnerable pattern
def insert(memory_text):
    query = f"INSERT INTO memories (content) VALUES ('{memory_text}')"  # BUG
    warehouse.execute(query)   # attacker text is now SQL syntax

# Simplified fixed pattern
def insert_fixed(memory_text):
    warehouse.execute(
        "INSERT INTO memories (content) VALUES (?)", (memory_text,)
    )   # value stays data, never becomes code

Because mem0's job is to store whatever the conversation contains, the injection vector is your own trusted memory pipeline — the most dangerous kind of second-order injection.

docs.title: Proof of concept (conceptual)
docs.text:
1. Attacker feeds crafted text to an AI app that uses mem0 — the text is saved as a memory.
  2. The Databricks vector store's insert()/update() interpolates that memory into a SQL string, unescaped.
  3. Hidden quotes/keywords in the memory bend the query; injected SQL runs on the Databricks warehouse.
  4. Attacker reads other users' memories, modifies or deletes stored data, and pivots inside the warehouse.

The accompanying poc.py demonstrates the pattern safely on a local SQLite database: the same memory text inserted via string interpolation (injection fires) versus a parameterized query (injection inert). Offline, no network, no Databricks, no exploit.

docs.title: Mitigation
docs.text:
• Upgrade now: mem0 1.0.8 or later.
  • Audit stored memories for tampering: unexpected entries, altered metadata, missing records.
  • Rotate Databricks warehouse credentials and check query history for anomalous statements during the exposure window.
  • Restore corrupted data from clean backups and monitor warehouse queries going forward.

docs.title: CVE-2026-115325 — Netmaker external-client authorization bypass
docs.text: Severity Product Type Vector HIGH 8.7 Netmaker through 1.7.0 Authorization bypass / broken object-level authorization (CWE-639) Network

docs.title: Affected versions
docs.text: Netmaker through 1.7.0. Fixed by upstream commit 332d8b9 (PR 4153); upgrade past 1.7.0.

docs.title: Root cause
docs.text: The updateExtClient handler (reachable via PUT /api/extclients/{network}/{clientid}) checks the caller's network-scoped role but never verifies that the targeted external client actually belongs to that network. A user scoped to network A can therefore modify external clients on network B: swap public keys, disable legitimate clients, and read WireGuard private keys from the API.

docs.title: Proof of concept (conceptual, educational only)
docs.text:
Educational purposes only. This demonstrates the authorization logic flaw — it performs no real network calls.

# scope_check_demo.py — the check Netmaker SHOULD have done
def update_ext_client(caller_network: str, target: dict, updates: dict) -> dict:
    """
    Conceptual authorization: the resource must belong to the caller's network.
    Vulnerable behavior allowed caller_network != target["network"].
    """
    if target.get("network") != caller_network:
        raise PermissionError(
            f"Denied: client belongs to network "
            f"{target.get('network')}, caller is scoped to {caller_network}"
        )
    target.update(updates)
    return target

client_b = {"network": "net-b", "clientid": "ext-01", "publickey": "aaa..."}
try:
    # attacker scoped to net-a tries to touch a net-b client
    update_ext_client("net-a", client_b, {"publickey": "attacker-key"})
except PermissionError as e:
    print(e)  # fixed behavior: denied

docs.title: Mitigation
docs.text:
• Upgrade Netmaker past 1.7.0 (fix: commit 332d8b9).
  • Rotate all WireGuard key pairs on affected networks.
  • Audit external clients for swapped public keys or unexplained disabled nodes.
  • Restrict who can manage external clients until every node is patched.
  • As a rule: enforce per-object authorization — always verify the resource belongs to the caller's scope.

docs.title: CVE-2026-115330 — Lotus SQL injection via stacked custom-metric queries
docs.text: Severity Product Type Vector HIGH 8.8 Lotus (open-source pricing/billing) SQL injection (CWE-89) Network (authenticated)

docs.title: Affected versions
docs.text: Lotus through 0.10.2 (custom billable metrics, POST /app/metrics/).

docs.title: Root cause
docs.text: Custom billable-metric queries are validated as "first statement only", but the backend executes the full submitted string. An authenticated organization user can append stacked, semicolon-separated SQL after the metric query, and the extra statements run against the shared multi-tenant database — reading or modifying usage, subscription, and billing data belonging to every tenant, not just the attacker's own organization.

docs.title: Proof of concept (conceptual, educational only)
docs.text:
Educational purposes only. Demonstrates why stacked statements are dangerous on a local database — no Lotus instance, no real data.

# stacked_query_demo.py — first-statement-only validation is not a boundary
import sqlite3

db = sqlite3.connect(":memory:")
db.execute("CREATE TABLE metrics (org TEXT, usage REAL)")
db.execute("INSERT INTO metrics VALUES ('acme', 42.0)")

def naive_validate(query: str) -> bool:
    # What the app effectively checked: only the first statement looks safe
    first = query.split(";")[0].strip().upper()
    return first.startswith("SELECT")

attacker = "SELECT usage FROM metrics; DROP TABLE metrics; --"
print("passes validation:", naive_validate(attacker))  # True — and that's the bug
print("fix: disable multi-statements at the driver level,")
print("     run queries through an allow-listed builder,")
print("     and scope every query to the caller's tenant.")

docs.title: Mitigation
docs.text:
• Upgrade Lotus past 0.10.2.
  • Disable multi-statement execution in the database driver.
  • Scope every metric query to the authenticated tenant (row-level enforcement).
  • Audit billing/usage data across tenants for tampering.
  • Prefer allow-listed query builders over raw SQL strings.

docs.text: Lotus through 0.10.2 (billable-metric property_name / categorical filters).

docs.title: Root cause
docs.text: Billable-metric counter, gauge, and rate queries are generated from Jinja templates into which the metric's property_name and categorical filter values are rendered unescaped. An authenticated organization user can embed SQL in those values; the rendered text becomes part of the executed query against the shared multi-tenant database, exposing or altering billing data across all tenants.

docs.title: Proof of concept (conceptual, educational only)
docs.text:
Educational purposes only. Shows the Jinja-interpolation hazard on a local string — no Lotus instance, no real database.

# jinja_sqli_demo.py — unescaped template values become SQL
from string import Template  # stdlib stand-in for the idea; Jinja behaves the same

def build_query_vulnerable(property_name: str) -> str:
    tpl = Template("SELECT SUM($prop) FROM usage_events")
    return tpl.substitute(prop=property_name)  # no escaping — the bug

def build_query_fixed(property_name: str, allowed: set) -> str:
    if property_name not in allowed:            # allow-list identifiers
        raise ValueError("unknown metric property")
    return f"SELECT SUM({property_name}) FROM usage_events"

attacker = "usage) FROM usage_events; -- "
print("vulnerable:", build_query_vulnerable(attacker))
try:
    build_query_fixed(attacker, {"usage", "events"})
except ValueError as e:
    print("fixed: blocked ->", e)
print("fixed:", build_query_fixed("usage", {"usage", "events"}))

docs.title: Mitigation
docs.text:
• Upgrade Lotus past 0.10.2.
  • Never render user input into SQL templates — validate identifiers against an allow-list.
  • Scope every metric query to the authenticated tenant.
  • Audit billing/usage data across tenants for tampering.
  • Use parameterized queries; keep identifiers and values strictly separated.

docs.title: CVE-2026-115332 — Lotus SQL injection via subscription filter keys
docs.text: Severity Product Type Vector HIGH 8.8 Lotus (open-source pricing/billing) SQL injection (CWE-89) Network (authenticated)

docs.title: Affected versions
docs.text: Lotus through 0.10.2 (subscription filter_keys).

docs.title: Root cause
docs.text: Subscription filter keys pass a keyword-only validation step that checks the key's shape but not its safety. The key is then rendered as an unquoted GROUP BY identifier in usage-aggregation queries. An authenticated organization user can register a subscription with a malicious filter key whose text breaks out of the identifier position and injects SQL — executed against the shared multi-tenant database, leaking or modifying every tenant's billing data.

docs.title: Proof of concept (conceptual, educational only)
docs.text:
Educational purposes only. Demonstrates the unquoted-identifier hazard on a local string — no Lotus instance, no real database.

# identifier_sqli_demo.py — keyword-only validation misses identifier breakout
import re

KEYWORD_OK = re.compile(r"^[a-zA-Z_][a-zA-Z0-9_.\"]*$")  # flawed check

def build_vulnerable(filter_key: str) -> str:
    assert KEYWORD_OK.match(filter_key), "keyword validation"  # passes...
    return f"SELECT org, SUM(usage) FROM events GROUP BY {filter_key}"  # ...but unquoted

def build_fixed(filter_key: str, allowed: set) -> str:
    if filter_key not in allowed:
        raise ValueError("unknown filter key")
    return f'SELECT org, SUM(usage) FROM events GROUP BY "{filter_key}"'

attacker = 'org", (SELECT 1) -- '
print("vulnerable:", build_vulnerable(attacker))
try:
    build_fixed(attacker, {"org", "plan"})
except ValueError as e:
    print("fixed: blocked ->", e)
print("fixed:", build_fixed("org", {"org", "plan"}))

docs.title: Mitigation
docs.text:
• Upgrade Lotus past 0.10.2.
  • Quote and allow-list every dynamic identifier; never interpolate raw keys.
  • Scope aggregation queries to the authenticated tenant.
  • Audit billing/usage data across tenants for tampering.

docs.title: CVE-2026-115346 — Avada theme arbitrary file upload leads to remote code execution
docs.text: Field Detail Severity HIGH 8.1 Product Avada theme for WordPress up to 7.16.2 Type CWE-434 (Unrestricted Upload of File with Dangerous Type) Vector Unauthenticated, network

docs.title: Affected versions
docs.text: • Avada up to and including 7.16.2 (fixed in 7.16.4)

docs.title: Root cause
docs.text: The theme's palette-image conversion function did not sufficiently validate file types before processing uploads. An unauthenticated attacker could upload files that may be executable, turning an image upload into remote code execution on the WordPress host.

docs.title: Proof of concept
docs.text:
Conceptually: an upload endpoint should accept only verified image content and store it non-executable. Here, weak validation let a disguised executable file through, and the server ran it.

See poc.py in this folder for a safe, educational demonstration. It does not exploit the vulnerability.

docs.title: Mitigation
docs.text:
• Update Avada to 7.16.4 or later immediately.
  • Scan the uploads directory for unexpected executable files and remove them.
  • Review administrator accounts and treat sites on 7.16.2 or older as potentially compromised.

docs.title: CVE-2026-115375 — Incus Path Traversal via Instance Backup (Host File Write)
docs.text:
Educational only. This writeup explains the vulnerability pattern for defensive learning. Test only in controlled environments you own.

Field Value Severity CRITICAL 9.9 (CVSS 3.1) Product Incus (container & VM manager) Type Path traversal (CWE-22) Vector Local/network: import a crafted instance backup Fixed in 7.0.2 / 7.5.0

docs.title: Affected versions
docs.text: Incus 7.0.0 before 7.0.2 and 7.1.0 before 7.5.0.

docs.title: Root cause
docs.text: Dependent custom volume names inside an instance backup's index.yaml were used without validation. A crafted backup with ../ sequences in volume names makes the daemon create root-owned directories with attacker-controlled content anywhere on the host filesystem.

docs.title: Proof of concept
docs.text: Conceptual illustration: poc.py shows a volume name containing ../ being used raw (vulnerable) versus canonicalized and confined to the storage pool (fixed).

docs.title: Mitigation
docs.text:
• Upgrade to 7.0.2 (7.0 line) or 7.5.0.
  • Only import backups from trusted sources; audit hosts for unexpected root-owned directories.
  • See also CVE-2026-115377 (migration symlink file write) — same release.

docs.title: CVE-2026-115377 — Incus Arbitrary File Write via Malicious Migration Source
docs.text:
Educational only. This writeup explains the vulnerability pattern for defensive learning. Test only in controlled environments you own.

Field Value Severity CRITICAL 9.9 (CVSS 3.1) Product Incus (container & VM manager, LXD successor) Type Arbitrary file write / symlink attack (CWE-59) Vector Network: malicious migration source Fixed in 6.0.7 / 7.0.2 / 7.5.0

docs.title: Affected versions
docs.text: Incus before 6.0.7, 6.1.0 before 7.0.2, and 7.1.0 before 7.5.0.

docs.title: Root cause
docs.text: During instance migration, the receiving daemon applied rsync/btrfs-receive streams without constraining symlinks to the transferred volume. An attacker-controlled stream can plant a symlink like rootfs -> / so subsequent file writes land on the host filesystem — executed as root.

docs.title: Proof of concept
docs.text: Conceptual illustration: poc.py shows a symlink resolved against the host root during extraction (vulnerable) versus resolving it inside the target volume (fixed).

docs.title: Mitigation
docs.text:
• Upgrade to 6.0.7, 7.0.2 (7.0 line), or 7.5.0.
  • Only accept migrations from trusted sources; scan hosts for unexpected root-owned files.
  • See also CVE-2026-115375 (path traversal in backup restore) — same release, same root-cause family.

docs.title: CVE-2026-115384 — Wasmtime Stack Buffer Overflow (Sandbox Escape)
docs.text:
Educational only. This writeup explains the vulnerability pattern for defensive learning. Test only in controlled environments you own.

Field Value Severity CRITICAL 9.9 (CVSS 3.1) Product Wasmtime (Bytecode Alliance WebAssembly runtime) Type Stack buffer overflow (CWE-20 Improper Input Validation) Vector Network-adjacent / local: run a malicious guest component Fixed in 48.0.4 / 49.0.2

docs.title: Affected versions
docs.text: Wasmtime 39.0.0 before 48.0.4, and 49.0.0 before 49.0.2.

docs.title: Root cause
docs.text: When the component-model async callback fires, the runtime copies the guest-supplied result into a fixed-size native stack buffer without validating the declared result type. A guest can declare a mistyped callback so the copy is far larger (~16KB) than the buffer, overwriting the stack frame including the return address.

docs.title: Proof of concept
docs.text: Conceptual illustration of the pattern: poc.py shows a fixed stack buffer receiving a caller-controlled size, contrasted with a version that validates the declared type/size before copying.

docs.title: Mitigation
docs.text:
• Upgrade Wasmtime to 48.0.4 or 49.0.2.
  • Audit every workload that executes guest-supplied components (edge functions, plugins, multi-tenant workers) and redeploy on patched runtimes.
  • Monitor host logs for unexpected guest crashes or trap anomalies.

docs.title: AWS MCP Server: Another App's Token Runs Your Cloud
docs.text:
Educational material only. Do not use against systems you do not own or have explicit permission to test.

Field Value CVE CVE-2026-115413 Severity High - CVSS 7.8 Product AWS API MCP Server (awslabs.aws-api-mcp-server, AI agent tool) Type Missing token audience validation (CWE-346, origin validation error) Vector In OAuth authentication mode, the server accepts access tokens without validating the expected audience or client ID. A local user holding an access token issued to a different application by the same identity provider can present it to the MCP server and run AWS operations using the server's configured AWS credentials.

docs.title: Affected versions
docs.text: AWS API MCP Server before 1.6.0. Update to 1.6.0 and configure the expected token audience or client ID.

docs.title: Root cause
docs.text:
A token proves two things: that an identity provider issued it, and who it was issued for. Checking only the first is half a check:

# Simplified vulnerable pattern
def authenticate(token):
    if token.issued_by_trusted_provider:  # BUG: audience never checked
        return grant_server_credentials()

# Simplified fixed pattern
def authenticate_fixed(token, expected_audience):
    if token.issued_by_trusted_provider and token.audience == expected_audience:
        return grant_server_credentials()
    return deny("wrong audience")
Tokens are scoped to an audience for exactly this reason: one application's login must not unlock another application's power.

docs.title: Proof of concept
docs.text:
Educational, conceptual demo only - it models the vulnerable pattern with synthetic, offline objects. It is not a working exploit and cannot be aimed at real systems.

  1. Local user obtains an access token issued to a different application by the same identity provider.
  2. The user presents that token to the MCP server in OAuth mode.
  3. The server verifies the issuer but never the audience, and accepts the token.
  4. The user runs AWS operations with the server's configured credentials.

The demo in poc.py shows that verifying a token's issuer is not enough: the audience must match the application it was issued for

docs.title: Mitigation
docs.text:
• Update now: AWS API MCP Server to 1.6.0.
  • Configure the expected token audience or client ID for the server.
  • Review recent AWS actions for operations you did not expect.
  • Rotate the server's AWS credentials and limit the server role to least privilege.

docs.title: CVE-2026-115417 — aws-c-mqtt: Excessive Allocation in MQTT 3.1.1 Adapter (Remote DoS)
docs.text: Field Value Severity High — CVSS 7.5 (v3.x) / 8.2 (CVSS 4.0) Product AWS aws-c-mqtt — the C MQTT client library behind the AWS IoT Device SDKs Type Uncontrolled memory allocation (CWE-789) in the MQTT 3.1.1 compatibility adapter Vector Remote actor supplies a value with an excessive size → the compatibility adapter allocates memory using that unchecked size → the client application crashes → denial of service

docs.title: Affected versions
docs.text: aws-c-mqtt before 0.16.2. Fixed in 0.16.2 and later, including the AWS Common Runtime and AWS IoT Device SDK releases that bundle it.

docs.title: Root cause
docs.text:
The MQTT 3.1.1 compatibility adapter lets a remote-supplied value decide how much memory to allocate, with no sanity ceiling. One absurd number in one field is enough: the adapter attempts the impossible allocation and the client application dies. Memory budgets must be set by the program, never by the peer — one unchecked size field should be rejected in a single comparison, long before any allocation is attempted.

# Simplified vulnerable pattern
def handle_packet(size_field):
    buf = allocate(size_field)   # remote value sets the budget — no ceiling

# Simplified fixed pattern
MAX_PACKET = 256 * 1024 * 1024
def handle_packet_fixed(size_field):
    if size_field > MAX_PACKET:
        raise ValueError("absurd size rejected before allocation")
    buf = allocate(size_field)

docs.title: Proof of concept (conceptual)
docs.text:
1. A remote actor reaches the MQTT client with a crafted value carrying an excessive size.
  2. The 3.1.1 compatibility adapter reads the size with no upper bound.
  3. The allocation is attempted against an impossible number.
  4. The client application crashes — for one laptop an annoyance, for an IoT fleet an outage.

The accompanying poc.py demonstrates the pattern safely: trusting vs. capping a remote size value, offline, with synthetic numbers. No MQTT, no network, no exploit.

docs.title: Mitigation
docs.text:
• Upgrade aws-c-mqtt to 0.16.2 or later.
  • Update the bundles: AWS Common Runtime and AWS IoT Device SDK releases that ship this library — most devices get the fix that way.
  • Watch your fleet for unexplained client restarts, which may be this bug being probed.
  • Never let peer-supplied values size your allocations anywhere in your own code.

docs.title: CVE-2026-115419 — Strands Agents SDK: Cross-Tenant Conversation Leak and Prompt Planting
docs.text: Field Value Severity High — CVSS 8.1 (v3.x) / 8.6 (CVSS 4.0) Product Amazon Strands Agents SDK — agent-to-agent (A2A) server component Type Missing authorization / cross-tenant state isolation failure — one caller can read and write another tenant's conversation state Vector Authenticated remote user sends plain HTTP requests to the A2A endpoint carrying a different context_id → the server returns other tenants' conversation history → the attacker plants persistent instructions in the shared state that alter model behavior for every subsequent caller

docs.title: Affected versions
docs.text:
• Python strands-agents before 1.43.0 (fixed in 1.43.0)
  • TypeScript @strands-agents/sdk before 1.5.0 (fixed in 1.5.0)

docs.title: Root cause
docs.text:
The A2A server treats the context_id as a label rather than a boundary: it never verifies that the caller actually owns the conversation they are requesting. Conversation state is effectively shared across tenants, so a request with someone else's identifier is served without question. Reads leak private chat history; writes plant instructions that persist in the shared state and steer the model's answers for innocent tenants who arrive later. Multi-tenant systems live or die on the ownership check — skipping it makes every tenant's data every tenant's data.

# Simplified vulnerable pattern
def get_history(context_id):
    return conversations[context_id]          # no ownership check

# Simplified fixed pattern
def get_history_fixed(context_id, caller):
    if not owns(caller, context_id):
        raise PermissionDenied("not your conversation")
    return conversations[context_id]

docs.title: Proof of concept (conceptual)
docs.text:
1. Attacker authenticates as an ordinary tenant of a Strands-powered agent service.
  2. They send HTTP requests to the A2A endpoint, swapping in another tenant's context_id.
  3. The server returns that tenant's conversation history — confidentiality broken.
  4. The attacker writes persistent instructions into the shared conversation state.
  5. Later callers receive model answers steered by the attacker's planted instructions — integrity broken.

The accompanying poc.py demonstrates the pattern safely: an in-memory multi-tenant session store with and without an ownership check, using synthetic data. No network, no SDK, no real tenants.

docs.title: Mitigation
docs.text:
• Upgrade: Python SDK to 1.43.0, TypeScript SDK to 1.5.0.
  • Enforce session boundaries at your own layer too — never rely on a single check.
  • Scrub any instructions in shared state that you did not write.
  • Audit recent conversation access for cross-tenant context_id usage.
  • Treat any multi-tenant AI deployment as compromised-by-design until isolation is verified.

docs.title: CVE-2026-115497 — Music Store: Directory Traversal Reads Any Server File
docs.text: Field Value Severity High — CVSS 7.5 (v3.1) Product Music Store – WordPress eCommerce plugin, up to and including 1.4.7 (ms-download.php) Type Directory traversal / path traversal (CWE-22) Vector Unauthenticated attacker obtains a valid purchase_id token with a single low-cost purchase (or a shared download link) → requests a download with the 'f' parameter set to ../../ sequences → ms-download.php resolves it as a filesystem path without neutralizing traversal → arbitrary file contents read from the server (wp-config.php, secrets)

docs.title: Affected versions
docs.text: Music Store – WordPress eCommerce plugin versions up to and including 1.4.7. Fixed in 1.4.8.

docs.title: Root cause
docs.text:
The download handler took the f request parameter and resolved it as a file path — without stripping ../ sequences. Anyone holding a valid purchase token (one cheap purchase, or a shared link) could walk the path up out of the download directory:

# Simplified vulnerable pattern
path = os.path.join(DOWNLOAD_DIR, request.params["f"])  # BUG: "../../" escapes

# Simplified fixed pattern
real = os.path.realpath(os.path.join(DOWNLOAD_DIR, request.params["f"]))
if not real.startswith(os.path.realpath(DOWNLOAD_DIR) + os.sep):
    return deny("invalid file")
User-supplied file names must always be canonicalized and pinned inside the intended directory — never trusted as raw path fragments.

docs.title: Proof of concept (conceptual)
docs.text:
1. Attacker makes one low-cost purchase (or receives a shared download link) to get a valid purchase_id token.
  2. Attacker requests a download with the f parameter set to a traversal path (e.g. ../../../../wp-config.php).
  3. ms-download.php joins it into a filesystem path without neutralizing the traversal.
  4. The server returns the contents of the arbitrary file — database credentials, secret keys.

The accompanying poc.py demonstrates the pattern safely: file paths from user input must be canonicalized and contained: the demo contrasts joining a raw parameter with a realpath prefix check. Offline, no server, no exploit.

docs.title: Mitigation
docs.text:
• Update now: Music Store 1.4.8.
  • Canonicalize and pin every user-supplied file path inside the intended directory (realpath + prefix check).
  • Rotate database credentials and salts if exposure is possible.
  • Prefer opaque file IDs over raw paths in download parameters.
