docs.title: CVE-2026-116006 — ruoyi-vue-pro: The SMS Code Is Always 9999, So Anyone Can Log In As Admin
docs.text: Field Value Severity High — CVSS 7.3 (NVD); the reporting researcher scores it 9.1 Critical on confidentiality/integrity impact Product YunaiV/ruoyi-vue-pro (Yudao) — up to 2026.09 Type Improper Authentication (CWE-287); also reported as hard-coded/predictable credential (CWE-798) and insecure default initialization (CWE-1188) Vector Unauthenticated, network → SMS login with a constant code → full account takeover

docs.title: Affected versions
docs.text:
• ruoyi-vue-pro up to 2026.09, branches master, master-jdk17, and master-jdk25. Verified on master-jdk17 and re-verified against upstream on 2026-10-21.
  • No fix is available as of 2026-10-21. The vendor was contacted early about this disclosure but did not respond. A public proof of concept exists.

docs.title: Root cause
docs.text:
The shipped base configuration pins the SMS verification-code range to a single value, left that way for testing convenience:

# yudao-server/src/main/resources/application.yaml
sms-code:
  begin-code: 9999  # testing convenience
  end-code: 9999    # testing convenience

The code generator draws an integer from [begin-code, end-code) and formats it as four digits — so with both ends at 9999, every code the system can ever produce is 9999. Worse, this block lives in the base configuration, not a test profile, and no shipped profile overrides it, so any deployment keeps it unless the operator explicitly changes both keys. The SMS-login endpoint is open to anonymous requests by design, and the login path (scene=21) has no CAPTCHA hook at all. The built-in admin account's phone number is published in the shipped SQL seed data.

docs.title: Proof of concept (conceptual)
docs.text:
The attack chain:

  1. The attacker, with no login and no CAPTCHA, asks the server for a login code for a victim's phone number (POST /admin-api/system/auth/send-sms-code, scene=21).
  2. The attacker logs in with the code 9999 — the only code the system can produce (POST /admin-api/system/auth/sms-login).
  3. The server returns a full access token for that account, including the built-in super administrator: control over users, roles, permissions, tenant data, and file storage. No password, no CAPTCHA, and no real text message are ever needed.

The accompanying poc.py demonstrates the pattern safely: a code generator with a pinned range versus one drawing from a wide random range, plus a login check, driven by synthetic offline data. Fully offline — no exploit, no network calls.

docs.title: Mitigation
docs.text:
• Set a wide random code range (for example 100000–999999) in the base configuration — never ship a constant verification code as a default.
  • Keep any test-only override in a test-only profile that production cannot load by accident.
  • Refuse to start (or log a loud warning) when begin-code == end-code outside a test profile.
  • Add a CAPTCHA / risk-control hook to the SMS-login path (scene=21 currently has none).
  • Disable SMS login for privileged accounts such as admin, or require an explicit confirmation for SMS login of admin accounts.
  • Force all sessions to re-login and audit recent logins for accounts you do not recognize — assume tokens may already have been issued.

docs.title: CVE-2026-116117 — Halo CMS: Path Traversal in the Theme View Resolver
docs.text: Field Value Severity High — CVSS 7.3 Product Halo CMS (open source, Java/Spring Boot) — up to 2.27.0-beta.1 Type Path traversal (CWE-22) Vector Remote, low complexity — a crafted template value in a page request escapes the theme directory and reaches files elsewhere on the server; exploit published

docs.title: Affected versions
docs.text: • Halo up to 2.27.0-beta.1. No fixed release was listed in the NVD record at the time of writing (record status: Deferred, October 26, 2026) — move off the beta and watch for the Halo security fix.

docs.title: Root cause
docs.text:
Halo's theme view resolver turns a template name into a file path so it can render the page, but it never verifies that the resolved path stays inside the theme folder. A template value containing directory-climbing segments is joined to the theme directory as-is, and the resulting path walks out of the theme directory. The resolver treats a file path as if it were harmless text — and a path in disguise obeys no folder boundary.

# Simplified vulnerable pattern
view_path = theme_dir + template_name   # template_name is attacker-controlled
open(view_path)                          # ".." segments walk out of theme_dir

# Simplified fixed pattern
candidate = resolve(theme_dir, template_name)
assert candidate.is_inside(theme_dir)    # reject anything that escapes
allowlist(template_name)                 # only known theme templates resolve

docs.title: Proof of concept (conceptual)
docs.text:
1. The attacker requests a page with a crafted template value containing directory-climbing segments.
  2. The theme view resolver builds a path from that value without a containment check.
  3. The resolved path lands outside the theme folder, and the server opens a file the theme was never meant to expose.

The accompanying poc.py demonstrates the pattern safely: a vulnerable resolver versus a fixed resolver, against purely synthetic offline directories created by the script itself. Fully offline, synthetic data — no exploit, no network, no system changes.

docs.title: Mitigation
docs.text:
• Move off 2.27.0-beta.1 in production: do not run the vulnerable beta publicly; upgrade to a fixed Halo release as soon as one ships.
  • Allowlist template names: only resolve template names your themes actually ship — reject anything else outright.
  • Canonicalize and verify: resolve the final path and confirm it stays inside the theme directory before opening it; never trust a string-prefix check alone.
  • Hunt: audit theme and access logs for template values containing .. or path separators.

docs.title: CVE-2026-116149
docs.text: Field Detail Severity HIGH 8.1 Product ImageMagick Type Stack-based Buffer Overflow (CWE-121) Vector CVSS:3.1/AV:N/AC:L/PR:L/UI:N/S:U/C:N/I:H/A:H

docs.title: Affected versions
docs.text: ImageMagick before 6.9.13-58 and 7.x before 7.1.2-33

docs.title: Root cause
docs.text: The bzip2-compressed image decoder copies decompressed data into a fixed-size stack buffer without validating that the data fits. A crafted image supplies more data than the buffer holds, overwriting adjacent stack memory and crashing the process or corrupting memory.

docs.title: Proof of concept
docs.text:
Educational only. This section illustrates the vulnerable pattern versus the fixed pattern in simplified form, for learning and defense. It is not a working exploit, and it must only ever be tested in controlled environments you own.

The demo below contrasts an unchecked fixed-buffer copy (vulnerable pattern) with a copy that refuses data larger than the buffer (fixed pattern), using only local dummy byte strings. It decodes nothing real and targets no system.

See poc.py in this folder for the runnable illustration using dummy values only.

docs.title: Mitigation
docs.text: Update ImageMagick to 6.9.13-58 or 7.1.2-33. Patch every host and container that processes untrusted images, run converters with least privilege, and consider disabling bzip2 coders for untrusted input until patched.

docs.text: Field Detail Severity HIGH 7.5 Product rclone Type Improper Verification of Cryptographic Signature (CWE-347) Vector CVSS:3.1/AV:N/AC:H/PR:N/UI:R/S:U/C:H/I:H/A:H

docs.title: Affected versions

docs.title: CVE-2026-116233 — Oray Pugongying X5 Pro: A DHCP Lease Time Smuggles a Newline into Dnsmasq (CRLF Injection)
docs.text: Field Value Severity Critical — CVSS 9.1 (CVSS:3.1/AV:N/AC:L/PR:H/UI:N/S:C/C:H/I:H/A:H) Product Oray Pugongying X5 Pro 7.6.1 Type CRLF Injection (CWE-74, CWE-93) Vector Network, low complexity, high privileges required, no user interaction, scope changed

docs.title: Affected versions
docs.text:
• Oray Pugongying X5 Pro firmware 7.6.1.
  • The vulnerable component is Dnsmasq: the rent_time (DHCP lease time) argument is written into a configuration file without neutralizing carriage-return / line-feed characters.
  • No vendor patch has been announced; the vendor was contacted before disclosure and did not respond.
  • This flaw is one of a cluster disclosed the same day against the same firmware: CVE-2026-116231 (Ser2net), CVE-2026-116232 (SNMP), CVE-2026-116234 (IPsec), CVE-2026-116235 (L2TP), and CVE-2026-116236 (PPPoE plugin upload).

docs.title: Root cause
docs.text:
User-controlled text is interpolated into a configuration file, but carriage returns (\r) and line feeds (\n) are never stripped or escaped. In a config file, a line break separates one directive from the next, so an attacker-controlled newline does not stay inside one value: it starts a brand new directive that the device then obeys as if an administrator wrote it (CWE-74: improper neutralization of special elements in output used by a downstream component, CWE-93: improper neutralization of CRLF sequences).

# Simplified vulnerable pattern (conceptual)
# lease-time value written straight into the dnsmasq config
rent_time = ATTACKER_VALUE
# attacker sends: "3600\n<new directive>"
# the config now contains a second, attacker-chosen line

docs.title: Proof of concept (conceptual)
docs.text:
The attack chain:

  1. The attacker holds a high-privilege account able to reach the device's DHCP/Dnsmasq configuration.
  2. They submit a lease time containing a hidden newline plus a crafted directive.
  3. Dnsmasq's configuration writer stores the value verbatim, and the hidden newline splits it into two lines.
  4. When the service reloads, the injected directive executes with the service's privileges, leading to root code execution.

The accompanying poc.py demonstrates the pattern safely and offline: a config writer that interpolates raw input (vulnerable) versus one that strips line breaks and validates the value as a number (fixed). No device, no network, no exploit.

docs.title: Mitigation
docs.text:
• Restrict management access to trusted networks only — do not expose the device's services to the internet.
  • Disable Dnsmasq's remote configurability where possible, and disable any services you do not use.
  • Watch configuration files for unexpected changes and audit device logs.
  • Check for a firmware update regularly, and replace the device if you cannot isolate it, since no patch has been announced.

docs.title: CVE-2026-116236 — Oray Pugongying X5 Pro: Unrestricted Plugin Upload via PPPoE Settings Leads to Root Code Execution

docs.title: Affected versions
docs.text:
• Oray Pugongying X5 Pro firmware 7.6.1.

# Simplified vulnerable pattern (conceptual)
# plugin options written straight to the upload directory

# the daemon later loads the plugin -> attacker code runs

  2. They submit crafted plugin options through the settings handler.
  3. The handler stores the options as a plugin file without validation.
  4. The daemon loads the plugin, and the attacker's code runs as root.

docs.title: CVE-2026-116241 — pgAdmin 4 Import/Export Quoting Bypass to Host Command Execution
docs.text: Field Detail Severity CRITICAL 9.9 (CVSS 3.1) / 9.4 (CVSS 4.0) Product pgAdmin 4, before 9.19 Type Improper neutralization / command injection via quoting confusion (CWE-78, CWE-115) Vector CVSS:3.1/AV:N/AC:L/PR:L/UI:N/S:C/C:H/I:H/A:H

docs.title: Affected versions
docs.text: pgAdmin 4 before 9.19. This is a bypass of the fix for CVE-2026-17566.

docs.title: Root cause
docs.text: The Import/Export Data tool wraps a user's export query inside a psql copy command and checks that the query's parentheses are balanced, so nothing can escape the wrapper. The check rejected a backslash inside a single-quoted string, but not inside a double-quoted identifier, where it treated the next double quote as closing the identifier. With standard_conforming_strings off, the database tool's parser applies the connection's escape character to whichever quote opened a token, so a backslash-escaped double quote does not close the identifier. pgAdmin's view of the quoting and the tool's view diverged: a closing parenthesis hidden from the check ended the wrapper, and a following TO PROGRAM clause was executed by psql on the pgAdmin host, as the operating-system account running pgAdmin, before the server rejected the statement. An ordinary database role can turn the setting off for itself, and the Import/Export permission is granted to non-administrators by default.

docs.title: Proof of concept
docs.text: Educational only. The accompanying poc.py demonstrates the core idea safely, with no database connection and no command execution: it shows how a naive parentheses-balance check can be fooled by a backslash inside a double-quoted identifier, and how the fixed check (reject any backslash inside a double-quoted identifier) catches it. It never runs a query, never invokes psql, and never executes a program clause.

docs.title: Mitigation
docs.text:
• Update pgAdmin 4 to 9.19 or later immediately. The fix rejects any backslash inside a double-quoted identifier, as was already done for single-quoted strings.
  • Restrict the Import/Export Data permission to trusted administrators on shared servers.
  • Audit recent exports on shared pgAdmin hosts for unusual queries, and review the host for abuse.

docs.title: CVE-2026-116506 — TOTOLINK A950RG command injection trio (with CVE-2026-116504 and CVE-2026-116505)
docs.text: Educational writeup only. The proof of concept below is conceptual and demonstrates the flaw in a controlled lab. Do not use it against systems you do not own.

docs.title: Summary
docs.text: Field Value Severity CRITICAL 9.9 (CVSS v3.1 primary; 8.6 under CVSS v4.0) Product TOTOLINK A950RG, firmware 4.1.2cu.5268_B20221104 Type Improper neutralization of special elements used in a command (CWE-74) — command injection Vector Network — router admin functions (firewall settings, cloud upgrade, device information) CWE CWE-74 (improper neutralization of special elements used in a command) Fixed in No fixed firmware version published in NVD at time of writing — see Mitigation

docs.title: Affected versions
docs.text:
TOTOLINK A950RG firmware 4.1.2cu.5268_B20221104. This writeup groups three same-product, same-class flaws disclosed together, all with public proof-of-concept code:

CVE Function CVSS v3.1 CVE-2026-116506 Firewall settings (apmib_set in firewall.so) 9.9 CRITICAL CVE-2026-116504 Cloud upgrade file name (setCloudUpgradeFW) 9.9 CRITICAL CVE-2026-116505 Device information handler (device address) 9.1 CRITICAL

docs.title: Root cause
docs.text: All three functions build shell commands by concatenating caller-supplied values — a firewall setting, an upgrade file name, and a device address — without sanitization or parameterization. A crafted value containing shell metacharacters breaks out of the intended command, so the router executes the attacker's command with the router process's privileges. An attacker who can reach the admin functions therefore gains control of the router, and with it visibility over the home network behind it.

docs.title: Proof of concept (conceptual, educational only)
docs.text:
See poc.py. It shows, against your own lab router (or a local command-building simulation) only:

  1. How to detect the vulnerable pattern: a value that reaches a shell command unchanged.
  2. The vulnerable pattern (string-concatenated shell command) versus the fixed pattern (fixed command with a parameterized argument and an allowlist check on the value).
  3. What a successful attack gains on a real device: router takeover, settings changes, and traffic visibility.

No working exploit is provided — only the pattern check and the vulnerable-vs-fixed comparison. The public proof-of-concept references are listed below for defenders, not reproduced here.

docs.title: Mitigation
docs.text:
• Check TOTOLINK for a firmware update for the A950RG and install it if one is published.
  • Turn off remote administration on the router.
  • Change the default admin credentials and use a strong password.
  • If no patch is available, isolate the device or replace it — public exploit code for all three flaws already exists.
  • Audit the router's settings and connected devices for changes you did not make.

docs.title: CKEditor 5: Pasted Styles Become Browser Code Execution
docs.text:
Educational material only. Do not use against systems you do not own or have explicit permission to test.

Field Value CVE CVE-2026-116688 Severity High - CVSS 8.1 Product CKEditor 5 (rich-text editor) Type Cross-site scripting via prototype pollution (CWE-79, via a vulnerable es-toolkit version) Vector Crafted editor content carrying a malicious style attribute value reaches a vulnerable helper library while CKEditor processes incoming styles. Prototype pollution alters shared object properties, steering editor code into unauthorized JavaScript execution in the browser of anyone who views the content.

docs.title: Affected versions
docs.text: CKEditor 5 from 45.0.0 until 47.7.4 and 48.5.1. Update to 47.7.4 or 48.5.1.

docs.title: Root cause
docs.text:
Prototypes are shared. Change a property on a prototype and every object inheriting from it sees the change. When untrusted style values can reach that machinery, one crafted input poisons the whole page:

# Simplified vulnerable pattern
def apply_style(obj, style_value):
    merge(obj.prototype, style_value)  # BUG: attacker-shaped keys merged

# Simplified fixed pattern
def apply_style_fixed(obj, style_value):
    clean = drop_dangerous_keys(style_value)
    return merge(obj.prototype, clean)
The fix is twofold: update the helper library so pollution is blocked, and treat style values as untrusted input that must be validated before it touches shared objects.

docs.title: Proof of concept
docs.text:
Educational, conceptual demo only - it models the vulnerable pattern with synthetic, offline objects. It is not a working exploit and cannot be aimed at real systems.

  1. Attacker crafts editor content with a malicious style attribute value.
  2. The content is saved and later displayed to a victim.
  3. Processing the style pollutes a shared prototype.
  4. Editor code follows the polluted property into script execution in the victim browser.

The demo in poc.py shows that untrusted style values must never reach shared prototype machinery without validation: the demo contrasts merging raw keys against dropping dangerous keys first

docs.title: Mitigation
docs.text:
• Update now: CKEditor 5 to 47.7.4 or 48.5.1.
  • Review saved content for suspicious style attribute values.
  • Clear cached editor bundles so old code stops serving.
  • Retest custom plugins that process pasted or imported styles.

docs.title: MLflow: A Prompt Trick Reads Server Files
docs.text:
Educational material only. Do not use against systems you do not own or have explicit permission to test.

Field Value CVE CVE-2026-116690 Severity High - CVSS 7.5 Product MLflow (AI / machine-learning experiment and model platform) Type Path traversal / improper limitation of a pathname (CWE-22) in prompt model-version creation Vector A remote caller creates a model version through the prompt branch of _create_model_version() with a schemeless relative source. Path validation only runs when the source has a URL scheme, so the local path is stored as the artifact location. The caller then reads it back through /api/2.0/mlflow/model-versions/get-artifact. Default unauthenticated servers require no privileges; basic-auth deployments are exposed to authenticated users who can create registered models.

docs.title: Affected versions
docs.text: MLflow from 3.10.0 until 3.17.0. Update to 3.17.0.

docs.title: Root cause
docs.text:
Validation that only runs on one shape of input is no validation at all. When a check is gated on 'has a URL scheme', every schemeless input takes the unchecked road:

# Simplified vulnerable pattern
def create_version(source):
    if has_scheme(source):
        validate_path(source)  # BUG: schemeless paths skip this
    return store_artifact_location(source)

# Simplified fixed pattern
def create_version_fixed(source):
    validate_path(source)  # every path, every time
    return store_artifact_location(source)
A second slip made it worse: a prompt tag was treated as true merely because the tag existed, rather than by checking its value.

docs.title: Proof of concept
docs.text:
Educational, conceptual demo only - it models the vulnerable pattern with synthetic, offline objects. It is not a working exploit and cannot be aimed at real systems.

  1. Caller creates a registered model and a prompt model version with a schemeless relative source.
  2. The server stores the local path as the artifact location without validating it.
  3. Caller requests the artifact through the model-versions get-artifact endpoint.
  4. The server returns file contents it can read.

The demo in poc.py shows that path validation must run on every input shape, not only on inputs that look like URLs, and tag presence must never stand in for a true value

docs.title: Mitigation
docs.text:
• Update now: MLflow to 3.17.0.
  • Require authentication in front of every MLflow server.
  • Never expose MLflow to the internet; bind it to localhost or a private network.
  • Audit model versions for artifact locations outside the artifact root.
  • Rotate credentials the server process could read.

docs.title: CVE-2026-116692 — MLflow: Unauthenticated Remote Code Execution via Third-Party Scorer Deserialization
docs.text: Field Value Severity Critical — CVSS 9.8 (v3.1) Product MLflow — open source AI engineering platform for agents, large language models, and machine learning models Type Improper control of generation of code / code injection (CWE-94) — third-party scorer deserialization accepts request-selected module descendants Vector An attacker uses MLflow artifact endpoints to place a Python module beneath a writable allowed scorer package, then submits its module and class through the scorer invoke endpoint (/ajax-api/3.0/mlflow/scorer/invoke). Scorer validation imports the module and constructs the class before trace processing. On authentication-disabled deployments no credentials are needed; on basic-auth deployments the attacker needs a principal able to create an experiment and run and upload artifacts.

docs.title: Affected versions
docs.text: MLflow from 3.12.0rc0 up to (but not including) 3.17.0. Fixed in 3.17.0.

docs.title: Root cause
docs.text:
Third-party scorer deserialization in the scorer module checked whether a requested module was a descendant of an allowed package, rather than requiring the exact allowed module. Any module nested under a writable allowed package passed the check, so attacker-controlled code was imported and instantiated by the server itself:

# Simplified vulnerable pattern
def load_scorer(module_name, class_name):
    if is_descendant(module_name, ALLOWED_PACKAGES):  # BUG: family check
        module = import_module(module_name)          # attacker code runs
        return module.get_class(class_name)()

# Simplified fixed pattern
def load_scorer_fixed(module_name, class_name):
    if module_name not in EXACT_ALLOWED_MODULES:     # exact check
        raise ValueError("scorer module not allowed")
    module = import_module(module_name)
    return module.get_class(class_name)()

A gate that checks the family instead of the exact module is no gate at all: the attacker just parks code inside the allowed family and the server imports it.

docs.title: Proof of concept (conceptual)
docs.text:
1. Attacker places a Python module beneath a writable allowed scorer package via MLflow artifact endpoints.
  2. Attacker calls the scorer invoke endpoint, naming the planted module and class.
  3. MLflow imports the module and constructs the class before trace processing.
  4. The attacker's code now runs on the MLflow server, with its models, runs, and data in reach.

The accompanying poc.py demonstrates the pattern safely: a family check lets a nested module through, while an exact-allowlist check rejects it. Offline, no server, no exploit.

docs.title: Mitigation
docs.text:
• Upgrade now: MLflow 3.17.0 or newer.
  • Never expose MLflow without authentication; authentication-disabled deployments allow this without credentials.
  • Restrict who can create experiments and runs and upload artifacts, especially on shared servers.
  • Audit recent scorer invocations for unknown modules or classes.
  • Ensure scorer packages are not writable by the server process where possible.

docs.title: CVE-2026-116755 — SoftIron HyperCloud Orchestrator Command Injection
docs.text: Field Value Severity HIGH — CVSS 3.1: 7.4 Product SoftIron HyperCloud (Orchestrator component) Type Improper Neutralization of Special Elements used in a Command (CWE-78) Vector CVSS:3.1/AV:A/AC:L/PR:L/UI:R/S:U/C:H/I:H/A:H Published 2026-10-31

docs.title: Affected versions
docs.text: SoftIron HyperCloud Orchestrator from 1.0 through 2.6.17. Fixed in 2.6.18.

docs.title: Root cause
docs.text:
When the Orchestrator delivers virtual machine template content to a hypervisor host, it wraps that content in a shell here-document whose terminator is not quoted. With an unquoted terminator, the shell performs expansion on the document body, and a crafted terminator line inside the content can end the document early — so attacker-controlled template text (for example, the VM DESCRIPTION field) is interpreted as shell commands instead of data.

Exploitation requires valid credentials, access to the management plane (owning a virtual machine alone is not sufficient), and a lifecycle operation that reaches the affected host, such as deploy, migrate, or network setup. Successful exploitation executes arbitrary operating system commands on hypervisor hosts as the privileged orchestration user.

docs.title: Proof of concept
docs.text: Educational, conceptual demo only — see poc.py. It shows, without running any attacker input, how an unquoted here-document terminator lets embedded content escape the document, and how quoting the terminator keeps the content literal. Do not test against systems you do not own.

docs.title: Mitigation
docs.text:
• Update HyperCloud to 2.6.18 immediately.
  • Until patched, restrict management plane access to trusted administrators only.
  • Audit virtual machine templates for suspicious description content.
  • Treat all template fields as untrusted input on the host side: quote here-document terminators and never pass template content through a shell unescaped.

docs.title: CVE-2026-116769 — Absolute Secure Access Authentication Bypass
docs.text: Field Value Severity CRITICAL (CVSS 4.0: 9.3) Product Absolute Secure Access server Type Authentication Bypass (CWE-287: Improper Authentication) Vector CVSS:4.0/AV:N/AC:L/AT:N/PR:N/UI:N/VC:N/VI:H/VA:N/SC:H/SI:H/SA:N Published 2026-11-02 Exploit Unauthenticated attacker can modify a client's security settings via the server; fixed in 14.61

docs.title: Affected versions
docs.text:
Absolute Secure Access servers starting with version 13.0 and prior to 14.61.

This writeup also covers a related flaw in the same server, CVE-2026-97718 (CRITICAL, CVSS 4.0: 9.4): a cross-site request forgery vulnerability in Secure Access server version 14.60, where a bypassed security control lets an attacker trick an admin into creating an account under the attacker's control.

docs.title: Root cause
docs.text: Secure Access servers in the affected range do not properly authenticate requests that change a client's security settings. An unauthenticated, network-reachable attacker can modify those settings through the server, weakening the protections applied to a client. Combined with the related request-forgery flaw, which turns an admin's own browser session into the tool that creates an attacker-controlled account, the server's access controls stop being a reliable boundary.

docs.title: Proof of concept
docs.text: poc.py in this folder is an educational simulation of the authorization logic: it shows a settings change going through when no authentication is required, and being rejected once authentication is enforced, plus a forged admin request being rejected once an anti-forgery check is required. It does not target any real server, sends no requests, and contains no working exploit.

docs.title: Mitigation
docs.text:
• Update Absolute Secure Access servers to 14.61 or later.
  • Restrict network access to the Secure Access server so it is not reachable by untrusted networks.
  • Audit client security settings and admin-created accounts for unexpected changes, and revert anything that does not match approved configuration.
  • Rotate credentials and review sessions for any client or account whose settings may have been modified.
  • Treat every settings-changing request as authenticated and authorized, and require anti-forgery checks on state-changing admin actions.

docs.title: OpenPanel: one alias escapes the JavaScript sandbox
docs.text:
Educational writeup only. The proof of concept below is conceptual and demonstrates the flaw in a controlled lab. Do not use it against systems you do not own or have explicit permission to test.

Field Value CVE CVE-2026-116811 Severity High — CVSS 8.8 Product OpenPanel (before 3.0.0) Type Code Injection / Sandbox Escape (CWE-94) Vector Network — a project member with write access stores a webhook JavaScript template that aliases the Function constructor past the AST allowlist and runs arbitrary code in the worker process.

docs.title: Affected versions
docs.text: OpenPanel before 3.0.0. Fixed in 3.0.0.

docs.title: Root cause
docs.text: The js-runtime validator checks template code against an AST allowlist, but it inspects the shape of the code rather than what it does. Reading the constructor through an alias (for example via a payload value's constructor property) hides the dangerous capability from the text-level check, so the allowlist passes code that still reaches the Function constructor at runtime.

docs.title: Proof of concept
docs.text: The script in poc.py models the checker flaw in pure string logic: a naive blocklist stops the literal dangerous name but passes the same capability written through an alias. No code is executed from the template; the demo only shows why text-level checks fail.

docs.title: Mitigation
docs.text:
• Update OpenPanel to 3.0.0.
  • Review webhook templates written by project members and restrict who can author templates.
  • Run template code in a truly isolated sandbox (no access to the Function constructor or host objects) with deny-by-default capabilities.
  • Audit worker logs for unexpected process activity.

docs.title: CVE-2026-116843 — Mistral Vibe: RCE via Git Filter Drivers in Worktree Mode
docs.text: Field Value Severity High — CVSS 8.8 (v3.1) Product Mistral Vibe — AI coding agent, worktree mode (--worktree) Type Inclusion of functionality from an untrusted control sphere (CWE-829) Vector An attacker crafts a repository whose .git/config defines git filter drivers. When the victim opens that repository in Vibe with --worktree, git worktree add applies .gitattributes and runs filter smudge, clean, or process commands before the trusted-folder check runs, executing attacker commands with the victim's privileges. User interaction is required (opening the repo), but no further action is needed.

docs.title: Affected versions
docs.text: Mistral Vibe before 3.0.3. Fixed in 3.0.3.

docs.title: Root cause
docs.text: The flaw is ordering, not a missing feature: the trusted-folder check exists, but it runs after the dangerous step. Adding a worktree applies the repository's own git configuration, including filter drivers that execute commands, and only afterwards does Vibe ask whether the folder is trusted. A safety gate that closes after the payload runs protects nothing.

docs.title: Proof of concept (conceptual)
docs.text:
1. Attacker publishes a repository with a malicious filter driver in its git configuration.
  2. Victim opens the repository in Mistral Vibe with worktree mode.
  3. git worktree add runs the filter commands with the victim's privileges.
  4. Attacker code executes before the trusted-folder check intervenes.

The accompanying poc.py demonstrates the pattern safely: a setup sequence that runs repository hooks before the trust check (vulnerable) versus one that checks trust first and refuses to run anything for untrusted folders (fixed). Offline, no git, no exploit.

docs.title: Mitigation
docs.text:
• Upgrade now: Mistral Vibe 3.0.3.
  • Never open untrusted repositories in worktree mode or with an AI agent that auto-runs repository configuration.
  • Review .gitattributes and .git/config before opening a stranger's repository.
  • Run coding agents with least privilege and keep credentials out of the agent's environment.

docs.title: WordPress Newsletters: One Click Hijacks the Admin (CSRF)
docs.text: Educational material only. Do not use against systems you do not own or have explicit permission to test. | Field | Value | |---|---| | CVE | CVE-2026-116863 | | Severity | Critical — CVSS 9.6 | | Product | Tribulant Software Newsletters plugin for WordPress (newsletters-lite) | | Type | Cross-Site Request Forgery (CWE-352) | | Vector | A logged-in WordPress administrator visits an attacker-crafted page while still authenticated. The page silently fires a request to the site, the browser attaches the admin session cookie, and the plugin executes the sensitive action because the request is not properly verified as coming from the admin's own dashboard. |

docs.title: Affected versions
docs.text: Newsletters (newsletters-lite) from n/a through 4.18.2. Update past 4.18.2 to the latest patched release.

docs.title: Root cause
docs.text:
A session cookie proves who the browser user is, not what they intended to do. When a sensitive action accepts a bare request without a per-action token tied to the admin dashboard, any page the admin visits can borrow that authority:

# Simplified vulnerable pattern
def handle_action(request):
    if request.user.is_admin:  # BUG: cookie alone = proof
        return apply_change(request.params)

# Simplified fixed pattern
def handle_action_fixed(request):
    if request.user.is_admin and valid_token(request.token):
        return apply_change(request.params)
    return deny("forgery check failed")
The fix is a token that only the site's own dashboard can produce, checked on every state-changing request.

docs.title: Proof of concept
docs.text:
Educational, conceptual demo only — it models the vulnerable pattern with synthetic, offline objects. It is not a working exploit and cannot be aimed at real systems.

  1. Attacker builds a page that silently fires a forged request at the target WordPress site.
  2. A logged-in administrator visits that page (a link, an ad, a comment).
  3. The browser attaches the admin session cookie to the forged request.
  4. The plugin runs the action as admin, with no dashboard visit involved.

The demo in poc.py shows that a cookie authenticates identity, not intent: the demo contrasts accepting any admin-cookie request against requiring a dashboard-issued per-action token.

docs.title: Mitigation
docs.text:
• Update now: Newsletters past 4.18.2 to the latest patched release.
  • Log out of WordPress when admin work is done; avoid browsing untrusted pages while logged in.
  • Review admin users, plugin settings, and subscriber lists for changes you did not make.
  • Force password resets for administrator accounts if any change looks unexplained.

docs.title: nest-admin: a leaked signing secret lets anyone forge admin tokens
docs.text:
Educational writeup only. The proof of concept below is conceptual and demonstrates the flaw in a controlled lab. Do not use it against systems you do not own or have explicit permission to test.

Field Value CVE CVE-2026-117564 Severity Critical — CVSS 9.8 Product nest-admin (before 1.0.1) Type Use of Hardcoded Credentials / Hardcoded Secret (CWE-321), Authentication Bypass Vector Network — unauthenticated. An attacker reads the hardcoded JWT secret from the committed .env.production file, signs a token claiming any user ID and the admin role, and the server trusts it.

docs.title: Affected versions
docs.text: nest-admin before 1.0.1. Fixed in 1.0.1 (rotate the leaked secret as well — updating alone does not un-leak it).

docs.title: Root cause
docs.text: The JWT signing secret was committed to the repository in .env.production. The server's JWT strategy and role guard verify only that a token's signature matches that secret; they never check who signed it. Once the secret is public, every token an attacker signs is indistinguishable from a legitimate one, including tokens claiming the admin role.

docs.title: Proof of concept
docs.text: The script in poc.py demonstrates the pattern locally with a dummy secret: it signs a token claiming the admin role and shows the server-side verification accepting it, because verification only checks the signature. No real system is contacted.

docs.title: Mitigation
docs.text:
• Update nest-admin to 1.0.1.
  • Rotate the leaked signing secret immediately and invalidate all tokens signed with the old secret.
  • Move secrets into a vault or secret manager; never commit .env files. Add .env* to .gitignore and scan history for committed secrets.
  • Verify roles server-side from a trusted store instead of trusting role claims in the token alone.

docs.title: CVE-2026-118147 — Visual Studio: Spoofing via Improper Certificate Validation
docs.text: Field Value Severity High — CVSS 3.1 score 7.4 (vector: AV:N/AC:H/PR:N/UI:N/S:U/C:H/I:H/A:N) Product Microsoft Visual Studio 2017, 2019, 2022, 2026 Type Spoofing via improper certificate validation (CWE-295) Vector Network, no privileges required, no user interaction — attacker must sit in the network path between Visual Studio and the requested resource (machine-in-the-middle)

docs.title: Affected versions
docs.text:
• Visual Studio 2017 version 15.9 — fixed in build 15.9.84
  • Visual Studio 2019 version 16.11 — fixed in build 16.11.62
  • Visual Studio 2022 version 17.14 — fixed in build 17.14.44
  • Visual Studio 2026 version 18.11 — fixed in build 18.11.3

Microsoft rates the issue "Important", reports it as not publicly disclosed and not exploited at publication time, and assesses exploitation as less likely.

docs.title: Root cause
docs.text: Visual Studio did not validate server certificates strictly enough. Certificates are how a client verifies that the server it talks to is really who it claims to be. When that check is weak, an attacker positioned in the logical network path — for example on public Wi-Fi or behind a compromised router — can present a fake certificate for the resource Visual Studio requested, and Visual Studio accepts it. From that point the attacker sits in the middle of the connection: they can view highly sensitive information in transit and tamper with what comes back. Microsoft describes the impact as a total loss of protection for the affected data, with no impact on availability.

docs.title: Proof of concept
docs.text: Educational, conceptual only — this demonstrates the pattern (lax vs. strict certificate validation) in plain Python. It is not an exploit against Visual Studio and does not target any real server. See poc.py: a mock certificate check shows how a lax validator accepts a certificate whose hostname and issuer do not match, while a strict validator rejects it.

docs.title: Mitigation
docs.text:
• Update Visual Studio to the October 2026 security release: VS 2022 build 17.14.44 (or the matching fixed builds for 2017, 2019, and 2026).
  • Until updated, avoid untrusted networks for development work that fetches remote resources.
  • Use a VPN on public Wi-Fi so an attacker cannot easily sit in your network path.
  • Keep Visual Studio and its components on automatic updates.

docs.title: Echo Go Framework: Proxy Tunnel Bypasses Router Authentication
docs.text:
Educational material only. Do not use against systems you do not own or have explicit permission to test.

Field Value CVE CVE-2026-118264 Severity Critical - CVSS 4.0 9.1 Product Echo Go web framework, 4.0.0 to before 4.16.1 and 5.0.0 to before 5.4.1 Type Inconsistent interpretation of HTTP requests (CWE-444) in the Proxy middleware Vector A remote unauthenticated attacker sends a WebSocket upgrade request through a proxy route; the upstream rejects the upgrade with an ordinary keep-alive response, but Echo already opened a raw tunnel, so later requests on the connection reach the upstream without passing Echo's router or route middleware.

docs.title: Affected versions
docs.text: Echo 4.0.0 to before 4.16.1, and Echo 5.0.0 to before 5.4.1. Update to 4.16.1 or 5.4.1.

docs.title: Root cause
docs.text:
The tunnel is selected before the upgrade is confirmed:

# Simplified vulnerable pattern
def proxy_upgrade(request):
    tunnel = open_raw_tunnel(request)   # BUG: tunnel first
    if not upstream_accepted(request):  # rejection never tears it down
        return keep_alive_response()
    # later requests on this connection skip the router entirely

# Simplified fixed pattern
def proxy_upgrade_fixed(request):
    if not upstream_accepted(request):
        return keep_alive_response()    # no tunnel without acceptance
    tunnel = open_raw_tunnel(request)   # tunnel only after confirmation

Authentication enforced only by Echo routes never runs for requests that never pass through the router.

docs.title: Proof of concept
docs.text:
Educational, conceptual demo only - it models the vulnerable pattern with synthetic, offline objects. It is not a working exploit and cannot be aimed at real systems.

  1. Attacker sends a WebSocket upgrade request to a proxy route.
  2. The upstream rejects the upgrade with a keep-alive response.
  3. The raw tunnel stays open anyway.
  4. Later requests on the connection reach the upstream directly, bypassing Echo authentication.

The demo in poc.py shows that ordering matters: a tunnel must only exist after the upgrade is confirmed.

docs.title: Mitigation
docs.text:
• Update now: Echo to 4.16.1 or 5.4.1.
  • Audit every proxy route for exposure to unauthenticated clients.
  • Enforce authorization at the upstream as well as in Echo routes.
  • Test rejected upgrades to confirm no tunnel survives a rejection.

docs.title: Google Chrome: a crafted page corrupts the V8 engine
docs.text:
Educational writeup only. The proof of concept below is conceptual and demonstrates the flaw in a controlled lab. Do not use it against systems you do not own or have explicit permission to test.

Field Value CVE CVE-2026-118359 Severity High — CVSS 8.8 Product Google Chrome (before 156.0.8078.73) Type Memory Corruption in V8 (CWE-119) Vector Network — a remote attacker lures a victim to a crafted HTML page; the page triggers memory corruption in V8 and potentially executes arbitrary code inside the sandbox. User interaction (visiting the page) is required.

docs.title: Affected versions
docs.text: Google Chrome before 156.0.8078.73. Fixed in 156.0.8078.73 (stable channel update for desktop, part of a large batch of fixes in the same release).

docs.title: Root cause
docs.text: V8, Chrome's JavaScript engine, mismanages memory when processing crafted page content, corrupting data structures the engine trusts. Corrupted structures can then be treated as valid objects or instructions, turning a rendering flaw into code execution inside the sandbox.

docs.title: Proof of concept
docs.text: The script in poc.py is a local version check only: it compares a Chrome version string against the fixed build and reports whether it is vulnerable. It contains no exploit code and contacts no system.

docs.title: Mitigation
docs.text:
• Update Chrome to 156.0.8078.73 and restart the browser so the patch takes effect.
  • Keep automatic updates enabled.
  • Be cautious with links from untrusted senders; this flaw needs only a page visit.

docs.title: llama.cpp ggml-rpc: A One-Byte Stack Slot Swallows 256 Kilobytes (RDMA Overflow)
docs.text:
Educational material only. Do not use against systems you do not own or have explicit permission to test.

Field Value CVE CVE-2026-118375 Severity Critical — CVSS 9.2 Product llama.cpp (ggml-rpc RDMA transport) Type Out-of-bounds Write / Stack-based Buffer Overflow (CWE-787) Vector An unauthenticated peer connects to the rpc server and advertises RDMA capabilities in its HELLO message. The RDMA receive path then copies up to 256 KiB into a 1-byte stack variable in the client-serving function, overflowing the stack. The server crashes, and the overflow may be bent toward code execution.

docs.title: Affected versions
docs.text: llama.cpp from b8841 up to, but not including, b11865. Fixed in b11865.

docs.title: Root cause
docs.text:
The receive path trusts a length that comes from the remote peer and never validates it against the destination buffer. The destination is a stack variable sized for a single byte, while the copy can run to 256 KiB. Any network-facing copy whose size is set by the peer and whose destination is tiny is an overflow waiting for a connection.

# Simplified vulnerable pattern (conceptual, not a working exploit)
def serve_client(peer):
    stack_slot = bytearray(1)          # destination fits one byte
    data = peer.recv()                 # size chosen by the peer, up to 256 KiB
    stack_slot[:len(data)] = data      # overflow: copy exceeds the buffer

# Simplified fixed pattern
def serve_client(peer):
    buffer = bytearray(MAX_MESSAGE)    # destination fits the largest legal message
    data = peer.recv()
    if len(data) > MAX_MESSAGE:
        raise ValueError("Message too large")
    buffer[:len(data)] = data

docs.title: Proof of concept
docs.text:
Educational demonstration only, on a local test setup you own:

  1. Build a vulnerable llama.cpp rpc server locally and a patched b11865 build side by side, on an isolated network.
  2. Point a test client at the vulnerable server, advertise RDMA support in the hello message, and send an oversized reply.
  3. Observe the vulnerable server crash; observe the patched server reject or handle the message without crashing.
  4. Confirm the operational fix: with the rpc server firewalled to trusted workers only, an untrusted-network client cannot reach it at all.

No working exploit is published here.

docs.title: Mitigation
docs.text:
• Update llama.cpp to b11865 or later.
  • If you cannot update yet, disable the RDMA transport path.
  • Never expose the rpc server to untrusted networks; firewall it so only your own workers can reach it.
  • Treat any unexpected rpc-server crash as a possible attack indicator and check logs for oversized hello messages.

docs.title: CVE-2026-118411 — Apache Roller CSRF creates an administrator account
docs.text: Severity Product Type Attack vector HIGH 8.8 Apache Roller 5.0.1 through 6.1.6 Cross-Site Request Forgery (CWE-352) Network — unauthenticated, requires a logged-in admin to open an attacker link

docs.title: Affected versions
docs.text:
• Apache Roller 5.0.1 through 6.1.6
  • Fixed in 6.1.7 and later

docs.title: Root cause
docs.text:
Roller applied its request-token (anti-CSRF) check only to POST requests — but administrative actions also accepted GET requests, which carried no token check at all. A browser attaches the admin's session cookie to any request, including one triggered by a link on another page, so an attacker can craft a URL that invokes the create-user action with administrator privileges and have a logged-in Roller administrator fire it by simply clicking the link.

Fixed in Roller 6.1.7 (see apache/roller#227): data-changing actions now require POST and a valid request token.

docs.title: Proof of concept
docs.text:
Conceptual only — illustrates the pattern behind the bug, not a working exploit.

# Admin actions accepted GET as well as POST, but the token check
# only ran on POST:
#
#     def handle_admin_action(request):
#         if request.method == "POST":
#             require_valid_token(request)   # GET skips this entirely
#         create_user(admin=True)            # ...runs either way
#
# Attacker link (sent to a logged-in admin):
#     https://roller.example.com/admin/create-user?role=admin
# One click, and the attacker's account is created with admin rights.

See poc.py for a safe, pure-Python simulation of the token-check gap vs. the fixed POST-plus-token behavior.

Educational use only. Do not build or distribute working exploits for this vulnerability — patch your dependencies instead.

docs.title: Mitigation
docs.text:
• Upgrade Apache Roller to 6.1.7 or later immediately.
  • Audit the user list for administrator accounts you did not create and revoke any you do not recognize.
  • For defense in depth, require POST plus a valid anti-CSRF token on every state-changing action — never accept GET for actions that change data.

docs.title: Sophos UTM: Unauthenticated Remote Code Execution as Root
docs.text:
Educational material only. Do not use against systems you do not own or have explicit permission to test.

Field Value CVE CVE-2026-118633 Severity Critical - CVSS 4.0 9.2 (CVSS 3.1 8.1) Product Sophos UTM (all versions, end of life) Type Path traversal (CWE-35) combined with a race condition Vector A remote unauthenticated attacker sustains repeated attacks for a few minutes against the email proxy with scanning enabled, wins a race condition, traverses outside the intended directory, and executes arbitrary code as root.

docs.title: Affected versions
docs.text: Sophos UTM, all versions. Sophos UTM is end of life and the patch must be installed manually. See the Sophos security advisory for the manual patch.

docs.title: Root cause
docs.text:
A path supplied through the email proxy is not confined to its intended directory, and a race between validation and use lets a crafted path escape:

# Simplified vulnerable pattern
def handle_email_path(path):
    if is_safe(path):          # check happens here...
        store(path)            # ...but the path can change before use
        # BUG: traversal escapes the safe folder, code runs as root

# Simplified fixed pattern
def handle_email_path_fixed(path):
    resolved = resolve_inside_safe_root(path)  # canonicalize first
    if resolved is None:
        return deny("path outside safe root")
    store(resolved)

High privilege plus an unguarded path is the core problem: the email scanner runs as root, so escaping its directory means escaping into root execution.

docs.title: Proof of concept
docs.text:
Educational, conceptual demo only - it models the vulnerable pattern with synthetic, offline objects. It is not a working exploit and cannot be aimed at real systems.

  1. Attacker sends crafted paths to the email proxy, repeatedly.
  2. A race condition lets one request escape the intended directory.
  3. The planted content lands where it executes with root privilege.
  4. The attacker now controls the firewall and can pivot inward.

The demo in poc.py shows why paths must be canonicalized inside a safe root before use, and why a check separated from use by a race is not a boundary.

docs.title: Mitigation
docs.text:
• Install the Sophos manual patch for UTM now - it does not install itself.
  • Disable email proxy scanning if you cannot patch immediately.
  • Restrict access to the UTM management interface to trusted hosts.
  • Plan migration off Sophos UTM, an end-of-life product.
  • Audit logs for repeated email-proxy requests and unexpected root activity.

docs.title: CVE-2026-118636: Apache MINA 3.0 Unsafe Deserialization to Remote Code Execution
docs.text: Field Detail Severity Critical — CVSS 9.8 (CVSS:3.1 AV:N/AC:L/PR:N/UI:N/S:U/C:H/I:H/A:H) Product Apache MINA 3.0 codec module (JavaNativeMessageDecoder) Type Deserialization of untrusted data (CWE-502) Vector Unauthenticated network attacker sends a crafted frame to an application that places JavaNativeMessageDecoder in front of an untrusted peer → the decoder calls ObjectInputStream.readObject() on frame bytes with no class filter → gadget-chain remote code execution

docs.title: Affected versions
docs.text: Apache MINA 3.0 (3.0 branch, including 3.0.0 through 3.0.0-M2). The 3.0.0 branch is inactive and no fixing release is planned. Users are recommended to move to the latest Apache MINA 2.2.X branch.

docs.title: Root cause
docs.text:
JavaNativeMessageDecoder in the MINA 3.0 codec module rebuilds Java objects from raw frame bytes using ObjectInputStream.readObject() with no class filter. Deserialization runs code from the classes named in the stream, so an attacker who controls the bytes controls which classes get rebuilt. With a gadget chain available on the classpath, that rebuild becomes arbitrary code execution on the server, before any application-level check ever sees the object.

# Simplified vulnerable pattern
frame = bytes_from_untrusted_peer()
obj = deserialize(frame)          # no class filter: any class may be rebuilt
handle(obj)                       # gadget chain already ran during rebuild

# Simplified fixed pattern
ALLOWED = {"com.example.SafeMessage"}
obj = deserialize(frame, allowed_classes=ALLOWED)  # unknown class rejected
handle(obj)

docs.title: Proof of concept
docs.text:
1. Attacker connects to a MINA 3.0 application that uses JavaNativeMessageDecoder on an untrusted-facing port.
  2. Attacker sends a single crafted frame containing a serialized gadget chain.
  3. The decoder rebuilds the object with no class filter, and the gadget chain executes code on the server.
  4. The attacker gains remote code execution with no authentication and no user interaction.

The educational demo in poc.py illustrates why a class filter is the only thing standing between network bytes and code execution.

Educational material only. Do not use against systems you do not own or have explicit permission to test.

docs.title: Mitigation
docs.text:
• Migrate now: move from MINA 3.0 to the latest Apache MINA 2.2.X release line. There will be no 3.0 fix.
  • Remove JavaNativeMessageDecoder from any service facing untrusted peers if migration is not immediately possible.
  • Never deserialize untrusted data: replace Java native serialization on the wire with a data-only format (e.g. JSON) plus schema validation.
  • If deserialization is unavoidable, enforce a strict class allowlist (JEP 290-style filters) and audit every decoder for a filter.

docs.title: n8n: Member Flaws Expose Every Project (Batch Update)
docs.text:
Educational material only. Do not use against systems you do not own or have explicit permission to test.

Field Value CVE CVE-2026-118649 (lead CVE of an n8n batch) Severity High - CVSS 4.0 8.7 (CVSS 3.1 8.3) Product n8n before 1.123.85, 2.x before 2.43.5, and 2.44.x before 2.44.1 Type Authorization bypass (CWE-1321 prototype pollution in project check); batch siblings: filter injection (CWE-943), credential exposure in error data, credential guard bypasses, stored XSS, SSRF Vector An authenticated member who can create and run workflows supplies a crafted workflow ID (such as a prototype-polluting value); the Data Table project check caches the owner project by that ID and matches every project, so the member can list, read, modify, and delete Data Table rows in all projects of the instance.

docs.title: Affected versions
docs.text: n8n before 1.123.85, 2.x before 2.43.5, and 2.44.x before 2.44.1. Update to 1.123.85, 2.43.5, or 2.44.1 depending on your release line.

docs.title: Root cause
docs.text:
Client-supplied identifiers are trusted as cache keys without validation, and a special value collides with the check itself:

# Simplified vulnerable pattern
def project_for(workflow_id):
    return cache.get(workflow_id)  # BUG: crafted id matches every project

# Simplified fixed pattern
def project_for_fixed(workflow_id):
    if not is_valid_workflow_id(workflow_id):
        return deny("invalid workflow id")
    return cache.get(workflow_id)  # only real ids, strict lookup

The batch shares one theme: input that should be validated is trusted, and secrets that should be scrubbed are kept in error data.

docs.title: Proof of concept
docs.text:
Educational, conceptual demo only - it models the vulnerable pattern with synthetic, offline objects. It is not a working exploit and cannot be aimed at real systems.

  1. Member creates a workflow with a crafted identifier.
  2. The Data Table project check matches every project.
  3. The member lists, reads, modifies, and deletes rows in other projects.
  4. Separately, failed operations expose credentials in error execution data.

The demo in poc.py shows a strict identifier check defeating the crafted value, and error data scrubbed of secrets.

docs.title: Mitigation
docs.text:
• Update now: n8n to 1.123.85, 2.43.5, or 2.44.1.
  • Rotate credentials that may have leaked into error execution data.
  • Review error workflows and who can view execution error data.
  • Audit member access and Data Tables for unexpected changes.
  • Review the full batch: filter injection in Quick Base, Outlook, and SharePoint nodes (CVE-2026-118645, CVE-2026-118641), credential storage in error data (CVE-2026-118643, CVE-2026-118647), and credential guard bypasses (CVE-2026-118642, CVE-2026-118675, CVE-2026-118676).

docs.title: MONAI: Malicious Bundle Runs Code When Loaded
docs.text:
Educational material only. Do not use against systems you do not own or have explicit permission to test.

Field Value CVE CVE-2026-118683 Severity High - CVSS 3.1 8.8 Product MONAI 1.2.0 to before 1.6.1 (medical imaging AI framework) Type Code injection (CWE-94) via bundle logging configuration Vector An attacker publishes a malicious bundle whose logging configuration is evaluated as code when a victim loads or runs the bundle, giving arbitrary Python execution on the victim's machine.

docs.title: Affected versions
docs.text: MONAI 1.2.0 to before 1.6.1. Update to 1.6.1 or later.

docs.title: Root cause
docs.text:
Bundle configuration is data from an untrusted publisher, but the loader evaluates part of it as code:

# Simplified vulnerable pattern
def load_workflow(bundle):
    logging_config = bundle.read("configs/logging.conf")
    apply_logging_config(logging_config)  # BUG: handler fields evaluated
    # attacker-controlled handler definition now runs as code

# Simplified fixed pattern
def load_workflow_fixed(bundle):
    if not bundle_is_trusted(bundle):
        raise ValueError("untrusted bundle")
    apply_logging_config_safely(bundle.read("configs/logging.conf"))

A download must never be an execution. Configuration should be parsed as data, never evaluated.

docs.title: Proof of concept
docs.text:
Educational, conceptual demo only - it models the vulnerable pattern with synthetic, offline objects. It is not a working exploit and cannot be aimed at real systems.

  1. Attacker publishes a bundle with a crafted logging configuration.
  2. Victim downloads and loads the bundle workflow.
  3. The loader evaluates the handler definition as code.
  4. Attacker code runs on the victim's machine.

The demo in poc.py contrasts evaluating a config field with parsing it as plain data, and shows why bundle contents must be inspected before use.

docs.title: Mitigation
docs.text:
• Update now: MONAI to 1.6.1 or later.
  • Load bundles only from trusted sources.
  • Inspect bundle configuration files before running a bundle.
  • Sandbox untrusted bundles and never run a stranger's bundle blind.
  • Check integrity of bundles (see also CVE-2026-118684, the MONAI hash-check weakness fixed in the same release).

docs.title: CVE-2026-118690 — Signal K Server: Missing Authentication on Log Download Leads to Admin Takeover
docs.text: Field Value Severity Critical — CVSS 9.8 Product Signal K Server — marine instrument data server for vessels Type Missing authentication for a critical function (CWE-306) — log archive endpoint has no login check Vector Unauthenticated remote attacker downloads log archives via /skServer/ziplogs → extracts the JWT secretKey from security.json in the ZIP → forges administrator tokens → creates persistent admin accounts

docs.title: Affected versions
docs.text: Signal K Server before 2.33.0. Fixed in 2.33.0.

docs.title: Root cause
docs.text:
Two failures combine. The log download endpoint performs no authentication, and its archive bundles the file holding the token signing secret. A secret that leaves the server in a download is no longer a secret:

# Simplified vulnerable pattern
def download_logs(request):
    # BUG: no auth check, archive includes the signing secret
    return bundle_logs(include=["logs", "security.json"])

# Simplified fixed pattern
def download_logs_fixed(request):
    if not request.is_authenticated_admin():
        raise PermissionError("admin login required")
    return bundle_logs(include=["logs"])  # secrets never exported
Sensitive endpoints need authentication, and secrets must never be included in downloadable output.

docs.title: Proof of concept
docs.text:
1. Attacker requests the log archive endpoint without logging in.
  2. The returned ZIP contains security.json with the JWT signing secret.
  3. The attacker signs a forged administrator token with that secret.
  4. The forged token creates a persistent admin account — full server control.

See poc.py for a safe, offline demo of a secret shipped in a public download: the demo contrasts an archive that bundles the signing secret with one that requires admin login and excludes secrets.

docs.title: Mitigation
docs.text:
• Update now: Signal K Server 2.33.0 or later.
  • Rotate the JWT signing secret — the old one must be treated as compromised.
  • Audit admin accounts for any you did not create.
  • Restrict network access to the server to trusted hosts.

docs.title: CVE-2026-118696 — JetBrains embedded browser trusts revoked intermediate certificates
docs.text: Field Detail Severity HIGH 8.0 Product JetBrains IntelliJ IDEA, PyCharm, PhpStorm, RubyMine, WebStorm, GoLand, Rider, CLion, DataGrip, RustRover, DataSpell Type CWE-299 (Improper Check for Certificate Revocation) Vector Network

docs.title: Affected versions
docs.text:
• IntelliJ IDEA, PyCharm, PhpStorm, RubyMine, WebStorm before 2026.3, 2026.2.4, 2026.1.5.1, 2025.3.6.2
  • GoLand, Rider, CLion, DataGrip, RustRover, DataSpell before their respective 2026.3 / patched branches (see JetBrains advisory)

docs.title: Root cause
docs.text: The embedded browser inside JetBrains IDEs trusted revoked eMudhra intermediate certificates, the same certificate authority incident behind CVE-2026-118697. A revoked badge was treated as valid, so pages served with a compromised chain looked trustworthy inside the IDE.

docs.title: Proof of concept
docs.text:
Conceptually: the IDE's embedded browser loads a page whose certificate chains to a revoked intermediate. With the revocation check missing, the browser shows a secure page; with the fix, it blocks it.

See poc.py in this folder for a safe, educational demonstration. It does not exploit the vulnerability.

docs.title: Mitigation
docs.text:
• Update your IDE to 2026.3 or the latest patched branch for your version line.
  • Update the Toolbox App alongside the IDEs (see CVE-2026-118697).
  • Treat any credentials entered in the embedded browser before patching as potentially exposed and rotate them.

docs.title: CVE-2026-118697 — JetBrains tools trust compromised intermediate certificates
docs.text: Field Detail Severity CRITICAL 9.0 Product JetBrains Toolbox App and IntelliJ IDEA (plus related IDEs) Type CWE-295 (Improper Certificate Validation) Vector Network

docs.title: Affected versions
docs.text:
• JetBrains Toolbox App before 3.9.1 and 3.8.2
  • IntelliJ IDEA before 2026.3 and 2026.2.4

docs.title: Root cause
docs.text: After a certificate authority incident, certain eMudhra intermediate certificates were revoked. The JetBrains daemon (jetbrainsd) kept trusting them, skipping the revocation check, so a certificate chained to a compromised intermediate was still accepted as valid.

docs.title: Proof of concept
docs.text:
Conceptually: a server presents a certificate chain rooted in a revoked intermediate. A client that checks revocation rejects it; the affected JetBrains daemon accepted it, so traffic to an impersonated service looked secure.

See poc.py in this folder for a safe, educational demonstration. It does not exploit the vulnerability.

docs.title: Mitigation
docs.text:
• Update the Toolbox App to 3.9.1 (or 3.8.2 branch) and IntelliJ IDEA to 2026.3 or 2026.2.4.
  • Update all other JetBrains tools, since the related embedded-browser issue (CVE-2026-118696) is fixed in the same releases.
  • Rotate credentials or tokens that may have crossed untrusted networks.

docs.title: CVE-2026-118762 - Monkeytype CI Workflow Privilege Escalation
docs.text: Field Value Severity CRITICAL (9.3) Product Monkeytype (repository CI workflow) Type CI Workflow Code Execution (CWE-829) Vector CVSS:3.1/AV:N/AC:L/PR:N/UI:R/S:C/C:H/I:H/A:N

docs.title: Affected versions
docs.text: Prior to version 26.43.0. The issue affects the repository CI workflow, not the Monkeytype application or user data.

docs.title: Root cause
docs.text: The fix-formatting workflow ran on pull_request_target with repository write permissions, checked out fork code, and executed a fork-controlled binary while the elevated token was still persisted in git config.

docs.title: Proof of concept
docs.text:
An external contributor whose pull request receives the format label could run arbitrary code with the workflow's elevated token, exfiltrate it, and push repository content or modify pull requests and issues.

See poc.py for an educational illustration of the vulnerable pattern versus the fixed pattern. Educational only, for controlled environments.

docs.title: Mitigation
docs.text:
• Update to Monkeytype 26.43.0 or later (workflow fix).
  • Avoid pull_request_target with write permissions combined with fork checkouts.
  • Never run fork-controlled binaries while an elevated token is persisted.

docs.text:

docs.title: CVE-2026-118772 — joi Multiple Email Rule Quadratic Regex (DoS)
docs.text: Field Value Severity HIGH 7.5 Product joi (hapijs/joi) 17.1.1–17.13.9 and 18.3.1 Type Inefficient regular expression complexity (CWE-1333) Vector CVSS:3.1/AV:N/AC:L/PR:N/UI:N/S:U/C:N/I:N/A:H Published 2026-10-29

docs.title: Affected versions
docs.text: joi from 17.1.1 until 17.13.9, and 18.3.1. Fixed in 17.13.9 and 18.3.1.

docs.title: Root cause
docs.text: The Joi.string().email({ multiple: true }) rule splits the value with a separator regular expression whose leading whitespace quantifier is retried at every position of a long whitespace run that contains no separator. The work is therefore quadratic in the length of the whitespace run, inside a single String.prototype.split call. Applications validating attacker-controlled values with the multiple option and no effective prior length limit can have the Node.js event loop blocked for seconds by one request. A .max() rule is not sufficient when abortEarly: false lets the email rule run after the length check fails.

docs.title: Proof of concept
docs.text:
Educational only. The demo below runs fully offline in Python and shows the pattern — a regex with a leading quantifier retried at every position of a whitespace run versus a linear split — with timing on synthetic strings. It never sends a request anywhere.

See poc.py. Run it with python3 poc.py. It demonstrates:

  1. Quadratic cost of the retrying separator pattern on whitespace runs.
  2. Linear cost of a plain split on the same input.
  3. How the gap grows with input length.

docs.title: Mitigation
docs.text:
• Upgrade joi to 17.13.9 or 18.3.1 immediately.
  • Enforce a strict length limit that actually runs before the email rule (do not rely on .max() with abortEarly: false).
  • Limit the size of multiple email lists on public endpoints.
  • Treat validators as security-critical code: they run first, on attacker input.

docs.title: References
docs.text:
• NVD: https://nvd.nist.gov/vuln/detail/CVE-2026-118772
  • joi fix PRs: https://github.com/hapijs/joi/pull/3162 and https://github.com/hapijs/joi/pull/3163

docs.title: node-forge 1.4.1 — Six Flaws Including a PKCS#12 Integrity Bypass
docs.text: Field Value Severity HIGH 7.5 (lead: CVE-2026-118782) Product node-forge (digitalbazaar/forge) before 1.4.1 Type PKCS#12 integrity bypass, denial of service, certificate chain confusion Vector CVSS:3.1/AV:N/AC:L/PR:N/UI:N/S:U/C:N/I:H/A:N (CVE-2026-118782) Published 2026-10-29

docs.title: CVEs in this batch
docs.text:
CVE Score Flaw CVE-2026-118779 7.5 PEM parsing regexes cause CPU exhaustion (DoS) CVE-2026-118782 7.5 PKCS#12 zero/negative iteration count yields a constant key, bypassing password integrity checks CVE-2026-119187 7.5 Recursive TLS record processing exhausts the call stack (DoS) CVE-2026-119188 7.5 Fragmented handshake interrupted by another record type triggers an uncaught TypeError (DoS) CVE-2026-119190 7.4 Deprecated extension OIDs parsed as basicConstraints; a leaf cert can be accepted as a CA CVE-2026-119191 7.5 ASN.1 BIT STRING decoding ignores maxDepth, causing quadratic memory use (DoS)

All fixed in node-forge 1.4.1.

docs.title: Affected versions
docs.text: node-forge before 1.4.1.

docs.title: Root cause
docs.text: The headline flaw (CVE-2026-118782) is in PKCS#12 handling: pki.pbe.generatePkcs12Key() accepted an iteration count of zero or less and then returned a constant key, independent of the password and salt. Crafted PKCS#12 input processed by forge.pkcs12.pkcs12FromAsn1() could therefore pass password-based integrity checks with any password, and predictable keys and IVs affected PKCS#12 PBE, shrouded key bags, encrypted SafeContents, and PKCS#8 encrypted private keys. The sibling flaws share one theme: parsers that trust counts, depths, and extension order from hostile input.

docs.title: Proof of concept
docs.text:
Educational only. The demo below runs fully offline and shows the pattern — a key-derivation function that must reject non-positive iteration counts versus one that silently returns a constant key. It uses no real crypto and never parses real PKCS#12 data.

See poc.py. Run it with python3 poc.py. It demonstrates:

  1. How a zero iteration count collapses key derivation to a constant.
  2. How two different passwords then "verify" against the same integrity value.
  3. How rejecting non-positive counts restores password dependence.

docs.title: Mitigation
docs.text:
• Upgrade node-forge to 1.4.1 immediately.
  • Audit where your app parses untrusted PEM, PKCS#12, or certificate data.
  • If a CA you trust copies extensions from certificate signing requests, verify that chains are re-validated after the upgrade.
  • Treat all crypto input as hostile: enforce counts, depths, and extension checks.

docs.title: References
docs.text:
• NVD: https://nvd.nist.gov/vuln/detail/CVE-2026-118782
  • node-forge 1.4.1 release: https://github.com/digitalbazaar/forge/releases/tag/v1.4.1
  • GHSA advisories: GHSA-7wch-p9px-956x, GHSA-jc66-7q78-782g, GHSA-hqq3-7jhf-c5jx, GHSA-8hrf-8g6f-7xwp, GHSA-5x38-2vff-x55p, GHSA-rhr8-3pm8-cq29

docs.title: CVE-2026-118869 — OS Command Injection in SHIRASAGI
docs.text: Field Value Severity HIGH — CVSS 3.0: 8.8 Product SHIRASAGI, v1.19.0–v1.21.0 Type OS command injection (CWE-78) Vector CVSS:3.0/AV:N/AC:L/PR:L/UI:N/S:U/C:H/I:H/A:H Affected versions SHIRASAGI v1.19.0 to v1.21.0 Fixed version SHIRASAGI v1.21.1

docs.title: Affected versions
docs.text: SHIRASAGI versions from v1.19.0 to v1.21.0. The same advisory also covers CVE-2026-117679 (cross-site scripting, v1.12.0–v1.21.0), fixed in the same release.

docs.title: Root cause
docs.text: An OS command injection flaw: a value the user controls is passed into a shell command without being sanitized. A shell command is just text, and the shell cannot tell where data ends and its instructions begin — so special characters in the value break out of the intended command and become a command of the attacker's choosing, executed with the server's privileges. The attacker only needs an ordinary logged-in account.

docs.title: Proof of concept
docs.text:
Educational only — this demonstrates the pattern, not a working exploit. Do not test against systems you do not own.

See poc.py: it shows, in a safe local simulation with no real shell execution and no network traffic, how a handler that glues user input into a command string lets a separator smuggle in a second command, and how a fixed handler that passes input as data only (never through a shell) blocks it.

Conceptual attack chain:

  1. The attacker logs in with an ordinary, low-privilege account.
  2. The attacker submits a value containing shell separators, like a semicolon followed by a command.
  3. The server builds its system command with that value inside.
  4. The shell runs the attacker's command as if the server itself had typed it.
  5. Result: arbitrary OS commands on the machine running the site — read configuration files, dump databases, plant backdoors, and pivot to other systems on the network.

docs.title: Mitigation
docs.text:
• Update SHIRASAGI to version v1.21.1, which fixes this flaw.
  • Review your server logs for unusual commands and unexpected logins.
  • Audit which accounts can reach the affected features, and restrict login access where possible.
  • As a standing rule, never build shell commands from user input: use fixed argument lists and pass input as data only.

docs.title: CVE-2026-118905 - nvm Version String Shell Command Injection
docs.text: Field Value Severity HIGH (7.0) Product Node Version Manager (nvm) Type OS Command Injection / Code Injection (CWE-78, CWE-94) Vector CVSS:3.1/AV:L/AC:H/PR:N/UI:R/S:U/C:H/I:H/A:H

docs.title: Affected versions
docs.text: Versions 0.31.2 through 0.40.5. Fixed in 0.40.6.

docs.title: Root cause
docs.text: nvm_ls built a sed program embedding the requested version pattern without escaping backslashes, so a version string containing a hash character closed the address early and the remainder was parsed as sed commands, including shell execution on GNU sed.

docs.title: Proof of concept
docs.text:
With an auto-switch hook (bash cdnvm or zsh load-nvmrc) installed, a user changing into a directory with a malicious .nvmrc runs the attacker's command. Scripts passing raw .nvmrc content to nvm use are affected the same way. A bare nvm use is not affected because nvm's own parser strips comments.

See poc.py for an educational illustration of the vulnerable pattern versus the fixed pattern. Educational only, for controlled environments.

docs.title: Mitigation
docs.text:
• Update nvm to 0.40.6 or later.
  • Avoid auto-switch hooks that pass raw .nvmrc content to nvm ls/version.
  • Treat .nvmrc files from untrusted repositories as untrusted input.

docs.title: References
docs.text:
• https://nvd.nist.gov/vuln/detail/CVE-2026-118905
  • https://github.com/nvm-sh/nvm/security/advisories/GHSA-vgqf-vc3m-4wv3

docs.title: CVE-2026-119145 — Frappe Path Traversal via File Upload Leads to RCE
docs.text: Field Value Severity CRITICAL 9.9 Product Frappe Framework (powers ERPNext) Type Path Traversal (CWE-22) Vector Network, low privileges, no user interaction, scope changed

docs.title: Affected versions
docs.text: Frappe before 15.121.0 and 16.x before 16.34.0. Patched in 15.121.0 and 16.34.0.

docs.title: Root cause
docs.text: Certain file-upload handling does not validate the destination path before writing to disk. An authenticated attacker can craft an upload whose path climbs out of the intended storage directory and lands inside application code, turning a file upload into remote code execution. Vendor advisory: GHSA-9pp9-wgp9-3p3j.

docs.title: Proof of concept
docs.text: Educational only: poc.py demonstrates the defensive pattern — canonicalizing an upload destination and rejecting anything that escapes the storage directory, plus a version check. It writes nothing outside a temporary directory.

docs.title: Mitigation
docs.text:
• Upgrade to Frappe 15.121.0 or 16.34.0 immediately. There is no workaround; upgrading is required.
  • Audit recent uploads for files written outside the storage directory.
  • Review server logs for traversal sequences in upload requests.

docs.title: CVE-2026-119167: TranslatePress Stored XSS via the Comment Parameter
docs.text: Field Value Severity HIGH (7.2) CVSS vector CVSS:3.1/AV:N/AC:L/PR:N/UI:N/S:C/C:L/I:L/A:N Product TranslatePress – Translate Multilingual sites with AI Translation for WordPress, up to and including 3.3.8 Vulnerability type Stored Cross-Site Scripting (CWE-79)

docs.title: Affected versions
docs.text: TranslatePress up to and including 3.3.8.

docs.title: Root cause
docs.text: Comment text flows through the translation rendering path without sufficient input sanitization and output escaping, so an unauthenticated attacker can inject arbitrary web scripts that execute whenever a user opens an injected page. Exploitation requires that at least one prior comment from the attacker's name and email pair has been approved under WordPress's default comment_previously_approved moderation setting, and that a secondary language is configured in TranslatePress.

docs.title: Proof of concept
docs.text:
The demo in poc.py models the safe pattern: comment text is escaped on output, so markup in a comment is displayed as plain text and never executes. It runs locally.

See poc.py in this folder. Educational only: the demo illustrates the vulnerable pattern's safe counterpart and performs no exploitation. Only test in controlled environments against systems you own or are authorized to test.

docs.title: Mitigation
docs.text:
• Update TranslatePress to version 3.3.9.
  • Review comments already stored on the site and remove injected payloads (updating does not delete stored payloads).
  • Tighten comment moderation and keep a second language only where it is needed.
  • Escape all user-supplied output.
