docs.title: CVE-2026-119168 — Nomad Allocation Migration Symlink Following
docs.text: Field Value Severity HIGH 8.8 Product HashiCorp Nomad and Nomad Enterprise Type Symlink Following (CWE-59) Vector CVSS:3.1/AV:L/AC:L/PR:L/UI:N/S:C/C:H/I:H/A:H Published 2026-10-29

docs.title: Affected versions
docs.text: Nomad before 2.1.0. Fixed in Nomad 2.1.0 and Nomad Enterprise 2.1.0, 1.11.12, and 1.10.18.

docs.title: Root cause
docs.text: During same-client allocation data migration, Nomad copies allocation data without verifying that a path inside the allocation directory is a symbolic link pointing outside it. A malicious workload can plant such a link, and the migration — running with host privileges — follows it, changing permissions and ownership of host directories. The trusted copy operation acts on workload-controlled paths.

docs.title: Proof of concept
docs.text:
Educational only. The demo below runs fully offline and shows the pattern — a migration copy that follows a symlink versus one that refuses to leave the allocation directory — using a local temp directory. It never touches a real Nomad cluster.

See poc.py. Run it with python3 poc.py. It demonstrates:

  1. How a planted symlink inside allocation data points outside the directory.
  2. How an unchecked copy follows the link onto the "host" path.
  3. How a scoped copy (refusing links that escape the directory) blocks it.

docs.title: Mitigation
docs.text:
• Upgrade to Nomad 2.1.0 (Enterprise: 1.11.12 or 1.10.18) immediately.
  • Audit recent allocation migrations for unexpected permission or ownership changes on host directories.
  • Restrict which workloads can run on shared clients.
  • Monitor host directories for permission changes outside maintenance windows.

docs.title: References
docs.text:
• NVD: https://nvd.nist.gov/vuln/detail/CVE-2026-119168
  • HashiCorp advisory (HCSEC-2026-53): https://discuss.hashicorp.com/t/hcsec-2026-53-nomad-allocation-data-migration-may-allow-host-directory-permission-modification-via-symlink-following/77931

docs.title: pyasn1 0.6.5 — Four Quadratic-Complexity Decoding Flaws
docs.text: Field Value Severity HIGH 7.5 (all four) Product pyasn1 before 0.6.5 Type Algorithmic complexity / denial of service (CWE-407) Vector CVSS:3.1/AV:N/AC:L/PR:N/UI:N/S:U/C:N/I:N/A:H Published 2026-10-29

docs.title: CVEs in this batch
docs.text:
CVE Flaw CVE-2026-119194 Schemaless container decoding grows a TagSet set with colliding hashes: quadratic CPU CVE-2026-119195 Constructed string / indefinite-length ANY decoding re-concatenates a growing bytes value CVE-2026-119196 Constructed BIT STRING decoding re-shifts and re-copies the accumulated bit value per fragment CVE-2026-119197 Binary REAL decoding rebuilds a large mantissa one octet at a time

All fixed in pyasn1 0.6.5. No confidentiality or integrity impact; the impact is availability — a small crafted input can pin a decoding worker.

docs.title: Affected versions
docs.text: pyasn1 from 0.3.3 (schemaless path) and earlier versions generally, before 0.6.5.

docs.title: Root cause
docs.text: Four decoders share the same anti-pattern: rebuilding a growing value from scratch on every step instead of appending efficiently. Work therefore grows with the square of the input size, and nothing capped total decode work. Attacker-controlled BER, CER, or DER input — many fragments, many distinct long tag IDs, or a large REAL mantissa — turns a small message into seconds of CPU per request.

docs.title: Proof of concept
docs.text:
Educational only. The demo below runs fully offline and shows the pattern — repeatedly concatenating a growing bytes value (quadratic) versus collecting fragments and joining once (linear) — with timing on synthetic data. It never decodes real ASN.1.

See poc.py. Run it with python3 poc.py. It demonstrates:

  1. Quadratic cost of re-concatenating a growing value per fragment.
  2. Linear cost of collecting fragments and joining once.
  3. How the gap explodes as fragment count grows.

docs.title: Mitigation
docs.text:
• Upgrade pyasn1 to 0.6.5 immediately.
  • Add input size limits and decode timeouts around any decoding of untrusted ASN.1.
  • Keep ASN.1 parsers off unauthenticated paths where possible.
  • Monitor decoder CPU; a single slow decode is a signal, not noise.

docs.title: References
docs.text:
• NVD: https://nvd.nist.gov/vuln/detail/CVE-2026-119194
  • pyasn1 0.6.5 release: https://github.com/pyasn1/pyasn1/releases/tag/v0.6.5
  • GHSA advisories: GHSA-fm9c-5rcf-2q5p, GHSA-9m75-vc3g-4x39, GHSA-2qm8-x737-gmw5, GHSA-mm57-4v3p-rchx

docs.title: CVE-2026-119283: joserfc Unbounded JWE Recipients CPU Exhaustion
docs.text: Field Detail Severity High — CVSS 7.5 Product joserfc — Python library for JSON Object Signing and Encryption (JOSE) Type Uncontrolled resource consumption (CWE-400) — unbounded recipient list in JWE decryption Vector Unauthenticated attacker submits a JWE with a huge recipients array to an endpoint using an RSA key-management algorithm → server performs one private-key decryption per recipient → CPU exhaustion

docs.title: Affected versions
docs.text: joserfc before 1.7.5. Fixed in 1.7.5.

docs.title: Root cause
docs.text:
The decrypt routine accepts a JWE General JSON Serialization recipients array with no count limit and calls the private-key decryption for every entry. The option that should stop early is only consulted after the loop has already processed every recipient, so it cannot reduce the work. Private-key operations are expensive, which turns the recipient count into an attacker-controlled CPU dial.

# Simplified vulnerable pattern
def decrypt_token(token):
    for recipient in token["recipients"]:  # BUG: no count limit
        decrypt_private_key(recipient)     # expensive, per entry

# Simplified fixed pattern
MAX_RECIPIENTS = 10
def decrypt_token_fixed(token):
    if len(token["recipients"]) > MAX_RECIPIENTS:
        raise ValueError("too many recipients")
    for recipient in token["recipients"]:
        decrypt_private_key(recipient)

docs.title: Proof of concept
docs.text:
1. Attacker builds a single JWE with thousands of recipients.
  2. Attacker submits it to an endpoint that decrypts tokens with an RSA key.
  3. The server runs one private-key decryption per recipient.
  4. Repeated submissions saturate service CPU; legitimate logins time out.

The educational demo in poc.py illustrates how an unbounded loop over an attacker-sized list turns one request into thousands of expensive operations.

Educational material only. Do not use against systems you do not own or have explicit permission to test.

docs.title: Mitigation
docs.text:
• Upgrade now: joserfc 1.7.5 or later.
  • Cap recipient counts and reject oversized tokens before decrypting.
  • Rate-limit token endpoints to bound repeated submission.

docs.text: Video walkthrough

docs.title: CVE-2026-119286: graphql-core Reused Validation Error Memory Exhaustion
docs.text: Field Detail Severity High — CVSS 7.5 Product graphql-core — Python port of the GraphQL.js reference implementation Type Uncontrolled resource consumption (CWE-400) / memory leak (CWE-401) — reused exception retains documents via growing tracebacks Vector Unauthenticated client repeatedly submits a small document with more than 100 validation errors → shared error object's traceback grows, retaining each document and context → worker memory exhaustion

docs.title: Affected versions
docs.text: graphql-core 3.3.0a3 through 3.3.0. Fixed in 3.3.1.

docs.title: Root cause
docs.text:
When a document exceeds the maximum error count, validation raises a module-level error object instead of a fresh one. Python appends a new traceback frame to that shared object on every raise, and each frame keeps its document, validation context, and error set alive for the lifetime of the process. Small invalid queries therefore leak memory on every request.

# Simplified vulnerable pattern
SHARED_ERROR = ValidationError("too many errors")  # module-level

def validate(doc):
    if error_count(doc) > MAX_ERRORS:
        raise SHARED_ERROR  # BUG: traceback grows, old docs retained

# Simplified fixed pattern
def validate_fixed(doc):
    if error_count(doc) > MAX_ERRORS:
        raise ValidationError("too many errors")  # fresh object, freed

docs.title: Proof of concept
docs.text:
1. Attacker sends a small GraphQL document with more than 100 validation errors.
  2. Validation raises the shared error object; its traceback grows.
  3. Each rejected document, context, and error set stays retained.
  4. Repeated requests grow worker memory until the worker is killed.

The educational demo in poc.py illustrates how reusing one exception object across requests turns tracebacks into an unbounded memory leak.

Educational material only. Do not use against systems you do not own or have explicit permission to test.

docs.title: Mitigation
docs.text:
• Upgrade now: graphql-core 3.3.1 or later.
  • Limit query size and depth at the gateway.
  • Alert on worker memory growth so a leak trips an alert before an outage.

docs.title: CVE-2026-119481 — Privilege Escalation in Crocoblock JetFormBuilder for WordPress
docs.text: Field Value Severity CRITICAL — CVSS 3.1: 9.8 Product Crocoblock JetFormBuilder (WordPress plugin) Type Incorrect Privilege Assignment / Privilege Escalation (CWE-266) Vector CVSS:3.1/AV:N/AC:L/PR:N/UI:N/S:U/C:H/I:H/A:H Affected versions JetFormBuilder from n/a through 3.6.7.1 Fixed version Update past 3.6.7.1

docs.title: Affected versions
docs.text: JetFormBuilder through version 3.6.7.1. Any WordPress site running the plugin with a form exposed to visitors is affected — no account is needed.

docs.title: Root cause
docs.text: A form submission could carry a user role, and the plugin trusted the role from the request without checking who was asking. Privileges must always be decided on the server, never taken from user input; here the form was allowed to assign roles, so any visitor could request the administrator role and the site created the account with full rights.

docs.title: Proof of concept
docs.text:
Educational only — this demonstrates the pattern, not a working exploit. Do not test against systems you do not own.

See poc.py: it shows, in a safe local simulation, how a form handler that copies the role from the request creates an administrator for any visitor, and how the fixed version (role decided server-side, never from the request) blocks it.

Conceptual attack chain:

  1. Attacker opens any form on the site — a contact form, a signup form.
  2. The submission carries a hidden role field set to administrator.
  3. The plugin creates the account with full administrator rights.
  4. The attacker logs in and owns the site: plugins, content, users.
  5. Result: full site takeover from a form anyone on the internet can fill in.

docs.title: Mitigation
docs.text:
• Update JetFormBuilder to a version past 3.6.7.1 immediately.
  • Open the WordPress user list and delete any administrator account you do not recognize.
  • Check for newly installed plugins, themes or content you did not add.
  • Review form plugins site-wide: no form submission should ever carry a role or capability.

docs.title: Video walkthrough
docs.text: Watch the explainer Short

docs.title: CVE-2026-119747 / CVE-2026-119749 — GetPaid for WordPress: Payment Bypass and Broken Authorization
docs.text: Field Value Severity HIGH — CVSS 4.0: 8.7 (CVE-2026-119749), 7.1 (CVE-2026-119747) Product GetPaid plugin for WordPress < 2.8.63 Type Improper Validation of Specified Quantity (CWE-1284) / Incorrect Authorization (CWE-863) Vector CVSS:4.0/AV:N/AC:L/AT:N/PR:N/UI:N/VC:N/VI:H/VA:N/SC:N/SI:N/SA:N (CVE-2026-119749) Affected versions All versions before 2.8.63 Fixed version 2.8.63

docs.title: Affected versions
docs.text: The GetPaid plugin for WordPress (invoicing, payment forms and Buy Now buttons), all versions before 2.8.63.

docs.title: Root cause
docs.text:
Two flaws in the same release, both fixed in 2.8.63:

  1. Negative quantity payment bypass (CVE-2026-119749). The process_item() routine never validates that an item quantity is positive. An unauthenticated attacker submits a negative quantity on a public payment form, producing a negative line subtotal that drags the invoice total to zero. A zero total routes the order through process_free_payment(), which marks the invoice as paid without any gateway charge.
  2. Incorrect authorization (CVE-2026-119747). The check_post_permissions() method in the plugin's REST posts controller maps REST operations to generic WordPress post capabilities instead of enforcing the plugin's manage_invoicing permission. Authenticated users with lower-privileged roles such as Editor or Author can list other users' invoices, mark pending invoices as paid without recording payment transactions, or create published items and new invoices through the REST API.

docs.title: Proof of concept
docs.text:
Educational only — this demonstrates the pattern, not a working exploit. Do not test against systems you do not own.

See poc.py: it shows, in a safe local simulation, how an unchecked negative quantity collapses an invoice total to zero and triggers the free-payment path, and how the fixed version (quantity must be a positive integer, free payments gated on a real zero-value product) breaks that chain.

Conceptual attack chain:

  1. Attacker opens a public GetPaid payment form (no login required).
  2. Attacker submits an item quantity of -1.
  3. The unchecked quantity produces a negative line subtotal.
  4. The invoice total drops to zero.
  5. The plugin treats the order as a free payment and marks the invoice as paid — no gateway charge ever happens.

docs.title: Mitigation
docs.text:
• Update GetPaid to version 2.8.63 immediately.
  • Audit recent invoices marked paid with no corresponding gateway transaction, especially zero-total orders.
  • Review Editor and Author accounts for invoice activity they should not have performed.
  • As a rule, validate quantities server-side (positive integers only) and enforce plugin-specific capabilities — never generic post capabilities — on invoicing endpoints.

docs.title: CVE-2026-119977 — WordPress Core upgrade-window staged-installer RCE
docs.text: Field Detail Severity HIGH 8.1 Product WordPress Core 4.7 through 7.1.3 Type CWE-367 (Time-of-check Time-of-use Race Condition) Vector Unauthenticated, network, during a core upgrade window

docs.title: Affected versions
docs.text:
• WordPress Core 4.7.0 through 7.1.3 (all branches in that range)
  • Fixed in 7.1.4 and the corresponding patched branch releases (e.g. 7.0.8, 6.9.11, 6.8.12, 4.7.39)

docs.title: Root cause
docs.text: During a full-package core upgrade, WordPress downloads and unpacks the new version into a staging folder whose name is predictable, and that folder is reachable from the web. The staged installer files therefore sit in a known, web-accessible location while the upgrade is still running. An unauthenticated attacker who requests the staged files inside that window can execute code on the server: a classic time-of-check time-of-use race between staging and installation.

docs.title: Proof of concept
docs.text:
Conceptually: an admin starts a core upgrade, the new package unpacks into a predictable staging path, and before the upgrade completes, an unauthenticated request to that path reaches the staged files and runs code with the web server's privileges.

See poc.py in this folder for a safe, educational demonstration. It does not exploit the vulnerability.

docs.title: Mitigation
docs.text:
• Update WordPress to 7.1.4 (or the patched release for your branch) immediately.
  • After updating, scan for unexpected files in wp-content and for admin accounts you did not create.
  • Keep automatic core updates enabled so future upgrade windows are patched.
  • Where possible, block direct web access to staging/upgrade directories at the server level.

docs.title: CVE-2026-119978 — Flowise sandbox escape via allowlisted modules
docs.text: Field Detail Severity HIGH 8.5 Product Flowise through 3.1.4 Type CWE-749 (Exposed Dangerous Method or Function) Vector Authenticated, network

docs.title: Affected versions
docs.text: • Flowise through 3.1.4 (when ALLOW_BUILTIN_DEP=true)

docs.title: Root cause
docs.text: Flowise executes user-supplied JavaScript in custom function nodes inside a vm2 sandbox. When builtin dependencies are allowed, allowlisted modules (langchain, mammoth) become a bridge out: submitted code can write a file into the mammoth package through its local file store and then require it, escaping the sandbox and executing OS commands as the Flowise process user.

docs.title: Proof of concept
docs.text:
Conceptually: code inside a sandbox should only touch virtual resources. Here, an allowlisted module gave the sandboxed code a handle to the real filesystem, so a write plus a require turned sandboxed code into host code.

See poc.py in this folder for a safe, educational demonstration. It does not exploit the vulnerability.

docs.title: Mitigation
docs.text:
• Upgrade past Flowise 3.1.4 when a fixed release is available.
  • Disable ALLOW_BUILTIN_DEP until then.
  • Audit custom function nodes and do not expose Flowise to untrusted users on a shared host.

docs.title: CVE-2026-119979 — LM Studio model downloader path traversal plants persistent plugins
docs.text: Field Detail Severity HIGH 8.8 Product LM Studio before 0.4.22+1 Type CWE-22 (Path Traversal) Vector User-assisted download

docs.title: Affected versions
docs.text: • LM Studio before 0.4.22+1

docs.title: Root cause
docs.text: The model downloader's download-request resolution did not neutralize backslash-separated traversal sequences in filenames. A crafted model repository could therefore write files outside the models directory, including a plugin manifest, install-state file and bridge config, so an attacker-supplied Python payload runs on every launch.

docs.title: Proof of concept
docs.text:
Conceptually: downloading a model writes files under the models folder. With traversal sequences in filenames, the same download writes files into the plugin directory instead, and the app loads them automatically at startup.

See poc.py in this folder for a safe, educational demonstration. It does not exploit the vulnerability.

docs.title: Mitigation
docs.text:
• Update LM Studio to 0.4.22 or later.
  • Inspect the plugin directory for entries you did not install and remove anything suspicious.
  • Only download models from sources you trust.

docs.title: CVE-2026-120043: SliceWP Affiliates SQL Injection via the Registration Email
docs.text: Field Value Severity HIGH (7.5) CVSS vector CVSS:3.1/AV:N/AC:L/PR:N/UI:N/S:U/C:H/I:N/A:N Product Affiliate Program Suite — SliceWP Affiliates for WordPress, up to and including 1.2.14 Vulnerability type SQL Injection (CWE-89)

docs.title: Affected versions
docs.text: SliceWP Affiliates up to and including 1.2.14.

docs.title: Root cause
docs.text: The plugin builds a customer lookup query by pasting the user-supplied email parameter into the SQL string without escaping it and without preparing the query. The injection is reachable without any account: the vulnerable code path runs on the user_register hook fired on every successful WooCommerce My Account registration, and the nonce it needs is obtainable by a guest. An unauthenticated attacker can append extra SQL to the existing query and extract sensitive information from the database.

docs.title: Proof of concept
docs.text:
The demo in poc.py models the safe pattern: the email is passed as a bound parameter to a prepared statement, so it can never rewrite the query. It runs locally.

See poc.py in this folder. Educational only: the demo illustrates the vulnerable pattern's safe counterpart and performs no exploitation. Only test in controlled environments against systems you own or are authorized to test.

docs.title: Mitigation
docs.text:
• Update SliceWP Affiliates to the latest release (fix in WordPress changeset 3786081).
  • Review database and registration logs for unusual signups.
  • Rotate any credentials or data that may have been exposed.
  • Use prepared statements with bound parameters for every database query.

docs.title: CVE-2026-120135: Apache Thrift Java Bindings Uncontrolled Recursion (Denial of Service)
docs.text: Field Detail Severity High — CVSS 8.2 (CVSS:4.0 AV:N/AC:L/AT:P/PR:N/UI:N/VC:N/VI:N/VA:H) Product Apache Thrift Java bindings Type Uncontrolled recursion (CWE-674) Vector Unauthenticated network attacker sends a deeply nested message to a Thrift Java service → the parser recurses once per nesting level with no depth limit → stack exhaustion → service crash (denial of service)

docs.title: Affected versions
docs.text: Apache Thrift before 0.24.0 (Java bindings). Fixed in 0.24.0. Users are recommended to upgrade to version 0.24.0.

docs.title: Root cause
docs.text:
The Thrift Java parser handles nested structures recursively: each nesting level triggers another parser call. No maximum depth is enforced, so the attacker — not the application — chooses how deep the recursion goes. Every program has a fixed stack, so once the attacker-supplied depth exceeds it, the process crashes. The message itself does not need to be large; depth, not size, is the weapon.

# Simplified vulnerable pattern
def parse(value, depth):
    if is_nested(value):
        return parse(value.inner, depth + 1)   # no limit: depth is attacker-chosen
    return value

# Simplified fixed pattern
MAX_DEPTH = 64
def parse(value, depth):
    if depth > MAX_DEPTH:
        raise ValueError("message nesting too deep")
    if is_nested(value):
        return parse(value.inner, depth + 1)
    return value

docs.title: Proof of concept
docs.text:
1. Attacker connects to a Thrift Java service (no authentication required).
  2. Attacker sends a single message nested thousands of levels deep.
  3. The parser recurses once per level until the stack is exhausted.
  4. The service process crashes; clients lose service until it restarts, and the trick can be repeated.

The educational demo in poc.py shows how an unbounded recursive parser falls over while a depth-limited one rejects the same input safely.

Educational material only. Do not use against systems you do not own or have explicit permission to test.

docs.title: Mitigation
docs.text:
• Upgrade now: Apache Thrift Java bindings to 0.24.0.
  • Enforce a maximum nesting depth in any parser you own, and reject messages that exceed it.
  • Reject overly nested messages at the edge (proxy/WAF rules on message structure) until patched.
  • Monitor for sudden service crashes that could signal recursion probing.

  • https://cwe.mitre.org/data/definitions/674.html

docs.title: CVE-2026-120201 — Jpom: Authentication Bypass to Super-Admin
docs.text: Field Value Severity Critical — CVSS 3.1 score 9.8 Product Jpom 2.10.0 through 2.11.12 Type Authentication bypass via query-condition injection (CWE-943) Vector Network, unauthenticated — a crafted JPOM-USER-TOKEN header value interpreted as a query condition

docs.title: Affected versions
docs.text:
• Jpom 2.10.0 through 2.11.12.
  • Fixed by upgrading past 2.11.12 to a vendor-fixed release (no specific fixed version is named in the NVD record — check the vendor's releases).

docs.title: Root cause
docs.text:
Jpom's login interceptor verifies the user session by building a database-style query out of the JPOM-USER-TOKEN header value, using Hutool's Condition parser. The parser treats parts of that value as query operators, not as data. An unauthenticated attacker can send a value such as is not null, which the parser reads as a condition instead of a token — so the lookup matches a super-administrator account without any password or valid session. Once signed in as super-admin, the attacker abuses Jpom's script features to execute commands on the servers Jpom manages.

# Simplified vulnerable pattern
user = find_user_by_token(header_token)  # header value spliced into the query
# header_token = "is not null" -> parsed as a CONDITION, not a value
# -> query matches a super-admin account, no password checked

# Simplified fixed pattern
user = find_user_by_token_parameterized(header_token)  # value bound, never parsed
if user is None or not verify_session(user, session):
    reject_request()  # identity must be proven, never inferred from a condition

docs.title: Proof of concept (conceptual)
docs.text:
1. The attacker sends a single unauthenticated request to the Jpom server with a crafted JPOM-USER-TOKEN header value.
  2. The Condition parser interprets the value as a query operator, and the login check matches a super-admin account.
  3. Signed in as super-admin, the attacker opens Jpom's script feature and runs commands on managed servers.

The accompanying poc.py demonstrates the pattern safely: a query builder that parses header input versus a parameterized lookup that treats input as data only. Fully offline, synthetic data — no exploit, no network, no system changes.

docs.title: Mitigation
docs.text:
• Upgrade past Jpom 2.11.12 now: move to a vendor-fixed release.
  • Keep Jpom off the public internet: restrict the server to trusted admin networks, behind VPN or a jump host.
  • Rotate administrator credentials: assume any exposed instance's admin sessions and stored credentials are compromised.
  • Audit script activity: review recent script runs and scheduled tasks for anything you did not authorize.
  • Hunt: look for requests carrying unusual JPOM-USER-TOKEN values (quotes, operators, is not null) in server logs.

docs.title: CVE-2026-120209 — AJ-Report: Hard-Coded JWT Secret to Remote Code Execution
docs.text: Field Value Severity Critical — CVSS 3.1 score 9.8 Product AJ-Report through 1.7.1 Type Use of hard-coded cryptographic key (CWE-321) leading to authentication bypass and remote code execution Vector Network, unauthenticated — a forged share token signed with the publicly known hard-coded secret

docs.title: Affected versions
docs.text:
• AJ-Report through 1.7.1.
  • No fixed release is named in the NVD record — treat every 1.7.1-and-earlier install as vulnerable until the vendor ships a fix.

docs.title: Root cause
docs.text:
AJ-Report signs its share tokens with a hard-coded JWT secret baked into the source code (JwtUtil), identical on every installation. Because the source is public, anyone can read the secret and sign arbitrary tokens offline — no account, no password, no interaction with the server needed. A forged token carrying a reportCode of dataSet reaches the testTransform endpoint, which passes attacker-supplied scripts to the Groovy class loader, giving unauthenticated remote code execution on the reporting server.

# Simplified vulnerable pattern
SECRET = "hard-coded-in-source"          # same on every install
token = sign({"reportCode": "dataSet"}, SECRET)   # anyone can mint this
verify(token, SECRET)                    # server trusts it -> endpoint reached

# Simplified fixed pattern
SECRET = load_from_secure_config()       # unique per deployment, never in code
token = sign({"reportCode": "dataSet"}, SECRET)
verify(token, SECRET)                    # a forged token fails: wrong secret

docs.title: Proof of concept (conceptual)
docs.text:
1. The attacker reads the hard-coded signing secret from AJ-Report's public source code.
  2. Offline, the attacker signs a share token with that secret, claiming report access.
  3. The server verifies the signature (it matches — the secret is the same) and the token opens the report test endpoint.
  4. The endpoint hands the attacker's script to the scripting engine, which runs it on the server.

The accompanying poc.py demonstrates the pattern safely: signing and verifying with a baked-in secret (forgeable by anyone) versus a per-deployment secret loaded from configuration (forgeries fail). Fully offline, synthetic data — no exploit, no network, no system changes.

docs.title: Mitigation
docs.text:
• Take AJ-Report off the public internet now: no fixed release is named yet, so exposure is the immediate risk. Restrict it to trusted networks behind VPN or a jump host.
  • Rotate the signing secret: replace the hard-coded value with a unique, randomly generated per-deployment secret stored outside the source code, and invalidate all previously issued tokens.
  • Upgrade the moment a vendor fix ships: watch the vendor's releases and apply the fixed version immediately.
  • Restrict the report test endpoint: it should never be reachable by unauthenticated users, even inside a trusted network.
  • Audit report activity: review recent share-token use and script executions for anything you did not authorize.

docs.title: CVE-2026-120213 — Path Restriction Bypass in @fastify/http-proxy
docs.text: Field Value Severity CRITICAL — CVSS 9.1 Product @fastify/http-proxy, versions 9.0.0 through 11.6.5 Type Path Traversal / Improper Encoding (CWE-22, CWE-436) Vector Network, low complexity, no privileges required, no user interaction

docs.title: Affected versions
docs.text:
• @fastify/http-proxy versions 9.0.0 through 11.6.5.
  • Fixed in 11.6.6 and later. There is no workaround other than upgrading.

docs.title: Root cause
docs.text: When an application uses parameterized prefix and rewritePrefix options to pin clients to a fixed upstream path, the plugin substitutes URL-decoded route parameters into rewritePrefix without re-encoding them. A parameter value encoding a path separator together with a fragment or query delimiter decodes into real separators and delimiters, injecting extra upstream path segments and stripping the mandatory suffix — without any dot-dot traversal. An unauthenticated remote attacker can reach upstream locations outside the intended prefix, enabling SSRF or authorization bypass in the proxied service.

docs.title: Proof of concept
docs.text: See poc.py: a local illustration of a decoded parameter reshaping a rewritten path, contrasted with a version that re-encodes values before substitution and validates the final path against the allowed prefix.

docs.title: Mitigation
docs.text:
• Update @fastify/http-proxy to 11.6.6 or later immediately (no workaround).
  • Review proxy logs for requests with encoded separators in parameters.
  • Re-check upstream authorization: do not rely on the proxy prefix alone.

docs.title: CVE-2026-120276: WAVLINK WN536AX6-A OS command injection (CWE-77)
docs.text: Field Detail Severity Critical — CVSS 10.0 Product WAVLINK WN536AX6-A (firmware V260507) Type OS command injection (CWE-77) Vector CVSS:3.1/AV:N/AC:L/PR:N/UI:N/S:C/C:H/I:H/A:H — a remote attacker with no privileges sends a web request to Web Management Interface (/bin/ioos) with a crafted group_name value; the router mishandles that value and the attacker gains control of the device

docs.title: Affected versions
docs.text: WAVLINK WN536AX6-A firmware V260507 (V260507_2.0.0 where noted). The vendor was contacted early about this disclosure; at the time of writing no fixed firmware version had been announced, so treat units on this firmware as affected and check WAVLINK for an update. This flaw is one of six critical flaws disclosed together in this router (CVE-2026-120276, CVE-2026-120277, CVE-2026-120279, CVE-2026-120280, CVE-2026-120281, CVE-2026-120282); all six are covered by the same walkthrough video.

docs.title: Root cause
docs.text: The router's web handler takes a user-supplied text field and uses it without proper validation. In the command-injection flaws, the value is interpolated into a shell command, so shell metacharacters in the field become code the router runs. In the buffer-overflow flaw, the value is copied into a fixed-size buffer with no length check, so an oversized value spills past the buffer and overwrites control data. Either way, untrusted text is never separated from the mechanism that acts on it.

docs.title: Proof of concept
docs.text:
1. Attacker reaches the router's web interface remotely.
  2. Attacker submits a request to Web Management Interface (/bin/ioos) with a crafted group_name value.
  3. The router mishandles the value: injected commands run, or the buffer overflows.
  4. Attacker commands run as the device, giving full control of the router.

The educational demo in poc.py shows the vulnerable pattern versus the fixed pattern. It runs no command on any real device.

Educational material only. Do not use against systems you do not own or have explicit permission to test.

docs.title: Mitigation
docs.text:
• Check WAVLINK for a firmware update for the WN536AX6-A and install it as soon as one is available.
  • Until a fix exists, disable remote administration from the internet and restrict the admin panel to the local network.
  • Isolate or replace the router if it cannot be updated and must stay exposed.
  • Validate every device setting against a strict allowlist and never build shell commands from user input; use argument arrays without a shell.

docs.title: CVE-2026-120279: WAVLINK WN536AX6-A OS command injection (CWE-77)
docs.text: Field Detail Severity Critical — CVSS 10.0 Product WAVLINK WN536AX6-A (firmware V260507) Type OS command injection (CWE-77) Vector CVSS:3.1/AV:N/AC:L/PR:N/UI:N/S:C/C:H/I:H/A:H — a remote attacker with no privileges sends a web request to openvpn_cli Handler (/protocol.csp) with a crafted file_id value; the router mishandles that value and the attacker gains control of the device

docs.title: Affected versions
docs.text: WAVLINK WN536AX6-A firmware V260507 (V260507_2.0.0 where noted). The vendor was contacted early about this disclosure; at the time of writing no fixed firmware version had been announced, so treat units on this firmware as affected and check WAVLINK for an update. This flaw is one of six critical flaws disclosed together in this router (CVE-2026-120276, CVE-2026-120277, CVE-2026-120279, CVE-2026-120280, CVE-2026-120281, CVE-2026-120282); all six are covered by the same walkthrough video.

docs.title: Root cause
docs.text: The router's web handler takes a user-supplied text field and uses it without proper validation. In the command-injection flaws, the value is interpolated into a shell command, so shell metacharacters in the field become code the router runs. In the buffer-overflow flaw, the value is copied into a fixed-size buffer with no length check, so an oversized value spills past the buffer and overwrites control data. Either way, untrusted text is never separated from the mechanism that acts on it.

docs.title: Proof of concept
docs.text:
1. Attacker reaches the router's web interface remotely.
  2. Attacker submits a request to openvpn_cli Handler (/protocol.csp) with a crafted file_id value.
  3. The router mishandles the value: injected commands run, or the buffer overflows.
  4. Attacker commands run as the device, giving full control of the router.

The educational demo in poc.py shows the vulnerable pattern versus the fixed pattern. It runs no command on any real device.

Educational material only. Do not use against systems you do not own or have explicit permission to test.

docs.title: CVE-2026-120283: Linksys E8450 Stack-based Buffer Overflow (CWE-119)
docs.text: Field Detail Severity Critical — CVSS 10.0 Product Linksys E8450 (firmware 1.2.00.360516) Type Stack-based buffer overflow (CWE-119) Vector CVSS:3.1/AV:N/AC:L/PR:N/UI:N/S:C/C:H/I:H/A:H — a remote attacker with no privileges sends a web request to the router portal with an oversized hidden timezone value; the value overflows a fixed stack buffer and hijacks control of the device

docs.title: Affected versions
docs.text: Linksys E8450 firmware 1.2.00.360516. The vendor was contacted early about this disclosure but did not respond, so at the time of writing no fixed firmware version had been announced. Treat units on this firmware as affected and check Linksys support for an update.

docs.title: Root cause
docs.text: The router portal copies a hidden timezone field into a fixed-size stack buffer with no length check. A value longer than the buffer spills past its end and overwrites the saved return address on the stack, so when the handler finishes it jumps to attacker-controlled data instead of back to normal router code. One missing length check turns an ordinary web field into control of the whole device.

docs.title: Proof of concept
docs.text:
1. Attacker reaches the router portal remotely, with no login.
  2. Attacker submits a request with a timezone value far longer than the buffer expects.
  3. The copy overflows the buffer and overwrites the return address.
  4. Attacker-controlled code runs on the router, giving full control of the device.

The educational demo in poc.py shows the vulnerable pattern (unchecked copy) versus the fixed pattern (bounded copy with rejection). It runs no code on any real device.

Educational material only. Do not use against systems you do not own or have explicit permission to test.

docs.title: Mitigation
docs.text:
• Check Linksys support for a firmware update for the E8450 and install it as soon as one is available.
  • Until a fix exists, disable remote administration from the internet and restrict the admin panel to the local network.
  • Replace the router if no patch arrives, since the vendor has not responded to the disclosure.

docs.title: CVE-2026-120311 — Network-AI Path Traversal via FileJobStore (plus related CVEs)
Overview
docs.text:
Field Value Severity HIGH — CVSS 8.8 Product Network-AI, versions 5.13.4 before 5.15.5 Type Path traversal (CWE-23) Vector CVSS:3.1/AV:N/AC:L/PR:L/UI:N/S:U/C:H/I:H/A:H

Network-AI before 5.15.5 contains a path traversal vulnerability in FileJobStore that allows attackers to read or delete arbitrary .json files by supplying traversal sequences in the job id. Attackers controlling the id passed to FileJobStore.get(), FileJobStore.delete(), or JobQueue.getJob() can disclose credentials and grant tokens or delete configuration files to weaken AuthGuardian authorization.

This video also covers three sibling flaws fixed in the same release: CVE-2026-120312 (path traversal in AgentVCR cassette names, 8.8), CVE-2026-120313 (path traversal in InputSanitizer.sanitizePath(), 7.5), and CVE-2026-120314 (missing authentication in the A2A server, 7.3).

docs.title: Affected versions
docs.text: • Network-AI from 5.13.4 before 5.15.5

docs.title: Root cause
docs.text: Job identifiers are stitched directly into filesystem paths without validating the resolved location. A job id containing folder-climbing sequences escapes the jobs directory, so the store reads or deletes files anywhere on disk. The same missing validation pattern appears in AgentVCR cassette handling, and a prefix check in the input sanitizer can be fooled by sibling directories sharing a name prefix.

docs.title: Proof of concept
docs.text: Educational only — see poc.py. It demonstrates the concept: a job id is resolved against the jobs directory, and a safe implementation rejects any resolved path that escapes the base directory. No real exploit is included.

docs.title: Mitigation
docs.text:
• Update Network-AI to 5.15.5 or later.
  • Configure a secret for the A2A server so task operations require authentication.
  • Rotate any credentials or grant tokens that may have been exposed.
  • Audit JSON configuration files for unexpected changes or deletions.

docs.text:
• https://github.com/Jovancoding/Network-AI/security/advisories/GHSA-v64j-mc7x-c7x7
  • https://www.vulncheck.com/advisories/network-ai-5.13.4-before-5.15.5-path-traversal-via-filejobstore-job-id
  • https://nvd.nist.gov/vuln/detail/CVE-2026-120311

docs.title: CVE-2026-120315 — LobeHub Chat Path Traversal via writeTempFile
Overview
docs.text:
Field Value Severity HIGH — CVSS 8.8 Product LobeHub Chat, versions 1.84.26 before 2.1.49 Type Path traversal (CWE-22) Vector CVSS:3.1/AV:N/AC:L/PR:L/UI:N/S:U/C:H/I:H/A:H

LobeHub Chat from 1.84.26 before 2.1.49 contains a path traversal vulnerability that allows authenticated users to write arbitrary files by supplying unsanitized file names to the temporary file writer. Attackers can create a file record via file creation with a traversal name, then trigger document parsing to overwrite application files like the server startup script, leading to code execution or denial of service.

docs.title: Affected versions
docs.text: • LobeHub Chat from 1.84.26 before 2.1.49

docs.title: Root cause
docs.text: User-supplied file names are never sanitized before being joined to the temporary directory path. Folder-climbing sequences survive to the filesystem, so the parser writes attacker content outside the temp folder and over application files.

docs.title: Proof of concept
docs.text: Educational only — see poc.py. It demonstrates the concept: a file name is resolved against the temp directory, and a safe implementation rejects any resolved path that escapes it. No real exploit is included.

docs.title: Mitigation
docs.text:
• Update LobeHub Chat to 2.1.49 or later.
  • Review recent uploads for suspicious file names.
  • Restrict file creation privileges if self-hosting.

docs.title: CVE-2026-120322 — Termix Path Traversal in File Manager Transfer
docs.text: Field Value Severity CRITICAL (CVSS 3.1: 9.9) Product Termix (Termix-SSH) web-based server management platform Type Path Traversal (CWE-22: Improper Limitation of a Pathname to a Restricted Directory) Vector CVSS:3.1/AV:N/AC:L/PR:L/UI:N/S:C/C:H/I:H/A:H Published 2026-11-02 Exploit Publicly disclosed; vendor did not respond

docs.title: Root cause
docs.text: The File Manager plugin's transferToHost endpoint (/plugin-api/file-manager/transferToHost) accepts a destPath argument and uses it to decide where an uploaded file lands on the host, without validating or sanitizing the path. A destPath containing ../ sequences is joined onto the upload directory as given, so the resolved path climbs out of the intended folder. The attack is remote, requires only a low-privilege authenticated account, and needs no user interaction.

docs.title: Proof of concept
docs.text: poc.py in this folder is an educational simulation of the path-resolution logic: it shows a crafted destination escaping the upload folder when the path is trusted as given, and being rejected once the resolved path is confined to the folder. It does not target any real server and contains no working exploit.

docs.title: Mitigation
docs.text:
Fixed in Termix core v26.10.0 and in the standalone File Manager plugin v1.0.0 (the transfer engine now always writes over SFTP). Until you upgrade:

  • Upgrade Termix core to 26.10.0 or the File Manager plugin to 1.0.0.
  • Limit which accounts can log in to Termix and audit low-privilege accounts.
  • Never expose the Termix dashboard to the open internet; restrict it to a trusted network or VPN.
  • Audit the host for unexpected files outside upload directories, especially startup scripts and web directories.

docs.title: CVE-2026-120338 — Prefab UI Generative UI Sandbox Escape
docs.text: Field Value Severity CRITICAL (CVSS 3.1: 10.0) Product Prefab UI (prefab-ui) Generative UI sandbox Type Code Injection (CWE-94: Improper Control of Generation of Code) Vector CVSS:3.1/AV:N/AC:L/PR:N/UI:N/S:C/C:H/I:H/A:H Published 2026-11-01 Exploit Sandbox escape design flaw; fixed in 0.21.0

docs.title: Affected versions
docs.text: prefab-ui 0.14.0 through 0.20.2. Fixed in 0.21.0.

docs.title: Root cause
docs.text:
Prefab UI's Generative UI sandbox runs caller-supplied Python inside Pyodide (Python compiled to WebAssembly) in a Deno subprocess. The feature is documented as isolation for untrusted code, including LLM-written UI — but the launcher started Deno with unrestricted --allow-read, --allow-write, and --allow-net, and the runner left the Deno API on the JavaScript global object. Pyodide's js module proxies that global, so the Python code could call Deno.readTextFileSync and Deno.writeTextFileSync. A caller who can supply code can read and write files as the server OS user, and can persist code execution by writing a .pth file into the server virtualenv's site-packages.

The usual remote path is FastMCP's GenerativeUI provider, which registers the MCP tool generate_prefab_ui and forwards that tool's code argument into the sandbox. On a FastMCP server with no authentication configured, any client who can reach the server can call the tool; with authentication, any client allowed to call tools can. Generative UI is opt-in, and the host must have Deno installed.

docs.title: Proof of concept
docs.text: poc.py in this folder is an educational simulation of the permission logic: it shows sandboxed code reaching the host runtime when permissions are left open, and being blocked once permissions are revoked before code runs. It does not target any real server and contains no working exploit.

docs.title: Mitigation
docs.text:
• Update to prefab-ui 0.21.0 or later. The fix revokes Deno read, write, and network permissions after the runtime and Prefab sources load and before accepting code, starts the process with --no-prompt so a permission request cannot re-grant them, and limits bootstrap network access to cdn.jsdelivr.net.
  • Do not expose FastMCP servers without authentication; require auth and restrict which clients may call tools.
  • Treat any "sandbox" for LLM-generated code as untrusted until its permission model is audited — an isolation claim is not isolation.
  • Audit servers that ran affected versions for unexpected .pth files in site-packages and unexpected file changes.

docs.title: References
docs.text:
• NVD: https://nvd.nist.gov/vuln/detail/CVE-2026-120338
  • Advisory: https://github.com/PrefectHQ/prefab/security/advisories/GHSA-595q-jv4r-q7j9
  • Fix: https://github.com/PrefectHQ/prefab/pull/538
  • Release: https://github.com/PrefectHQ/prefab/releases/tag/v0.21.0

docs.title: CVE-2026-120422 — Sogou Input Method Config Hijack Leads to Malware Delivery
docs.text: Field Value Severity HIGH — CVSS 4.0: 8.9 Product Sogou Input Method for Windows (SGTool.exe) Type Cleartext configuration retrieval / insecure channel Vector CVSS:4.0/AV:N/AC:L/AT:P/PR:N/UI:P/VC:H/VI:H/VA:N Affected versions Versions before 16.10 Fixed version 16.10 (released 2026-10-29, migrates affected requests to HTTPS)

docs.title: Affected versions
docs.text: Sogou Input Method for Windows, versions before 16.10.

docs.title: Root cause
docs.text:
The SGTool.exe component retrieves configuration data over unencrypted HTTP. An attacker capable of manipulating network traffic can replace legitimate server responses with malicious configurations. The fake configuration can instruct SGTool.exe to download attacker-controlled files to arbitrary locations, including paths used by legitimate application components, resulting in arbitrary code execution when the downloaded files are subsequently executed or loaded.

In the campaign documented by ESET, attackers tampered with DNS resolution for the configuration host so the app's request landed on a staging server, which served the malicious configuration through the app's brand-promotion mechanism.

docs.title: Proof of concept
docs.text:
Educational only — this demonstrates the pattern, not a working exploit. Do not test against systems you do not own.

See poc.py: it shows, in a safe local simulation, how a cleartext config response can be swapped for a malicious one, and how the fixed version (HTTPS with server verification) rejects the swap.

Conceptual attack chain (ESET "SlippyNunchucks" / DarkVigil campaign, observed from July 2026):

  1. Attacker hijacks DNS resolution for the configuration host.
  2. The app's HTTP config request lands on an attacker staging server.
  3. The staging server returns a malicious configuration.
  4. SGTool.exe downloads attacker files to sensitive locations.
  5. The downloaded files execute or load — the DarkVigil backdoor is installed, with no suspicious click by the user.

docs.title: Mitigation
docs.text:
• Update Sogou Input Method to version 16.10 or later, which migrates the affected HTTP requests to HTTPS, and verify the update actually installed.
  • Until patched, avoid untrusted networks for affected machines.
  • Check machines for unexpected downloads made by the helper tool.
  • Remove Sogou Input Method where it is not needed.

docs.title: CVE-2026-120442 — Authentication Bypass via Hardcoded JWT Key in ape-volo-admin
docs.text: Field Value Severity CRITICAL — CVSS 9.8 Product ape-volo-admin, all versions before 3.6.1 Type Authentication Bypass / Hardcoded Credentials (CWE-1394) Vector Network, low complexity, no privileges required, no user interaction

docs.title: Affected versions
docs.text:
• ape-volo-admin versions before 3.6.1.
  • Fixed in 3.6.1 and later.

docs.title: Root cause
docs.text: ape-volo-admin shipped a hardcoded JWT signing key inside appsettings.json, visible in the public source and identical across installations. Anyone can read the key and sign their own tokens offline; by setting the jti claim to the seeded administrator id, an unauthenticated attacker obtains a fully valid administrator token and full API control.

docs.title: Proof of concept
docs.text: See poc.py: a local demonstration of why a shared, public signing key cannot authenticate anyone — a token signed with a known key verifies successfully — contrasted with a fixed setup that loads a unique per-installation secret from the environment.

docs.title: Mitigation
docs.text:
• Update ape-volo-admin to 3.6.1 or later.
  • Rotate the JWT signing key to a fresh, unique secret stored outside source code.
  • Invalidate existing sessions and force all users to log in again.
  • Never commit secrets to source control; scan repositories for leaked keys.

docs.title: Video walkthrough
docs.text: Video walkthrough: Watch the explainer Short

docs.title: References
docs.text: • NVD: https://nvd.nist.gov/vuln/detail/CVE-2026-120442

docs.title: CVE-2026-120554 — WordPress Plugin Privilege Escalation
docs.text: Field Value Severity HIGH 8.8 Product Import and export users and customers (import-users-from-csv-with-meta) Type Incorrect Authorization (CWE-863) Vector Authenticated attacker with a delegated role that can create users but cannot promote users

docs.title: Affected versions
docs.text: Versions up to and including 2.5.11.

docs.title: Root cause
docs.text: The plugin's cron settings save handler writes the new options (cron activation flag, configured-by user, user id, and import file path) before the authorization gate runs. Because the write happens first, a user who should be blocked still gets their settings stored. A delegated role that can create users but cannot promote users can therefore repoint the scheduled import file at a file under attacker control.

docs.title: Proof of concept
docs.text:
Educational, conceptual demonstration only. This is not a working exploit.

# Conceptual flow (no real requests, no real site):
# 1. Attacker holds a delegated role: can create users, cannot promote users.
# 2. Attacker saves cron settings pointing the import file at their own file.
# 3. The plugin stores the settings BEFORE checking authorization.
# 4. On the next unattended cron tick (after a prior admin cron save),
#    the scheduled import runs and creates the attacker account as Administrator.

The key lesson: authorization must be checked before any state-changing write, not after it.

docs.title: Mitigation
docs.text:
• Update the plugin past version 2.5.11.
  • Disable or closely scrutinize any scheduled user imports.
  • Audit administrator accounts for accounts you did not create.
  • Never grant the create-users capability to roles you do not fully trust.

docs.title: Video walkthrough
docs.text: Short video explaining the vulnerability, the attack chain, and the fix. Watch the short walkthrough.

docs.title: CVE-2026-121606-group — Firmware Signature Verification Bypass in Qihoo 360 Routers
docs.text: Field Value Severity CRITICAL — CVSS 3.1: 10.0 (CVE-2026-121606, CVE-2026-121607, CVE-2026-121609) Product Qihoo 360 home routers (D621-2, D603-2, D600-2, D619, D606-6, D706, Whole Home Router M5) Type Improper Verification of Cryptographic Signature (CWE-345) Vector CVSS:3.1/AV:N/AC:L/PR:N/UI:N/S:C/C:H/I:H/A:H Affected versions Firmware up to 6.4.9 (D-series); Whole Home Router M5 4.0.17.1566 Fixed version None — vendor did not respond; replace the device

docs.title: The batch
docs.text:
Three 10.0 flaws in the same firmware family, all with public exploits:

  • CVE-2026-121606 (10.0) — The verify_sign function of fs2/bin/iscm (Firmware Signature Verification) fails to verify the signature argument properly. A crafted sign value passes as genuine. Affects D621-2, D603-2, D600-2, D619, D606-6 and D706 up to 6.4.9.
  • CVE-2026-121607 (10.0) — The testspeed_ function in the same firmware family is remotely exploitable with the same impact.
  • CVE-2026-121609 (10.0) — The Home function of the Whole Home Router M5 (4.0.17.1566) is remotely exploitable.
  • Related: CVE-2026-121608 (7.3) in the same D-series firmware.

The vendor was contacted early about the disclosure but did not respond in any way. There is no patch.

docs.title: Affected versions
docs.text: Qihoo 360 D621-2, D603-2, D600-2, D619, D606-6 and D706 up to firmware 6.4.9, and Whole Home Router M5 version 4.0.17.1566. These are consumer home routers, commonly exposed to the internet for remote management.

docs.title: Root cause
docs.text: Firmware updates are the one operation that must never trust the network: the router verifies a cryptographic signature before installing an image. In this firmware the verification function accepts a signature argument and does not verify it correctly, so a crafted value is accepted as genuine. The only guard between the internet and the device's firmware is a check that does not check — and once an attacker can install arbitrary firmware, they own the box permanently.

docs.title: Proof of concept
docs.text:
Educational only — this demonstrates the pattern, not a working exploit. Do not test against systems you do not own.

See poc.py: it shows, in a safe local simulation, how a signature check that never really compares the value lets forged firmware pass, and how a correct check (verify the signature against the vendor's public key before installing anything) rejects it.

Conceptual attack chain:

  1. Attacker crafts a malicious firmware image and a forged signature.
  2. The router's broken verification accepts both as genuine.
  3. The router installs the attacker's firmware.
  4. The attacker owns the router: traffic visible, devices redirected, persistence inside the box.
  5. Result: the whole home network is exposed through the device that was supposed to guard it.

docs.title: Mitigation
docs.text:
• Replace affected routers with a supported model — there is no patch and the vendor has not responded.
  • Until replaced, do not expose the router's management interface to the internet and never install firmware from unofficial sources.
  • Put smart-home and IoT devices on a separate network segment so a compromised router cannot reach them directly.
  • Watch for unknown admin logins and unexpected firmware version changes on the device.

docs.title: CVE-2026-121932 / CVE-2026-121933 — Linksys E5350 Setup Wizard Remote Takeover
docs.text: Field Value Severity CRITICAL — CVSS 3.1: 10.0 (both) Product Linksys E5350, firmware 1.0.00.037 Type OS command injection (CWE-78) / Missing authentication (CWE-287, CWE-306) Vector CVSS:3.1/AV:N/AC:L/PR:N/UI:N/S:C/C:H/I:H/A:H Affected versions 1.0.00.037 Fixed version None released (vendor did not respond)

docs.title: Affected versions
docs.text: Linksys E5350, firmware version 1.0.00.037, both flaws in the setup wizard endpoint (/wizard/apply.cgi).

docs.title: Root cause
docs.text:
Two flaws in the same wizard endpoint, both remotely reachable with no authentication:

  1. CVE-2026-121932 — OS command injection. The ping and traceroute diagnostic functions pass the caller-supplied address argument straight into a system command, so crafted input is executed by the router instead of being treated as data.
  2. CVE-2026-121933 — missing authentication. The setup wizard's save function lets a caller change the router password (including emptying the admin password) without any login check, handing over the admin account itself.

Exploits for both flaws are public. The vendor was contacted early about the disclosure and did not respond, so no patch has been released.

docs.title: Proof of concept
docs.text:
Educational only — this demonstrates the pattern, not a working exploit. Do not test against systems you do not own.

See poc.py: it shows, in a safe local simulation, how diagnostic input is concatenated into a command string in the vulnerable pattern versus validated against an allow-list in the fixed pattern, and how a password change with no session check succeeds in the vulnerable pattern versus being rejected in the fixed pattern. Nothing here executes attacker input.

Conceptual attack chain:

  1. An unauthenticated remote attacker reaches the setup wizard endpoint.
  2. Either they hide a command inside a diagnostic address field and the router runs it, or they call the setup save function and overwrite the admin password.
  3. Either path yields full control of the router and the home network behind it.

docs.title: Mitigation
docs.text:
There is no patch — treat the device as untrusted until the vendor ships one:

  • Block the setup wizard from the internet and disable remote management completely.
  • Administer the router only from your local network, and change the admin password from the local network only.
  • If you cannot lock the wizard down, replace the E5350: a router with public exploits and no fix should not guard a home network.

docs.title: CVE-2026-121952-group — Memory Corruption Batch in FreeRDP before 3.32.2
docs.text: Field Value Severity CRITICAL — CVSS 3.1: 9.8 (lead CVE-2026-121952; batch includes 9.8, 8.8, 8.1 and HIGH 7.5 flaws) Product FreeRDP Type Out-of-Bounds Write / Use-After-Free / Heap Buffer Overflow (CWE-787, CWE-416, CWE-122) Vector CVSS:3.1/AV:N/AC:L/PR:N/UI:N/S:U/C:H/I:H/A:H (lead CVE-2026-121952) Affected versions FreeRDP before 3.32.2 Fixed version FreeRDP 3.32.2

docs.title: The batch
docs.text:
One release, 3.32.2, closes a batch of memory-safety flaws on both sides of the connection. Headline members:

  • CVE-2026-121952 (9.8) — Out-of-bounds write in the proxy: the bitmap cache v2 parser rejects only counts above 5, but the cell array is later accessed at fixed indices 0 through 4. A client declaring fewer than five caches corrupts the heap, leaking data or crashing the proxy.
  • CVE-2026-121953 (9.8) — Use-after-free in the client's RDPGFX dynamic virtual channel: a duplicate-name channel frees memory that is still in use.
  • CVE-2026-121958 (8.8) — Heap out-of-bounds write in the RDPGFX client: the delete-surface callback truncates surface hash keys to 16 bits, so a malicious server can make the client write past its key array.
  • CVE-2026-121962 (8.1) — Heap buffer overflow in the transport reader when handling partial Early User Authorization PDUs.
  • Plus HIGH 7.5 flaws in the same release: server-side input parsing (121951), smartcard handling (121955), Kerberos ticket handling (121956), RDPGFX use-after-free (121957), shadow-server denial of service (121960) and RD Gateway RPC (121964).

docs.title: Affected versions
docs.text: FreeRDP before 3.32.2 — clients, servers and proxies. Any application embedding FreeRDP (for example xfreerdp, GNOME Remote Desktop, KDE krdp) is affected through its bundled copy.

docs.title: Root cause
docs.text: The flaws share one root cause: data supplied by the other side of the connection was trusted before it was validated. The proxy believed a client-declared cache count and then accessed fixed array positions without checking the count covered them. The client believed a server's surface identifiers and channel names without checking them against its own tables. Each unchecked value reached a memory operation that assumed it was safe, and the result was heap corruption on either side.

docs.title: Proof of concept
docs.text:
Educational only — this demonstrates the pattern, not a working exploit. Do not test against systems you do not own.

See poc.py: it shows, in a safe local simulation, how a cache count that is only checked on one side lets a client write past a fixed-size array, and how the fixed version (validate the full range before any access) blocks it.

Conceptual attack chain:

  1. A malicious client connects to the FreeRDP proxy and declares fewer than five bitmap caches in its Confirm Active.
  2. The proxy trusts the count and writes to fixed cache slots 0–4.
  3. The write lands past the allocated array and corrupts the heap.
  4. Heap data leaks back to the backend, or the proxy process crashes.
  5. Result: data exposure or denial of service on the proxy; the same release's client flaws let a rogue server attack the client instead.

docs.title: Mitigation
docs.text:
• Update FreeRDP to 3.32.2 on clients, servers and proxies alike.
  • Update distributions' FreeRDP packages (for example Debian's freerdp3 to 3.32.2+dfsg-1).
  • Treat unknown or untrusted RDP servers as hostile — the client-side flaws need only a connection to a malicious server.
  • Monitor proxy processes for crashes, which can be the first sign of exploitation attempts.

docs.title: CVE-2026-121966 — ForwardAuth Identity Leak in Traefik
docs.text: Field Value Severity HIGH — CVSS 3.1: 8.7 Product Traefik Type Exposure of Connection-Bound Authentication / Identity Leak (CWE-488) Vector CVSS:3.1/AV:N/AC:H/PR:N/UI:N/S:C/C:H/I:H/A:N Affected versions Traefik 2.x before 2.11.60 and 3.x before 3.7.16 Fixed version Traefik 2.11.60 / 3.7.16

docs.title: Affected versions
docs.text: Traefik 2.x before 2.11.60 and 3.x before 3.7.16, when ForwardAuth is used with an authentication server that relies on connection-bound authentication (NTLM or Negotiate). In 3.7, Ingress NGINX auth-url requests are affected the same way.

docs.title: Root cause
docs.text: Traefik sends ForwardAuth subrequests through an authentication-server connection pool shared by all clients. Some authentication methods — NTLM and Negotiate — bind the authenticated identity to the connection, not to the request. Sharing the connection therefore shares the login: an unauthenticated attacker can reuse another user's authenticated connection and receive that user's identity in the auth response headers, reaching backends as the victim.

docs.title: Proof of concept
docs.text:
Educational only — this demonstrates the pattern, not a working exploit. Do not test against systems you do not own.

See poc.py: it shows, in a safe local simulation, how a shared auth connection pool hands one user's identity to another user's request, and how the fixed version (one connection per client, never shared across users) blocks it.

Conceptual attack chain:

  1. A victim signs in through the proxy; the auth server verifies them.
  2. Their identity sticks to a connection in the shared pool.
  3. The attacker requests the same pooled connection — no login needed.
  4. The proxy returns the victim's identity in the auth response headers.
  5. Result: the attacker reaches backends as the victim, with their permissions and their data.

docs.title: Mitigation
docs.text:
• Update Traefik to 2.11.60 or 3.7.16 now.
  • Where possible, prefer header-based authentication methods over NTLM / Negotiate for ForwardAuth.
  • Review auth-server logs for connection reuse patterns that do not match normal user behavior.
  • Until patched, restrict who can reach the proxy and monitor for unexpected identities in backend access logs.

docs.title: CVE-2026-121971 — Symfony HttpClient Leaks Scoped Credentials to Foreign Origins
docs.text: Field Value Severity HIGH — CVSS 4.0: 8.2 Product Symfony HttpClient (ScopingHttpClient) Type Information Exposure / Credential Disclosure (CWE-200, CWE-522) Vector CVSS:4.0/AV:N/AC:L/AT:P/PR:N/UI:N/VC:H/VI:N/VA:N/SC:N/SI:N/SA:N Affected versions 5.x before 5.4.56, 6.x before 6.4.50, 7.x before 7.4.23, 8.x before 8.1.11 Fixed version 5.4.56 / 6.4.50 / 7.4.23 / 8.1.11

docs.title: Affected versions
docs.text: Symfony HttpClient, in versions 5.x prior to 5.4.56, 6.x prior to 6.4.50, 7.x prior to 7.4.23, and 8.x prior to 8.1.11.

docs.title: Root cause
docs.text:
ScopingHttpClient merges the options of its default scope (such as auth_bearer or auth_basic) into a request before resolving a relative URL against the base_uri. A network-path reference such as //evil.example/steal resolves to a different origin, but the request still carries the default scope's credentials — so the credentials are disclosed to an attacker-controlled server. The same happens with a different port or a user-info part on the same host.

This is reachable whenever an attacker controls the beginning of a URL passed to a client built with a base_uri and credentials, including clients created with HttpClient::createForBaseUri() or configured under framework.http_client.scoped_clients.

The fix: after resolving a relative URL against the base URI of the default scope, ScopingHttpClient now compares the scheme and authority of the result with those of the base URI, parsed the way the request is sent.

docs.title: Proof of concept
docs.text:
Educational only — this demonstrates the pattern, not a working exploit. Do not test against systems you do not own.

See poc.py: it shows, in a safe local simulation, how a network-path reference escapes the base origin while keeping the scoped credentials, and how the fixed version (compare scheme and authority after resolution, strip credentials on mismatch) breaks that chain.

Conceptual attack chain:

  1. Application builds a scoped client with a base URI and a secret token for its real API.
  2. Attacker controls the beginning of a URL the application requests (for example through a webhook target, redirect target or user-supplied path).
  3. The attacker supplies a network-path reference pointing at their own server.
  4. The client resolves it to the foreign origin but keeps the default scope's credentials attached.
  5. The attacker's server receives the request — and the token.

docs.title: Mitigation
docs.text:
• Update Symfony to 5.4.56, 6.4.50, 7.4.23 or 8.1.11 depending on your release line.
  • Rotate any bearer token or basic-auth credential that may have been sent to an untrusted origin.
  • Never build request URLs from untrusted input; validate and allow-list URL prefixes before handing them to a scoped client.
  • Audit logs for requests whose resolved host differs from the configured base URI.

docs.title: CVE-2026-122006 — Arbitrary File Write and Read in Ruby on Rails Active Storage
docs.text: Field Value Severity CRITICAL — CVSS 3.1: 9.8 Product Ruby on Rails Active Storage (activestorage gem) Type Insecure ImageMagick Policy / Arbitrary File Write and Read (CWE-1188) Vector CVSS:3.1/AV:N/AC:L/PR:N/UI:N/S:U/C:H/I:H/A:H Affected versions activestorage before 8.0.5.2 and 8.1 before 8.1.4.1 Fixed version Rails 8.1.4.1 / 8.0.5.2 (with mini_magick 5.1 or newer)

docs.title: Affected versions
docs.text: The activestorage gem before 8.1.4.1 for Ruby on Rails, when ImageMagick attachment processing occurs. Apps are exposed when the :mini_magick variant processor is used (the default for apps created with load_defaults 6.1 or earlier) and ImageMagick runs without a strict security policy — the policies shipped by Debian and Ubuntu do not block the dangerous coders. Apps using libvips instead of ImageMagick are not affected by this specific flaw.

docs.title: Root cause
docs.text: When a file is attached, Active Storage runs an ImageMagick analyzer on it immediately — before any preview or variant is requested. ImageMagick chooses how to read a file from its contents, not its name, and some of its handlers ("coders") act on files named inside the image: the MSL (Magick Scripting Language) coder, for example, can read and write files on the server. Active Storage constrained none of them, so a crafted upload could reach any coder the host policy allowed. With the Disk service, the same path can also read files the application process can read — including secret_key_base, the key that signs and encrypts Rails cookies. The fix ships a strict ImageMagick security policy with Active Storage and applies it through mini_magick.

docs.title: Proof of concept
docs.text:
Educational only — this demonstrates the pattern, not a working exploit. Do not test against systems you do not own.

See poc.py: it shows, in a safe local simulation, how an analyzer with no policy dispatches a crafted upload to a dangerous file handler, and how the fixed version (an allowlist policy that only permits safe image coders) blocks it.

Conceptual attack chain:

  1. Attacker uploads a file disguised as an image — no account needed.
  2. Active Storage attaches it and the ImageMagick analyzer runs at once.
  3. The crafted content reaches a dangerous coder, which writes files anywhere on the server.
  4. On Disk service deployments, the attacker also reads files the app can read, including secret_key_base.
  5. Result: arbitrary file write, stolen secrets, forged sessions, full server takeover.

docs.title: Mitigation
docs.text:
• Update Rails to 8.1.4.1 or 8.0.5.2 immediately.
  • If you use :mini_magick, upgrade mini_magick to 5.1 or newer — older versions cannot apply the new policy and the app fails at boot.
  • Rotate secret_key_base and every other secret the application process could read, especially on Disk service deployments.
  • Consider switching the variant processor to libvips, which is not affected by this flaw.
  • Review upload handling: never let attachment processing reach dangerous file handlers.

docs.title: CVE-2026-122051 — Edimax BR-6208AC Unauthenticated Remote Command Injection
docs.text: Field Value Severity CRITICAL — CVSS 3.1: 10.0 Product Edimax BR-6208AC router, firmware 1.32 Type Command injection (CWE-74) Vector CVSS:3.1/AV:N/AC:L/PR:N/UI:N/S:C/C:H/I:H/A:H Affected versions Firmware 1.32 Fixed version None released at disclosure — vendor did not respond

docs.title: Affected versions
docs.text: Edimax BR-6208AC running firmware 1.32. The vulnerable functionality is the /goform/mp endpoint.

docs.title: Root cause
docs.text: The /goform/mp endpoint takes attacker-controlled input from a web request and passes it to the system shell without validation or authentication. Because the request needs no login, anyone who can reach the router's web interface can get a command executed with the router's own privileges. A public exploit has been published for this flaw, and the vendor was contacted early about the disclosure but did not respond.

docs.title: Proof of concept
docs.text:
Educational only — this demonstrates the pattern, not a working exploit. Do not test against systems you do not own.

See poc.py: it shows, in a safe local simulation with no real shell execution and no network traffic, how an unfiltered endpoint handler passes raw input straight through, and how a fixed handler that rejects anything outside a strict allowlist breaks the chain.

Conceptual attack chain:

  1. The attacker sends a single crafted web request to /goform/mp on an internet-reachable router — no account needed.
  2. The endpoint passes the hidden input to the system shell.
  3. The shell runs the command with the router's privileges.
  4. The attacker gains remote control of the router and can change settings, observe traffic, or use it as a launchpad.

docs.title: Mitigation
docs.text:
• Block internet access to the router's admin pages immediately, and turn off remote management.
  • If the router cannot be isolated from the internet, replace it: no patch was available at disclosure.
  • Check the router's settings for changes you did not make, and review connected devices and DNS settings for tampering.
  • Segment the router from sensitive devices on your network until it is replaced or patched.

docs.title: Mistral Vibe Repository-Triggered Code Execution Group (CVE-2026-122133, CVE-2026-122134, CVE-2026-122135)
docs.text: Field Value Severity HIGH 8.8 (all three) Product Mistral Vibe (AI coding agent) Type Untrusted search path / inclusion of functionality from untrusted control sphere (remote code execution) Vector CVSS:3.1/AV:N/AC:L/PR:N/UI:R/S:U/C:H/I:H/A:H

docs.title: Affected versions
docs.text:
• CVE-2026-122133: Mistral Vibe before 2.25.5 on Windows (untrusted search path: a git.exe placed in the repository root runs at session start).
  • CVE-2026-122134: Mistral Vibe before 2.25.7 (malicious Git clean / process filter drivers configured in a repository run during startup status collection).
  • CVE-2026-122135: Mistral Vibe before 3.0.3 (repository-configured signing program abused during project context collection with a signed commit).
  • Fixed in: 2.25.5, 2.25.7, and 3.0.3 respectively.

docs.title: Root cause
docs.text: Startup order. When Vibe opens a project, it runs version-control commands at session start to build project context, before any trust prompt is shown. Those commands obey settings stored inside the repository itself: which helper binary to run, which filter drivers to invoke, and which signing program to execute. A crafted repository therefore controls code that runs with the developer's privileges, and the trust prompt arrives too late to matter.

docs.title: Proof of concept
docs.text: Educational only. The included poc.py models the concept with local strings: a repository configuration naming an untrusted helper program, and the vulnerable startup path that would execute it versus the fixed path that prompts for trust first and allow-lists helpers. It executes no repository commands and opens no real project. See poc.py and the video walkthrough for the conceptual chain: crafted repository -> victim opens project -> startup commands run -> repository setting selects attacker program -> code execution as the developer.

docs.title: Mitigation
docs.text:
• Update Mistral Vibe to 2.25.7 (or 3.0.3 on the 3.x line) immediately.
  • Do not open repositories from strangers or untrusted sources.
  • Inspect repository configuration (helpers, filters, signing settings) before opening unfamiliar projects.
  • Treat every cloned project as untrusted until proven otherwise, and prefer opening unknown code in an isolated sandbox or container.
  • After updating, review recently opened projects for suspicious helper or filter settings.

docs.title: CVE-2026-122192 — Guest-to-Host Memory Access in Firecracker
docs.text: Field Value Severity HIGH — CVSS 3.1: 7.5 Product Firecracker microVMs Type Improper Handling of a Failed Memory Remap (CWE-390) Vector CVSS:3.1/AV:L/AC:H/PR:H/UI:N/S:C/C:H/I:H/A:H Affected versions Firecracker 0.23.0 through 1.16.1 Fixed version Firecracker 1.16.2 / 1.17.0

docs.title: Affected versions
docs.text: Firecracker versions 0.23.0 through 1.16.1, for microVMs restored from a snapshot with the File memory backend, when the host fails to create the replacement mapping. The attacker needs root privileges inside the guest.

docs.title: Root cause
docs.text: When a guest asks to discard memory through balloon or virtio-mem devices, Firecracker must replace the mapping — and if that replacement fails, the failure must stop the operation. In the affected versions a failed remap went unhandled: the old mapping stayed in place and the guest could use it to read or modify memory belonging to the Firecracker VMM process itself. A silent failure in the one place that enforces isolation breaks isolation.

docs.title: Proof of concept
docs.text:
Educational only — this demonstrates the pattern, not a working exploit. Do not test against systems you do not own.

See poc.py: it shows, in a safe local simulation, how a discard request whose remap fails but is ignored leaves host memory reachable from the guest, and how the fixed version (verify every remap, abort when one fails) blocks it.

Conceptual attack chain:

  1. Attacker holds root inside a guest microVM restored from a snapshot with the File memory backend.
  2. The guest sends a balloon or virtio-mem discard request.
  3. The host fails to create the replacement mapping and does not notice.
  4. The guest reads or modifies Firecracker VMM process memory through the stale mapping.
  5. Result: guest-to-host escape — the isolation a VM promises is broken.

docs.title: Mitigation
docs.text:
• Upgrade Firecracker to 1.16.2 or 1.17.0.
  • Until upgraded, avoid restoring snapshots with the File memory backend.
  • Limit root access inside guests where possible.
  • Audit snapshot restores and monitor for unusual guest memory activity.

docs.title: CVE-2026-122220 — WPO365 LOGIN SAML Replay Authentication Bypass
docs.text: Field Value Severity CRITICAL — CVSS 4.0: 9.1 Product WPO365 | LOGIN plugin for WordPress (wpo365-login) Type Authentication bypass by capture-replay (CWE-294) Vector CVSS:4.0/AV:N/AC:L/AT:P/PR:N/UI:N/VC:H/VI:H/VA:N/SC:N/SI:N/SA:N Affected versions Before 45.2 Fixed version 45.2

docs.title: Affected versions
docs.text: WPO365 | LOGIN (wpo365-login) plugin for WordPress, all versions before 45.2.

docs.title: Root cause
docs.text: SAML single sign-on logins carry a unique message ID, and the plugin's anti-replay check is supposed to record every ID it has already processed, so a captured login message can only be used once. A logic error in the check makes it return before it ever saves the processed ID to the plugin's transient store. The list of seen message IDs therefore stays empty forever, and the duplicate check never triggers — a validly signed SAMLResponse captured once can be replayed to the assertion consumer endpoint again and again within the assertion's validity window, logging the attacker in as the victim, including administrators, with no detection.

docs.title: Proof of concept
docs.text:
Educational only — this demonstrates the pattern, not a working exploit. Do not test against systems you do not own.

See poc.py: it shows, in a safe local simulation, how a replay check that returns before recording a message ID accepts the same login message twice, and how the fixed version (record the ID on first use, reject any repeat) breaks the chain.

Conceptual attack chain:

  1. A legitimate user signs in through SAML; the signed login message crosses the network.
  2. An attacker captures that one valid, signed message.
  3. The attacker replays the exact message to the login endpoint.
  4. The replay check consults its never-written list, finds no duplicate, and grants a session as the victim.
  5. Within the assertion validity window the replay can be repeated, including against administrator accounts.

docs.title: Mitigation
docs.text:
• Update the WPO365 LOGIN plugin to 45.2 or later now.
  • Review administrator login history for repeated logins from the same message, and force administrators to sign in fresh.
  • Rotate any administrator credentials that could have been replayed, and treat unexplained repeat logins as compromise until ruled out.
